Hilbert functions of filtered graphical zonotopal algebras

Boris Shapiro ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, Stockholm University, SE-106 91 Stockholm, Sweden and Department of MCS, Guangdong Technion Israel Institute of Technology, 241 Daxue Road, Jinping District, 515063, Shantou, Guangdong province, China, shapiro@math.su.se    Ilya Smirnov ††thanks: BCAM – Basque Center for Applied Mathematics, Mazarredo 14, 48009 Bilbao, Spain  and  IKERBASQUE, Basque Foundation for Science, Plaza Euskadi 5, 48009 Bilbao, Spain, ismirnov@bcamath.org    Arkady Vaintrob ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, University of Oregon, Eugene, OR 97403, USA, vaintrob@uoregon.edu
Abstract

The external zonotopal algebra of a graph is generated by nilpotent vertex elements XvX_{v} and determines the graphical matroid after deleting loops. Replacing these generators by f⁡(Xv)f(X_{v}), for a power series f⁡(u)f(u), and filtering by word length gives a family of filtered algebras. We extend filtered graph reconstruction from simple graphs to loopless multigraphs without isolated vertices when the linear and quadratic coefficients of ff are nonzero. Nevertheless, even the family of Hilbert functions indexed by all polynomials does not determine the graph: two nonisomorphic ten-vertex trees have the same Hilbert function for every ff, answering a question of Nenashev and the first author. For forests and series whose first nonconstant term has degree k≥2k\geq 2, we give a monomial presentation indexed by partial score vectors whose entries are divisible by kk.

For normalized nondegenerate functions, a boundary-state calculus gives a common finite parameter partition for all trees of a fixed maximum degree. In maximum degrees three and four, exact symbolic calculations identify these partitions by the vanishing of specified coefficients of f−1f^{-1}. For functions with nonzero quadratic coefficient, the same calculus gives explicit recurrences for attached or connecting paths. Symmetry reductions, including commuting actions of 𝔰​𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_{2} and the symmetric group on the leaves of a star, determine the generic Hilbert series of stars and two-vertex multigraphs and also apply to parallel edges and leaves in larger graphs. For cycles, we determine the highest-degree term and the first three nonconstant coefficients in the stable range. A weighted independent-set formula describes the trace sequence in the remaining conjecture.

Keywords. Zonotopal algebras, filtered algebras, Hilbert functions, graph reconstruction, boundary states, Hilbert stratification.

1 Introduction

How much information about a graph can be recovered from an algebra associated with it, and how much remains after the algebra is replaced by its Hilbert function? The external zonotopal algebra 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} gives a particularly concrete setting for these questions. Its isomorphism type is equivalent to the graphical matroid of GG, after deleting loops [21, 11, 12]. Thus it recovers which sets of edges are forests, but not how all the edges meet at vertices. In particular, all trees with the same number of edges have isomorphic external zonotopal algebras.

Keeping the algebra and changing its filtration can recover the missing information. Nenashev and the first author [13] replaced the nilpotent vertex generators XvX_{v} by exp⁡(Xv)\exp(X_{v}) and filtered by the number of factors in products of these generators. The resulting filtered algebra determines a loopless multigraph without isolated vertices [13, Theorem 5]. For any fixed series with nonzero linear and quadratic coefficients, they proved the same statement for simple graphs without isolated vertices [13, Theorem 6]. Our Theorem 3.8 extends this to loopless multigraphs without isolated vertices. In all these cases the underlying algebra remains 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G}. Thus the additional information is in the filtration.

These results describe two extremes: the graded algebra retains only the graphical matroid, whereas an appropriate filtered algebra retains the whole graph. Direct comparison of filtered algebras, however, requires both multiplication and filtration data in a space whose dimension is the number of spanning forests—already 2N2^{N} for a tree with NN edges. We therefore study the more accessible Hilbert functions of these filtrations. They require ranks of spaces of products, rather than the construction or exclusion of algebra isomorphisms. Our main questions are which graphs they distinguish, how they depend on ff, and how they can be computed under graph attachment.

1.1 Definitions and notation for the results

Throughout, 𝐤\mathbf{k} is a field of characteristic zero. Graphs are finite undirected multigraphs. Loops are allowed, but are excluded from the degree count and do not affect 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f}; they still index variables of the ambient edge algebra ΦG\Phi_{G}. Write Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G) for the maximum non-loop vertex degree. A leaf is a vertex of non-loop degree one; its incident non-loop edge is a leaf edge. We call vertices of non-loop degrees two and three bivalent and trivalent, respectively. A tree is connected, and a forest need not be. In the enumeration statements, a unicyclic graph is connected and has exactly one cycle. A subcubic graph has maximum degree at most three.

Choose an orientation of the non-loop edges and put

ΦG=𝐤[φe:e∈E(G)]/(φe2),Xv=∑e​ leaving ​vφe−∑e​ entering ​vφe,𝒞G=𝐤[Xv:v∈V(G)]⊆ΦG.\Phi_{G}=\mathbf{k}[\varphi_{e}:e\in E(G)]/(\varphi_{e}^{2}),\qquad X_{v}=\sum_{e\text{ leaving }v}\varphi_{e}-\sum_{e\text{ entering }v}\varphi_{e},\qquad\mathscr{C}_{G}=\mathbf{k}[X_{v}:v\in V(G)]\subseteq\Phi_{G}.

Changing the orientation changes signs of edge variables and gives an isomorphic algebra. The standard grading assigns degree one to every φe\varphi_{e}. The dimension of 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} counts spanning forests, and its graded Hilbert series is a specialization of the Tutte polynomial [16, 15, 21].

For any polynomial or formal power series ff, put Yv=f⁡(Xv)Y_{v}=f(X_{v}) and let 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f} be the subalgebra generated by 11 and the YvY_{v}, with filtration

𝒞Gf,d=Span{Yv1⋯Yvj:0≤j≤d},𝒞Gf,−1=0.\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f,d}=\Span\{Y_{v_{1}}\cdots Y_{v_{j}}:0\leq j\leq d\},\qquad\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f,-1}=0.

The empty product is 11. Its Hilbert function is the sequence hd​(G,f)=dim(𝒞Gf,d/𝒞Gf,d−1)h_{d}(G,f)=\dim(\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f,d}/\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f,d-1}), and its Hilbert series is the polynomial

ℋGf​(t)=∑d≥0hd​(G,f)​td.\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f}(t)=\sum_{d\geq 0}h_{d}(G,f)t^{d}.

Thus dim𝒞Gf,d=∑j=0dhj​(G,f)\dim\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f,d}=\sum_{j=0}^{d}h_{j}(G,f). We use [td]​H[t^{d}]H for the coefficient of tdt^{d} in a series HH, and ltt⁡H\operatorname{lt}_{t}H for its highest-degree term.

Adding a constant to ff, or multiplying it by a nonzero scalar, does not change this filtration. A series is nondegenerate if f′​(0)≠0f^{\prime}(0)\neq 0; in that case we normalize

f⁡(u)=u+α​u2+β​u3+γ​u4+δ​u5+⋯,f(u)=u+\alpha u^{2}+\beta u^{3}+\gamma u^{4}+\delta u^{5}+\cdots,

and 𝒞Gf=𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f}=\mathscr{C}_{G} as unfiltered algebras. We write g=f−1g=f^{-1} for its compositional inverse. A nonconstant degenerate series, after subtracting its constant term, has the form c​uk+⋯cu^{k}+\cdots, where c≠0c\neq 0 and k≥2k\geq 2; its order is kk. If GG has a non-loop edge, such a series generates a proper subalgebra of 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G}. Constant functions give the algebra 𝐤\mathbf{k}.

Since Xvdeg⁡v+1=0X_{v}^{\deg v+1}=0, only coefficients through degree Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G) matter. For nondegenerate functions we therefore use the parameter space

𝒜D={u+a2​u2+⋯+aD​uD}≃𝔸𝐤D−1,D≥max⁡(1,Δ⁡(G)).{\mathscr{A}}_{D}=\{u+a_{2}u^{2}+\cdots+a_{D}u^{D}\}\simeq\mathbb{A}_{\mathbf{k}}^{D-1},\qquad D\geq\max(1,\Delta(G)).

For a fixed graph the Hilbert series is constant on a nonempty Zariski open subset of this space. This is the generic Hilbert series; its cumulative dimensions, not necessarily its individual coefficients, are maximal [13, Proposition 3]. A Hilbert stratum consists of the parameters giving a specified series. We call a nondegenerate parameter Hilbert-exceptional for GG if its series is not the generic one. This terminology makes no assertion about singularities of the stratum. Here a stratification means a finite partition into locally closed subsets; no smoothness or frontier condition is imposed on its parts.

We write CnC_{n} for the simple cycle on n≥3n\geq 3 vertices, SnS_{n} for the star K1,n−1K_{1,n-1}, and EmE_{m} for two vertices joined by mm parallel edges. The tree T⁡(a,b,c)T(a,b,c) has three paths of edge lengths a,b,ca,b,c attached at one common endpoint; in particular D6=T⁡(1,1,3)\mathrm{D}_{6}=T(1,1,3) and E6=T⁡(1,2,2)\mathrm{E}_{6}=T(1,2,2). A partial orientation orients a subset of the edges. Its score vector a=(av)a=(a_{v}) counts the selected edges directed away from each vertex. Let

sk​(G,t)=∑a​ a partial score vectork|av​for all ​vt|a|/k,|a|=∑vav,s_{k}(G;t)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a\text{ a partial score vector}\\ k\mid a_{v}\ \text{for all }v\end{subarray}}t^{|a|/k},\qquad|a|=\sum_{v}a_{v},

where each distinct score vector is counted once, irrespective of the number of partial orientations producing it. Finally, hmf​(t)h_{m}^{f}(t) denotes the Hilbert series of 𝐤⁡[x]/(xm+1)\mathbf{k}[x]/(x^{m+1}) filtered by products of xx and f⁡(x)f(x). These one-variable filtrations enter the star formula below.

For a graph GG with marked vertex vv, let GnG_{n} be obtained by attaching a path with nn edges at vv. For disjoint marked graphs (G′,v′)(G^{\prime},v^{\prime}) and (G′′,v′′)(G^{\prime\prime},v^{\prime\prime}), let G′∗nG′′G^{\prime}\ast_{n}G^{\prime\prime} join their marked vertices by such a path. For a sequence of polynomials put

L⁡(an)=an−an−1−3​t​an−2+2​t​an−3.L(a_{n})=a_{n}-a_{n-1}-3t\,a_{n-2}+2t\,a_{n-3}.

For a fixed graph, call the map f↦ℋGff\mapsto\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f} its all-polynomial Hilbert profile when ff ranges over 𝐤⁡[u]\mathbf{k}[u], and its nondegenerate Hilbert profile when f′​(0)≠0f^{\prime}(0)\neq 0. Equality of profiles always means pointwise equality at the same ff, not merely equality of the sets of possible series. Two graphs are universally Hilbert equivalent when their nondegenerate profiles agree (see Section 6.9).

Example 1.1 (The path with two edges).

For the path 1−2−31-2-3, write a=φ12a=\varphi_{12} and b=φ23b=\varphi_{23}, with both edges oriented in increasing vertex order. Then

X1=a,X2=b−a,X3=−b,Y1=a,Y2=b−a−2​α​a​b,Y3=−b.X_{1}=a,\quad X_{2}=b-a,\quad X_{3}=-b,\qquad Y_{1}=a,\quad Y_{2}=b-a-2\alpha ab,\quad Y_{3}=-b.

If α≠0\alpha\neq 0, the ordinary degree-two element a​bab already belongs to 𝒞Gf,1\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f,1}. Hence ℋGf=1+3​t\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f}=1+3t, whereas ℋGu=1+2​t+t2\mathscr{H}_{G}^{u}=1+2t+t^{2}. This change records when an element can be expressed in the new generators, not a change in the underlying algebra.

1.2 Main results

The limits of Hilbert functions.
Theorem A (Failure of all-polynomial reconstruction).
  1. (i)

    The two nonisomorphic ten-vertex trees denoted T​31,T​32T3_{1},T3_{2} in Figure 8 satisfy

    ℋT​31f​(t)=ℋT​32f​(t)for every ​f∈𝐤⁡[u].\mathscr{H}_{T3_{1}}^{f}(t)=\mathscr{H}_{T3_{2}}^{f}(t)\qquad\text{for every }f\in\mathbf{k}[u].
  2. (ii)

    Among trees with at most ten vertices, there are just three pairs of nonisomorphic universally Hilbert equivalent trees, all on ten vertices. Among connected unicyclic simple graphs with at most eight vertices, there is one such pair, on eight vertices. They are the four pairs in Figure 8. The polynomial u2u^{2} separates the two graphs in each pair other than T​3T3.

Part (i) answers [13, Problem 5] with its original quantifier over all polynomials: passing to Hilbert functions loses information that no choice of ff recovers. The proof combines the complete nondegenerate parameter tests with an algebraic result about degenerate functions; the remaining finite calculations are exact. The uniqueness assertions in part (ii) additionally use exhaustive enumeration (Propositions 6.15, 6.16 and 6.18).

For a forest and a function of order k≥2k\geq 2, the stronger structural statement is that 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f} has a monomial presentation with basis indexed by the partial score vectors all of whose entries are divisible by kk (Theorem 3.20). In particular, ℋGf=sk​(G,t)\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f}=s_{k}(G;t), and the filtered algebra, not just its Hilbert function, depends only on GG and kk. This answers [13, Problem 4] for forests and makes the degenerate part of the T​3T3 comparison finite. For cycles there is a closely related formula, with a one-dimensional correction for even cycle length (Proposition 3.29).

Uniform control of the parameters.

Although different graphs need not be distinguished, the dependence on ff can be controlled simultaneously for an infinite class of graphs. The relevant inverse coefficients begin with

g⁡(u)=u−α​u2+(2​α2−β)​u3+(−5​α3+5​α​β−γ)​u4+⋯.g(u)=u-\alpha u^{2}+(2\alpha^{2}-\beta)u^{3}+(-5\alpha^{3}+5\alpha\beta-\gamma)u^{4}+\cdots. (1.1)
Theorem B (A uniform parameter partition for trees).
  1. (i)

    For every D≥1D\geq 1, there is a finite locally closed partition of 𝒜D{\mathscr{A}}_{D} on each part of which ℋTf\mathscr{H}_{T}^{f} is constant in ff simultaneously for every tree TT with Δ⁡(T)≤D\Delta(T)\leq D.

  2. (ii)

    For D=3D=3, the coarsest such partition is given by the four vanishing patterns of [u2]​g[u^{2}]g and [u3]​g[u^{3}]g. On α≠0\alpha\neq 0, a tree distinguishes β=2​α2\beta=2\alpha^{2} from the other parameters exactly when it has a trivalent vertex with at least two non-leaf neighbors. Its coefficient of t2t^{2} then drops by one on that locus.

  3. (iii)

    For D=4D=4, the coarsest common partition consists of the eight vanishing patterns of [u2]​g,[u3]​g,[u4]​g[u^{2}]g,[u^{3}]g,[u^{4}]g.

Part (i) has an algebraic proof, using finitely many local calculations independent of the size of the tree (Theorem 6.5). The explicit partitions in parts (ii) and (iii) use exact symbolic local rank calculations; the latter is stated as a computer-assisted theorem (Theorems 6.7 and 6.10). The graphical criterion in part (ii) has a proof from the local rules (Proposition 6.9). The pattern does not persist in degree five: already the star with five leaves detects a condition not given by the vanishing of an individual inverse coefficient (Remark 6.11).

Attaching paths.
Theorem C (Tails and necks).

Suppose f=u+α​u2+⋯f=u+\alpha u^{2}+\cdots with α≠0\alpha\neq 0.

  1. (i)

    For Hn=ℋGnfH_{n}=\mathscr{H}_{G_{n}}^{f}, one has L⁡(Hn)=0L(H_{n})=0 for n≥4n\geq 4.

  2. (ii)

    For Hn=ℋG′∗nG′′fH_{n}=\mathscr{H}_{G^{\prime}\ast_{n}G^{\prime\prime}}^{f}, the polynomial L⁡(Hn)L(H_{n}) is independent of nn for n≥5n\geq 5. It is determined explicitly by the two marked graphs, and vanishes under an explicit condition on either end. The end graphs are unrestricted. Theorems 4.9 and 4.16 give the formulas, including forked and doubled tail variants. The recurrence for paths was first found experimentally by Per Alexandersson. Its generating function is given in Corollary 4.14.

Symmetry and generic Hilbert functions.
Theorem D (Stars).

For normalized nondegenerate ff and N≥0N\geq 0,

ℋSN+1f​(t)=∑p=0⌊N/2⌋((Np)−(Np−1))​tp​hN−2​pf​(t),(N−1)=0.\mathscr{H}_{S_{N+1}}^{f}(t)=\sum_{p=0}^{\lfloor N/2\rfloor}\left(\binom{N}{p}-\binom{N}{p-1}\right)t^{p}h_{N-2p}^{f}(t),\qquad\binom{N}{-1}=0.

Moreover, ℋSnf=ℋSnf−1\mathscr{H}_{S_{n}}^{f}=\mathscr{H}_{S_{n}}^{f^{-1}}, and f=eu−1f=e^{u}-1 realizes the generic Hilbert series on every star.

Theorem 5.11, Corollary 5.18 and Proposition 5.17 prove these assertions. Explicit formulas for f=u+c​urf=u+cu^{r} follow from the same reduction. Parallel edges admit a complementary reduction, which determines the generic series of every EmE_{m} (Theorem 5.4). Both reductions extend to suitable groups of edges in an arbitrary larger graph.

The exponential is not generic on every graph, as Nenashev and the first author already showed [13, Example 2]. It is generic on all trees with Δ≤4\Delta\leq 4 by Theorem B, whereas small graphs with cycles can detect its special coefficient identities. Section 6.10 compares exact examples, symbolic parameter classifications and finite-field scans, and states the status of each.

Cycles.
Theorem E (The first coefficients and the top term for cycles).

Let Hn=ℋCnfH_{n}=\mathscr{H}_{C_{n}}^{f} with f=u+α​u2+⋯f=u+\alpha u^{2}+\cdots and α≠0\alpha\neq 0. For n≥7n\geq 7,

Hn=1+n​t+((n+12)−1)​t2+((n+23)−3​n)​t3+O⁡(t4).H_{n}=1+nt+\left(\binom{n+1}{2}-1\right)t^{2}+\left(\binom{n+2}{3}-3n\right)t^{3}+O(t^{4}).

For every n≥3n\geq 3, its degree is ⌈n/2⌉+1\lceil n/2\rceil+1, and

ltt⁡H2​m+1=tm+2​(m≥1),ltt⁡H2​m=(2m−1+1)​tm+1​(m≥2).\operatorname{lt}_{t}H_{2m+1}=t^{m+2}\ (m\geq 1),\qquad\operatorname{lt}_{t}H_{2m}=(2^{m-1}+1)t^{m+1}\ (m\geq 2).

The low-degree formula follows from a complete description of the cubic relations (Theorem 7.1); the top term uses dual path calculations (Theorem 7.3). A conjecture for the remaining coefficients is stated separately in Section 7.6. Neither these partial formulas nor the path recurrence proves it.

1.3 Why boundary data are needed

The Hilbert series of two pieces do not by themselves determine the series after attachment. The graded deletion–contraction sequence need not remain exact at each level of the new filtration. We give sufficient conditions for filtered exactness and examples with arbitrarily large discrepancies even when both endpoints of the chosen edge have degree three. Also, attaching a leaf at specified vertices distinguishes a pair whose nondegenerate profiles agree. We therefore retain information about how elements use the attaching edge.

For normalized nondegenerate ff, take a graph with a marked leaf edge, with variable rr and r2=0r^{2}=0. Its algebra is U⊕r​UU\oplus rU, where UU is the algebra of the contracted graph. Omit the generator at the leaf vertex and let PdP_{d} be the span of products of the remaining generators of length at most dd. For u∈Uu\in U, ask when some lift congruent to uu modulo rr belongs to PdP_{d}, and when r​uru itself belongs to PdP_{d}. These questions define two filtrations on UU. A basis adapted to both records a pair of levels [p,q][p,q] for each basis vector. These are the boundary states; their multiplicities are independent of the adapted basis. The first level concerns a lift modulo rr, not necessarily the rr-free representative uu.

We give rules for joining two independent pieces along an edge, for meeting branches at a vertex, and for extending a path by one edge. Only the variables at the new vertex enter each local calculation. Moreover, the difference q−pq-p is bounded by the maximum degree. Up to a common shift of p,qp,q, there are therefore finitely many local types for bounded-degree trees. This explains the uniformity in Theorem B. Along a path, a three-by-three transfer matrix and a stationary part of the boundary data give Theorem C. The symmetry reduction for attached leaves respects these same boundary data, so it can be used before further attachments.

The stationary boundary quotients also suggest an interpretation in terms of Rees modules and filtered comparison complexes. We leave this interpretation, and the additional compatibility required for cyclic gluing, to subsequent work.

1.4 Related constructions and organization

Zonotopal algebras connect graphical power ideals, box splines and lattice-point enumeration [5, 1, 10]. Other deformations change the algebra rather than its generators. Kirillov and Nenashev replace φe2=0\varphi_{e}^{2}=0 by φe2=qe​φe\varphi_{e}^{2}=q_{e}\varphi_{e} [7, 8]. The external bizonotopal algebra uses two opposite arrows per edge with an additional zero-product relation; its Hilbert series counts partial score vectors [9]. This is not ordinary parallel-edge doubling. Grinberg, Kirillov and Shapiro study the matching algebra, in which products of incident edges vanish, and the subalgebra generated by the signed incidence sums [4]. For a cycle their unicyclic formula computes the Hilbert series of a quotient of our filtered algebra. It explains the independent-set contribution but not the full cycle filtration (Remark 7.10).

Sections 2 and 3 provide a proof-based foundation, including the external and central presentations, deletion–contraction, the forest and spanning-tree activity formulas, and reconstruction. Presentation and exactness are proved together by cut-power antiderivatives, without the dimension formulas. These classical results have an independent expository role here. The degenerate-forest presentation is then obtained by a leaf-induction argument.

The boundary calculus and path recurrences occupy Section 4. Section 5 gives the symmetry reductions, retaining the symmetric-group decomposition as a separate result. Section 6 treats parameter dependence and graph collisions, including the generic/exponential computations. Section 7 treats cycles, and Section 8 lists the remaining questions. Appendix A describes the computer calculations and the supplementary repository [18], which also contains tables of Hilbert functions of small graphs. Readers interested in the collisions need the filtration and degenerate-function results of Section 3, the local calculus of Section 4, and Section 6.

2 Graded graphical zonotopal algebras

This section collects the graded theory: the presentation of 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} by cut-power relations, the deletion–contraction sequence, the forest and spanning-tree formulas for the Hilbert series, and the reconstruction of the graphical matroid. These results are due to [16, 15, 21, 5, 11, 12]. We give complete proofs because the original arguments are spread over several sources and because the proofs below use the same constructions as the filtered theory. In particular, presentation and exactness are proved together, by cut-power antiderivatives, without using the dimension formulas (Theorem 2.7). A reader who knows these results can read the definitions in Section 2.2 and the statement of Theorem 2.7, and continue with Section 3.

2.1 Preliminaries on graphs

By a graph we understand a finite undirected multigraph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), possibly with loops, with vertex set VV and edge multiset EE. A leaf is a vertex of non-loop degree one, and its incident non-loop edge is a leaf edge.

Throughout, deg⁡v\deg v and Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G) count incident non-loop edges; loops are kept in EE but make no contribution to these degrees.

Graphs form a category 𝒢​r\mathscr{G}r with morphisms

f:G=(V,E)→G′=(V′,E′)f\colon G=(V,E)\to G^{\prime}=(V^{\prime},E^{\prime})

defined as maps of pairs

(γ,λ):(V,E)→(V′,E′),(\gamma,\lambda)\colon(V,E)\to(V^{\prime},E^{\prime}), (2.1)

injective on edges and preserving incidences between vertices and edges (that is, if e∈Ee\in E is an edge in GG connecting uu and vv, then λ⁡(e)\lambda(e) is an edge in G′G^{\prime} connecting γ⁡(u)\gamma(u) and γ⁡(v)\gamma(v)). Orientations used below are auxiliary choices, not part of a graph morphism; in particular, a morphism need not preserve them.

For an edge e∈Ee\in E we define two special graph morphisms, the deletion of ee:

je:G−e→Gj_{e}\colon G-e\to G

and the contraction of ee (assuming that ee is not a loop):

πe:G→Ge,\pi_{e}\colon G\to G_{e},

where G−eG-e is the subgraph of GG obtained by removing the edge ee from EE, and GeG_{e} is the graph obtained from GG by identifying the endpoints uu and vv of ee and replacing them with a new vertex ww and replacing each edge connecting uu and vv (including ee) by a loop at ww (Figure 1).

2.2 Graph algebras, orientations, and functoriality

By an algebra in this paper we understand a commutative unital algebra over a fixed field 𝐤\mathbf{k} of characteristic 00.

Definition 2.1.

Given a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), its edge algebra ΦG\Phi_{G} is the quotient of the polynomial algebra in edge variables φe,e∈E\varphi_{e},e\in E, by their squares,

ΦG:=𝐤[φe:e∈E]/(φe2).\Phi_{G}:=\mathbf{k}[\varphi_{e}:e\in E]/(\varphi_{e}^{2}). (2.2)

The edge algebra is a local algebra of dimension 2|E|2^{|E|} isomorphic to the tensor product of |E||E| copies of the algebra of dual numbers 𝐤⁡[ε]/(ε2)\mathbf{k}[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^{2}), namely

ΦG≃⨂e∈E(𝐤⁡[φe]/(φe2)).\Phi_{G}\simeq\bigotimes_{e\in E}\big(\mathbf{k}[\varphi_{e}]/(\varphi_{e}^{2})\big).

It inherits the standard grading from the polynomial algebra. A basis of the kkth graded component is given by square-free monomials of length kk in the edge variables φe\varphi_{e}. Each such monomial corresponds to a unique subset of EE which we can identify with a spanning subgraph of GG.

The edge algebra has an unsigned contravariant functoriality, independent of orientations. Every graph morphism (2.1)

(γ,λ):G→G′(\gamma,\lambda)\colon G\to G^{\prime}

induces a natural homomorphism of algebras

λ∗:ΦG′→ΦG,\lambda^{*}\colon\Phi_{G^{\prime}}\to\Phi_{G},

defined on generators φe′∈ΦG′\varphi_{e^{\prime}}\in\Phi_{G^{\prime}} by

λ∗​(φe′):=∑e∈λ−1​(e′)φe.\lambda^{*}(\varphi_{e^{\prime}}):=\sum_{e\in\lambda^{-1}(e^{\prime})}\varphi_{e}. (2.3)

Thus, λ∗​(φλ⁡(e))=φe\lambda^{*}(\varphi_{\lambda(e)})=\varphi_{e} and λ∗​(φe′)=0\lambda^{*}(\varphi_{e^{\prime}})=0, if e′∈E′e^{\prime}\in E^{\prime} is not in the image of λ\lambda.

Definition 2.2.

Choose an orientation of each non-loop edge of G=(V,E)G=(V,E), independently of the other edges. The zonotopal algebra of GG is the subalgebra 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} of ΦG\Phi_{G} generated by

Xv=∑e∈Ecv,e​φe,v∈V,X_{v}=\sum_{e\in E}c_{v,e}\varphi_{e},\qquad v\in V, (2.4)

where

cv,e={1,e​ has tail ​v​ and head different from ​v,−1,e​ has head ​v​ and tail different from ​v,0,otherwise, in particular if ​e​ is a loop.c_{v,e}=\begin{cases}1,&e\text{ has tail }v\text{ and head different from }v,\\ -1,&e\text{ has head }v\text{ and tail different from }v,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise, in particular if }e\text{ is a loop}.\end{cases} (2.5)

A linear order on VV gives one possible orientation, from the smaller to the larger endpoint, but no compatibility with a vertex order is required.

Remark 2.3.

Orientations are suppressed in the notation 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G}. If an orientation ω′\omega^{\prime} is obtained from ω\omega by reversing some edges, let ηe=−1\eta_{e}=-1 on those edges and ηe=1\eta_{e}=1 on the other edges, including loops. The graded automorphism

ηG:ΦG⟶ΦG,φe⟼ηe​φe,\eta_{G}:\Phi_{G}\longrightarrow\Phi_{G},\qquad\varphi_{e}\longmapsto\eta_{e}\varphi_{e},

sends XvωX_{v}^{\omega} to Xvω′X_{v}^{\omega^{\prime}}. These reorientation maps compose by multiplying their edge signs, and identify the corresponding zonotopal algebras. Loop variables occur in none of the XvX_{v}; deleting loops therefore leaves 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} unchanged under the natural identification inside the algebra on the remaining edge variables. We retain loops because they arise under contraction.

The unsigned map (2.3) does not in general preserve the zonotopal subalgebras. To define their functoriality, fix an orientation for each graph and let ϕ=(γ,λ):G→G′\phi=(\gamma,\lambda):G\to G^{\prime} be a graph morphism. If ee is oriented from uu to vv and λ⁡(e)\lambda(e) is not a loop, set εϕ​(e)=1\varepsilon_{\phi}(e)=1 when λ⁡(e)\lambda(e) is oriented from γ⁡(u)\gamma(u) to γ⁡(v)\gamma(v), and εϕ​(e)=−1\varepsilon_{\phi}(e)=-1 otherwise. If λ⁡(e)\lambda(e) is a loop, set εϕ​(e)=1\varepsilon_{\phi}(e)=1; this includes every loop of GG. Define a signed homomorphism of edge algebras by

ϕ♯​(φe′)={εϕ​(e)​φe,e′=λ⁡(e),0,e′∉λ⁡(E).\phi^{\sharp}(\varphi_{e^{\prime}})=\begin{cases}\varepsilon_{\phi}(e)\varphi_{e},&e^{\prime}=\lambda(e),\\ 0,&e^{\prime}\notin\lambda(E).\end{cases} (2.6)

It is well-defined because λ\lambda is injective and each image has square zero.

Proposition 2.4 (Signed pullbacks).

For every graph morphism ϕ=(γ,λ):G→G′\phi=(\gamma,\lambda):G\to G^{\prime}, the restriction of (2.6) gives a graded algebra homomorphism ϕ∗:𝒞G′→𝒞G\phi^{*}:\mathscr{C}_{G^{\prime}}\to\mathscr{C}_{G} satisfying

ϕ∗​(Xv′G′)=∑v∈γ−1​(v′)XvG.\phi^{*}(X_{v^{\prime}}^{G^{\prime}})=\sum_{v\in\gamma^{-1}(v^{\prime})}X_{v}^{G}. (2.7)

These restrictions define a contravariant functor on 𝒢​r\mathscr{G}r. Changing the chosen orientations gives a naturally isomorphic functor via the reorientation maps of Remark 2.3.

Proof.

For every e∈Ee\in E and v′∈V′v^{\prime}\in V^{\prime}, the incidence coefficients satisfy

εϕ​(e)​cv′,λ⁡(e)G′=∑v∈γ−1​(v′)cv,eG.\varepsilon_{\phi}(e)c^{G^{\prime}}_{v^{\prime},\lambda(e)}=\sum_{v\in\gamma^{-1}(v^{\prime})}c^{G}_{v,e}.

For a non-loop image this is the definition of the sign. If λ⁡(e)\lambda(e) is a loop, the left side is zero; on the right, either both endpoints of a non-loop edge belong to the same fibre and their coefficients cancel, or ee itself is a loop and both coefficients are zero. This proves (2.7), and hence preservation of the subalgebras. Choices of signs on target loop variables do not affect this restriction, since such variables do not occur in 𝒞G′\mathscr{C}_{G^{\prime}}. For a second graph morphism ψ:G′→G′′\psi:G^{\prime}\to G^{\prime\prime}, applying the displayed formula twice gives

ϕ∗​ψ∗​(Xv′′G′′)=∑v∈(γψ∘γ)−1​(v′′)XvG=(ψ∘ϕ)∗​(Xv′′G′′).\phi^{*}\psi^{*}(X_{v^{\prime\prime}}^{G^{\prime\prime}})=\sum_{v\in(\gamma_{\psi}\circ\gamma)^{-1}(v^{\prime\prime})}X_{v}^{G}=(\psi\circ\phi)^{*}(X_{v^{\prime\prime}}^{G^{\prime\prime}}).

It also gives the identity map for the identity morphism. Since the XvX_{v} generate, this proves functoriality. The reorientation maps commute with these restrictions by the same generator formula, which proves the last assertion. ∎

Remark 2.5.

If ϕ\phi preserves the orientation of every edge with non-loop image, then ϕ♯\phi^{\sharp} is the unsigned map λ∗\lambda^{*} of (2.3). In general the chosen signed extensions ϕ♯\phi^{\sharp} need not compose on the full edge algebras: their composites can differ on a target loop variable when an edge is collapsed. Functoriality holds for the restrictions ϕ∗\phi^{*}, where these variables are absent. Thus the unsigned edge-algebra functor and the zonotopal functor are distinct constructions; no order-compatibility assumption is implicit.

For deletion and contraction, choose the inherited orientation on every edge that remains non-loop. For a non-loop edge e=u​ve=uv, the graph GeG_{e} of Figure 1 retains ee as a loop e~\widetilde{e}, whereas G/eG/e is obtained by deleting that loop. Any other parallel edges become loops as well. The chosen signed extension of πe:G→Ge\pi_{e}:G\to G_{e} is then the unsigned edge-bijection isomorphism ΦGe→ΦG\Phi_{G_{e}}\to\Phi_{G}. Since loop variables do not occur in the incidence generators, its restriction identifies 𝒞G/e\mathscr{C}_{G/e} with 𝒞Ge\mathscr{C}_{G_{e}} and gives an injective homomorphism

πe∗:𝒞G/e=𝒞Ge⟶𝒞G.\pi_{e}^{*}:\mathscr{C}_{G/e}=\mathscr{C}_{G_{e}}\longrightarrow\mathscr{C}_{G}. (2.8)

It sends the generator at w={u,v}w=\{u,v\} to Xu+XvX_{u}+X_{v} and sends the generator at any other vertex to the corresponding XpX_{p}. All coefficients of edges between uu and vv cancel in Xu+XvX_{u}+X_{v}. The image is therefore independent of the edge variables that become loops, including φe\varphi_{e}.

2.3 Presentation and deletion–contraction

The deletion and contraction maps give the maps in the exact sequence below. We use the inherited orientations throughout. Let e∈Ee\in E be a non-loop edge with tail uu and head vv. Consider two algebra homomorphisms, the projection

je∗:𝒞G→𝒞G−e,j_{e}^{*}\colon\mathscr{C}_{G}\to\mathscr{C}_{G-e}, (2.9)

produced by sending φe∈ΦG\varphi_{e}\in\Phi_{G} to 00, and the embedding (2.8)

πe∗:𝒞G/e=𝒞Ge→𝒞G,\pi_{e}^{*}\colon\mathscr{C}_{G/e}=\mathscr{C}_{G_{e}}\to\mathscr{C}_{G},

which maps XwX_{w} to Xu+XvX_{u}+X_{v}.

Denote by

∂e:=∂∂φe:ΦG→ΦG/(φe),\partial_{e}:=\frac{\partial}{\partial\varphi_{e}}\colon\Phi_{G}\to\Phi_{G}/(\varphi_{e}), (2.10)

the “partial derivative” with respect to the edge variable φe∈ΦG\varphi_{e}\in\Phi_{G}. Modulo the ideal (φe)(\varphi_{e}), the map ∂e\partial_{e} is well-defined.

The identification

ΦG/(φe)≃ΦG−e\Phi_{G}/(\varphi_{e})\simeq\Phi_{G-e}

endows ΦG−e\Phi_{G-e} with a structure of a ΦG\Phi_{G}-algebra with respect to which ∂e\partial_{e} becomes a ΦG−e\Phi_{G-e}-valued derivation

δe:ΦG→ΦG−e.\delta_{e}\colon\Phi_{G}\to\Phi_{G-e}~.

For a reorientation map ηG\eta_{G} as in Remark 2.3, coefficient extraction satisfies

δe∘ηG=ηe​ηG−e∘δe.\delta_{e}\circ\eta_{G}=\eta_{e}\,\eta_{G-e}\circ\delta_{e}.

In particular, reversing ee changes this map by an overall sign under the reorientation identifications. The contraction maps commute with these identifications on the zonotopal algebras. Exactness and the strictness assertions below are therefore independent of orientations.

To prove exactness without using a dimension formula, we will establish it simultaneously with the power-algebra presentation, originally established in [21, 16]. For a graph HH and a subset I⊆V⁡(H)I\subseteq V(H), let DIHD_{I}^{H} be the number of edges crossing the cut I|V⁡(H)−II\mid V(H)-I, and put

RH=𝐤[xp:p∈V(H)],ρI=∑p∈Ixp,ℐH=(ρIDIH+1:I⊆V(H)).R_{H}=\mathbf{k}[x_{p}:p\in V(H)],\qquad\rho_{I}=\sum_{p\in I}x_{p},\qquad\mathcal{I}_{H}=(\rho_{I}^{D_{I}^{H}+1}:I\subseteq V(H)).

The evaluation homomorphism

evH:RH⟶𝒞H,xp⟼Xp,\operatorname{ev}_{H}\colon R_{H}\longrightarrow\mathscr{C}_{H},\qquad x_{p}\longmapsto X_{p},

satisfies ℐH⊆ker⁡evH\mathcal{I}_{H}\subseteq\ker\operatorname{ev}_{H}: the element ρI​(X)\rho_{I}(X) is a signed sum of the DIHD_{I}^{H} square-zero edge variables crossing the cut.

For use also with the central quotient below, write

ℐH(ϵ)=(ρV⁡(H),ρIDIH+ϵ:∅≠I⊊V(H)),ϵ∈{0,1}.\mathcal{I}_{H}^{(\epsilon)}=\left(\rho_{V(H)},\ \rho_{I}^{D_{I}^{H}+\epsilon}:\varnothing\neq I\subsetneq V(H)\right),\qquad\epsilon\in\{0,1\}. (2.11)

Thus ℐH(1)=ℐH\mathcal{I}_{H}^{(1)}=\mathcal{I}_{H}. Exponent zero is allowed when ϵ=0\epsilon=0, with the convention ρI0=1\rho_{I}^{0}=1. The relation ρV⁡(H)\rho_{V(H)} is written separately in both cases.

Lemma 2.6 (Cut-power antiderivatives).

Let e=u​ve=uv be a non-loop edge of GG, and set 𝒟e=∂xu−∂xv\mathcal{D}_{e}=\partial_{x_{u}}-\partial_{x_{v}} on RG=RG−eR_{G}=R_{G-e}. For ϵ=0,1\epsilon=0,1,

𝒟e​(ℐG(ϵ))=ℐG−e(ϵ)\mathcal{D}_{e}(\mathcal{I}_{G}^{(\epsilon)})=\mathcal{I}_{G-e}^{(\epsilon)} (2.12)

as vector subspaces of RGR_{G}. Every homogeneous element on the right of degree dd has a homogeneous 𝒟e\mathcal{D}_{e}-antiderivative in the ideal on the left of degree d+1d+1.

Proof.

For a proper nonempty subset I⊆VI\subseteq V, put cI=𝒟e​ρI∈{0,1,−1}c_{I}=\mathcal{D}_{e}\rho_{I}\in\{0,1,-1\}. If cI=0c_{I}=0, then DIG=DIG−eD_{I}^{G}=D_{I}^{G-e} and ρI\rho_{I} is invariant. If cI≠0c_{I}\neq 0, then DIG=DIG−e+1D_{I}^{G}=D_{I}^{G-e}+1. Differentiating any multiple of a generator of ℐG(ϵ)\mathcal{I}_{G}^{(\epsilon)} therefore gives an element of ℐG−e(ϵ)\mathcal{I}_{G-e}^{(\epsilon)}. This also holds for the invariant linear relation ρV\rho_{V}.

Conversely, consider ρIN​q\rho_{I}^{N}q with N=DIG−e+ϵN=D_{I}^{G-e}+\epsilon. If cI=0c_{I}=0, choose QQ with 𝒟e​Q=q\mathcal{D}_{e}Q=q and use 𝒟e​(ρIN​Q)=ρIN​q\mathcal{D}_{e}(\rho_{I}^{N}Q)=\rho_{I}^{N}q. Such a QQ exists because, in the linear coordinates xu,xu+xv,xpx_{u},x_{u}+x_{v},x_{p} for p≠u,vp\neq u,v, the operator is differentiation with respect to xux_{u}. If cI≠0c_{I}\neq 0, write

RG=(ker⁡𝒟e)​[ρI],q=∑j≥0qj​ρIj,𝒟e​qj=0.R_{G}=(\ker\mathcal{D}_{e})[\rho_{I}],\qquad q=\sum_{j\geq 0}q_{j}\rho_{I}^{j},\qquad\mathcal{D}_{e}q_{j}=0.

Then

H=1cI​∑j≥0qj​ρIN+j+1N+j+1H=\frac{1}{c_{I}}\sum_{j\geq 0}\frac{q_{j}\rho_{I}^{N+j+1}}{N+j+1}

satisfies 𝒟e​H=ρIN​q\mathcal{D}_{e}H=\rho_{I}^{N}q and lies in (ρIN+1)⊆ℐG(ϵ)(\rho_{I}^{N+1})\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{G}^{(\epsilon)}. Multiples of ρV\rho_{V} are integrated as in the invariant case. These operations preserve homogeneity with degree increased by one. There is no exception when N=0N=0: in particular, a bridge cut in the central case integrates the generator 11 of the deletion ideal to ±ρI\pm\rho_{I}. ∎

For a graded algebra A=⨁k≥0A(k)A=\bigoplus_{k\geq 0}A^{(k)}, write

HA​(t)=∑k≥0dimA(k)​tk.H_{A}(t)=\sum_{k\geq 0}\dim A^{(k)}t^{k}. (2.13)
Theorem 2.7 (Presentation and deletion–contraction).

Let GG be a graph. Then:

  1. (i)

    Evaluation xv↦Xvx_{v}\mapsto X_{v} induces a graded algebra isomorphism

    𝒞G≃𝐤[xv:v∈V]/((∑v∈Ixv)DI+1:I⊆V),\mathscr{C}_{G}\simeq\mathbf{k}[x_{v}:v\in V]/\left(\left(\sum_{v\in I}x_{v}\right)^{D_{I}+1}:I\subseteq V\right), (2.14)

    where DID_{I} is the number of edges crossing the cut I|V−II\mid V-I.

  2. (ii)

    For every non-loop edge ee, the derivation δe\delta_{e} lowers degree by one and the sequence of graded vector spaces

    0⟶𝒞G/e→πe∗𝒞G→δe𝒞G−e​[−1]⟶00\longrightarrow\mathscr{C}_{G/e}\xrightarrow{\pi_{e}^{*}}\mathscr{C}_{G}\xrightarrow{\delta_{e}}\mathscr{C}_{G-e}[-1]\longrightarrow 0 (2.15)

    is exact.

  3. (iii)

    Consequently,

    H𝒞G​(t)=H𝒞G/e​(t)+t​H𝒞G−e​(t).H_{\mathscr{C}_{G}}(t)=H_{\mathscr{C}_{G/e}}(t)+tH_{\mathscr{C}_{G-e}}(t). (2.16)
Proof.

We prove (i) and (ii) simultaneously by induction on the number of non-loop edges; (iii) then follows by taking graded dimensions. If there are no non-loop edges, every XpX_{p} is zero and ℐG=(xp:p∈V)\mathcal{I}_{G}=(x_{p}:p\in V), so the presentation holds and there is no exactness assertion to check. Otherwise, choose a non-loop edge ee with tail uu and head vv, and write X¯p=je∗​Xp\overline{X}_{p}=j_{e}^{*}X_{p}. The action of δe\delta_{e} on the generators (2.4) is

δe​(Xp)={1,p=u,−1,p=v,0,p∉{u,v}.\delta_{e}(X_{p})=\begin{cases}1,&p=u,\\ -1,&p=v,\\ 0,&p\notin\{u,v\}.\end{cases} (2.17)

Since δe\delta_{e} is a je∗j_{e}^{*}-derivation, formula (2.17) gives, for every F∈RGF\in R_{G},

δe​(F⁡(X))=(𝒟e​F)​(X¯).\delta_{e}(F(X))=(\mathcal{D}_{e}F)(\overline{X}). (2.18)

This proves the assertion about degree. It also proves surjectivity: if Q⁡(X¯)Q(\overline{X}) is an element of 𝒞G−e\mathscr{C}_{G-e}, choose a polynomial FF with 𝒟e​F=Q\mathcal{D}_{e}F=Q. When QQ is homogeneous of degree dd, the antiderivative FF can be chosen homogeneous of degree d+1d+1. The map πe∗\pi_{e}^{*} is injective by (2.8), and its image is annihilated by δe\delta_{e}.

It remains to prove exactness at 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} and the presentation

ker⁡evG=ℐG.\ker\operatorname{ev}_{G}=\mathcal{I}_{G}. (2.19)

Assume the presentation is known for graphs with fewer non-loop edges. Let Z=F⁡(X)∈𝒞GZ=F(X)\in\mathscr{C}_{G} satisfy δe​Z=0\delta_{e}Z=0. By (2.18) and the inductive hypothesis for G−eG-e, we have 𝒟e​F∈ℐG−e\mathcal{D}_{e}F\in\mathcal{I}_{G-e}. Lemma 2.6 gives H∈ℐGH\in\mathcal{I}_{G} with 𝒟e​H=𝒟e​F\mathcal{D}_{e}H=\mathcal{D}_{e}F. Consequently

P:=F−H∈ker𝒟e=𝐤[xu+xv,xp:p≠u,v].P:=F-H\in\ker\mathcal{D}_{e}=\mathbf{k}[x_{u}+x_{v},\,x_{p}:p\neq u,v].

Since H⁡(X)=0H(X)=0, we have Z=P⁡(X)Z=P(X). The evaluations of polynomials in this last ring form precisely the image of πe∗\pi_{e}^{*}: the variable at the contracted vertex ww maps to Xu+XvX_{u}+X_{v}, and the remaining variables map to XpX_{p}, p≠u,vp\neq u,v. This proves ker⁡δe=im⁡πe∗\ker\delta_{e}=\operatorname{im}\pi_{e}^{*}. All these constructions can be made homogeneously by the last assertion of Lemma 2.6, so exactness holds in every degree.

It remains to prove (2.19) for GG and thereby close the induction. If F⁡(X)=0F(X)=0, the same construction gives F=H+PF=H+P, with H∈ℐGH\in\mathcal{I}_{G} and P∈ker⁡𝒟eP\in\ker\mathcal{D}_{e}. Identify RG/eR_{G/e} with ker⁡𝒟e\ker\mathcal{D}_{e} by sending xwx_{w} to xu+xvx_{u}+x_{v}. The polynomial corresponding to PP evaluates to zero in 𝒞G/e\mathscr{C}_{G/e}, because its image P⁡(X)P(X) under the injective map πe∗\pi_{e}^{*} is zero. By the inductive hypothesis for G/eG/e, it belongs to ℐG/e\mathcal{I}_{G/e}. Hence P∈ℐGP\in\mathcal{I}_{G}, and therefore F∈ℐGF\in\mathcal{I}_{G}. This proves (2.19) and completes the induction. ∎

Remark 2.8 (Bizonotopal algebras).

Kirillov, Nenashev and the first and third authors use the same scheme for the external bizonotopal algebra ℬG\mathcal{B}_{G}, generated by vertex elements in the square-free algebra of the arrows of both orientations of the edges [9]. A derivation and the embedding of the algebra of the loopy contraction, which is the graph GeG_{e} above, give an exact sequence 0→ℬGe→ℬG→ℬG−e​[−1]→00\to\mathcal{B}_{G_{e}}\to\mathcal{B}_{G}\to\mathcal{B}_{G-e}[-1]\to 0 modeled on (2.15) [9, Proposition 3.7 and Corollary 3.8]. The difference lies in the loops: they do not contribute to 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G}, so that 𝒞Ge=𝒞G/e\mathscr{C}_{G_{e}}=\mathscr{C}_{G/e}, whereas the loops of GeG_{e} contribute to ℬGe\mathcal{B}_{G_{e}}. The Hilbert series therefore satisfy the same relation as in (2.16), with GeG_{e} in place of G/eG/e, but they are not specializations of the Tutte polynomial.

2.4 Spanning forests and Hilbert series

The exact sequence (2.15) gives the formulas for the dimension and the Hilbert series of 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G}, first proved in [21, 16].

A spanning forest of G=(V,E)G=(V,E) is an acyclic spanning subgraph, equivalently an acyclic subset of EE. We recall external activity before stating the Hilbert-series formula.

Definition 2.9.

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a graph with some linear order on the set of edges EE. Let F⊂EF\subset E be a spanning forest of GG. An edge e∈E−Fe\in E-F is called externally active for FF, if the subgraph F∪{e}F\cup\{e\} contains a cycle and the edge ee is the smallest element of this cycle.

The number α⁡(F)\alpha(F) of externally active edges for FF is called the external activity of FF.

Although α⁡(F)\alpha(F) depends on the edge order, the joint distribution of |F||F| and α⁡(F)\alpha(F) does not. More precisely, if r⁡(G)=|V⁡(G)|−c⁡(G)r(G)=|V(G)|-c(G), where c⁡(G)c(G) is the number of connected components, then

∑F​ spanning forest of ​Gzr⁡(G)−|F|​wα⁡(F)=TG​(1+z,w)[20, 2].\sum_{F\text{ spanning forest of }G}z^{r(G)-|F|}w^{\alpha(F)}=T_{G}(1+z,w)\qquad\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{Tut,Bjo}{}{}]}.

The joint counts are therefore coefficients of a shifted Tutte polynomial. The following theorem uses the coarser distribution of |E|−|F|−α⁡(F)|E|-|F|-\alpha(F); it does not recover the two statistics separately. Every loop is externally active for every forest, so α⁡(F)\alpha(F) is at least the number of loops.

Theorem 2.10 ([16, 21]).

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a graph.

  1. (i)

    The dimension of the algebra 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} is equal to the number of spanning forests of GG.

  2. (ii)

    The dimension of the kkth graded component 𝒞G(k)\mathscr{C}_{G}^{(k)} of 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} is equal to the number of spanning forests F⊆EF\subseteq E with the external activity

    α⁡(F)=|E|−|F|−k.\alpha(F)=|E|-|F|-k.
Proof.

Since dim𝒞G=∑k≥0dim𝒞G(k)\displaystyle\dim\mathscr{C}_{G}=\sum_{k\geq 0}\dim\mathscr{C}_{G}^{(k)}, part (i) follows from (ii).

Fix a linear order on EE, and give every graph obtained from GG by deleting or contracting edges the induced order on its remaining edges. Let ak​(G)=|{F⊂E|α⁡(F)=|E|−|F|−k}|a_{k}(G)=\bigl|\{F\subset E\,|\,\alpha(F)=|E|-|F|-k\}\bigr| be the number of spanning forests of a graph GG with the external activity |E|−|F|−k|E|-|F|-k, and let

FG​(t)=∑k≥0ak​(G)​tkF_{G}(t)=\sum_{k\geq 0}a_{k}(G)t^{k}

be its generating function. Then (ii) is equivalent to the equality H𝒞G​(t)=FG​(t)H_{\mathscr{C}_{G}}(t)=F_{G}(t). We prove this equality for every graph and every order, by induction on the number of non-loop edges.

If GG is a graph without non-loop edges, then it has only one spanning forest F=∅F=\emptyset for which all edges (loops) are externally active. Thus α⁡(F)=|E|=|E|−|F|\alpha(F)=|E|=|E|-|F| and FG​(t)=1F_{G}(t)=1. Since H𝒞GH_{\mathscr{C}_{G}} satisfies (2.16) and the two series agree when GG has no non-loop edges, to prove (ii) it is sufficient, by induction on the number of non-loop edges, to show that FGF_{G} satisfies the analogous deletion-contraction relation:

FG​(t)=FG/e​(t)+t​FG−e​(t)F_{G}(t)=F_{G/e}(t)+tF_{G-e}(t)

or, equivalently, that for every GG we have

ak​(G)=ak​(G/e)+ak−1​(G−e),k≥0.a_{k}(G)=a_{k}(G/e)+a_{k-1}(G-e),\ k\geq 0. (2.20)

Denote by ℱ⁡(G)\mathscr{F}(G) the set of forests in a graph GG. If e∈Ee\in E is a non-loop edge, then ℱ⁡(G)=ℱ+​(G)⊔ℱ−​(G)\mathscr{F}(G)=\mathscr{F}_{+}(G)\sqcup\mathscr{F}_{-}(G), where

ℱ+​(G)={F∈ℱ⁡(G)|e∈F}\mathscr{F}_{+}(G)=\{F\in\mathscr{F}(G)\,|\,e\in F\}

and

ℱ−​(G)={F∈ℱ⁡(G)|e∉F}.\mathscr{F}_{-}(G)=\{F\in\mathscr{F}(G)\,|\,e\not\in F\}.

These subsets can be identified with the sets of forests ℱ⁡(G/e)\mathscr{F}(G/e) and ℱ⁡(G−e)\mathscr{F}(G-e) by the bijections

f+:ℱ⁡(G/e)→ℱ+​(G),F↦F⊔{e}f_{+}\colon\mathscr{F}(G/e)\to\mathscr{F}_{+}(G),\ F\mapsto F\sqcup\{e\}

and

f−:ℱ⁡(G−e)→ℱ−​(G),F↦F.f_{-}\colon\mathscr{F}(G-e)\to\mathscr{F}_{-}(G),\ F\mapsto F.

To verify relation (2.20), we need to keep track of the numbers aka_{k}. We do not reorder the edges: we take for ee the largest non-loop edge in the given order. Then α⁡(f±​(F))=α⁡(F)\alpha(f_{\pm}(F))=\alpha(F) both for F∈ℱ⁡(G/e)F\in\mathscr{F}(G/e) and F∈ℱ⁡(G−e)F\in\mathscr{F}(G-e). Indeed, let e′∉F∪{e}e^{\prime}\notin F\cup\{e\}. If e′e^{\prime} is a loop of GG, it is active on both sides. Otherwise the cycle of F∪{e,e′}F\cup\{e,e^{\prime}\} in GG, respectively of F∪{e′}F\cup\{e^{\prime}\} in G−eG-e, contains the non-loop edge e′<ee^{\prime}<e, and contraction of ee identifies it with the cycle of F∪{e′}F\cup\{e^{\prime}\} in G/eG/e after removing ee; this does not change the smallest edge. Finally, ee itself is never externally active for F∈ℱ−​(G)F\in\mathscr{F}_{-}(G): a cycle through the non-loop edge ee contains another non-loop edge, which is smaller than ee. In the first case, the term |E|−|F||E|-|F| stays the same, so forests from ℱ⁡(G/e)\mathscr{F}(G/e) and ℱ+​(G)\mathscr{F}_{+}(G) contribute to the same coefficient aka_{k}. In the second case the difference |E|−|F||E|-|F| changes by 11, therefore forests from ℱ⁡(G−e)\mathscr{F}(G-e) contribute to ak−1a_{k-1}, as required. Since the order was arbitrary and H𝒞GH_{\mathscr{C}_{G}} does not depend on it, this also proves that the numbers ak​(G)a_{k}(G) are independent of the order. ∎

2.5 Central algebras and spanning trees

The same antiderivative argument gives the central, or spanning-tree counting, algebra of Postnikov and Shapiro. We include its presentation and Hilbert formula to parallel the external theory above; see [15, Theorem 9.1 and Corollary 10.5] and [13, Section 4, Theorem 7]. Filtered central algebras, generated by the elements f⁡(Xv)f(X_{v}) in the quotient ΦGc\Phi_{G}^{\mathrm{c}} below, are introduced in [13, Section 4]. They are not used in the subsequent sections; see Section 8.

Let GG be a connected graph with nonempty vertex set. Define its central zonotopal algebra as the power quotient

𝒞Gc=RG/ℐG(0)=𝐤[xv:v∈V]/(ρV,ρIDI:∅≠I⊊V).\mathscr{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{c}}=R_{G}/\mathcal{I}_{G}^{(0)}=\mathbf{k}[x_{v}:v\in V]\big/\left(\rho_{V},\ \rho_{I}^{D_{I}}:\varnothing\neq I\subsetneq V\right). (2.21)

Eliminating one variable with ρV=0\rho_{V}=0 gives the usual rooted presentation. The full-set relation is linear, not ρVDV=1\rho_{V}^{D_{V}}=1. For the deletion–contraction induction we use the same quotient on a disconnected graph. A proper union of connected components has cut size zero, so this auxiliary quotient is zero. This is the spanning-tree convention, not the tensor product of central algebras of the components.

To realize the quotient without using its dimension, set

ΦGc=ΦG/(φS:G−S​ is disconnected),φS=∏e∈Sφe.\Phi_{G}^{\mathrm{c}}=\Phi_{G}/(\varphi_{S}:G-S\text{ is disconnected}),\qquad\varphi_{S}=\prod_{e\in S}\varphi_{e}. (2.22)

A set S⊆ES\subseteq E is called slim when G−SG-S is connected. The slim monomials form a basis of ΦGc\Phi_{G}^{\mathrm{c}}. For disconnected GG, the empty support is nonslim and this algebra is zero, consistently with the convention above. Write 𝒞~Gc\widetilde{\mathscr{C}}_{G}^{\mathrm{c}} for its subalgebra generated by the incidence sums XvX_{v}. Reorientation sign changes preserve the nonslim-monomial ideal, so these incidence subalgebras are identified under reorientation as in Remark 2.3. The deletion and contraction maps below use inherited orientations. These sums satisfy ∑vXv=0\sum_{v}X_{v}=0 and, for a proper cut of size DI>0D_{I}>0,

(∑v∈IXv)DI=±DI!∏e∈δ⁡(I)φe=0.\left(\sum_{v\in I}X_{v}\right)^{D_{I}}=\pm D_{I}!\prod_{e\in\delta(I)}\varphi_{e}=0.

Consequently evaluation induces a surjection 𝒞Gc→𝒞~Gc\mathscr{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{c}}\to\widetilde{\mathscr{C}}_{G}^{\mathrm{c}}.

Lemma 2.11 (Slim deletion and contraction).

For every non-loop edge ee, the inclusion of ee-free monomials and coefficient extraction induce an exact sequence of graded vector spaces

0⟶ΦG/ec→ιeΦGc→δeΦG−ec​[−1]⟶0.0\longrightarrow\Phi_{G/e}^{\mathrm{c}}\xrightarrow{\iota_{e}}\Phi_{G}^{\mathrm{c}}\xrightarrow{\delta_{e}}\Phi_{G-e}^{\mathrm{c}}[-1]\longrightarrow 0. (2.23)

The first map is an injective algebra homomorphism and sends the contracted incidence generator to Xu+XvX_{u}+X_{v}.

Proof.

For S⊆E∖{e}S\subseteq E\setminus\{e\}, the edge ee remains in G−SG-S. Contracting it does not change connectedness, so

G−S connected⟺(G/e)−S connected.G-S\text{ connected}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(G/e)-S\text{ connected}.

This identifies the ee-free slim monomials with the basis on the left of (2.23). The slim monomials containing ee are φe​φT\varphi_{e}\varphi_{T} with (G−e)−T(G-e)-T connected, and coefficient extraction identifies them with the basis on the right. With inherited orientations, the incidence formula for ιe\iota_{e} follows from cancellation at the endpoints of every edge joining uu to vv, including ee; all other edge coefficients agree. ∎

Setting φe=0\varphi_{e}=0 also gives an algebra map je∗:ΦGc→ΦG−ecj_{e}^{*}:\Phi_{G}^{\mathrm{c}}\to\Phi_{G-e}^{\mathrm{c}}. It need not identify ΦGc/(φe)\Phi_{G}^{\mathrm{c}}/(\varphi_{e}) with ΦG−ec\Phi_{G-e}^{\mathrm{c}}: deletion can impose further nonslim-monomial relations. Nevertheless δe\delta_{e} is a je∗j_{e}^{*}-derivation. In particular, for ee oriented from uu to vv,

δe​(F⁡(X))=(𝒟e​F)​(X¯),X¯p=je∗​Xp.\delta_{e}(F(X))=(\mathcal{D}_{e}F)(\overline{X}),\qquad\overline{X}_{p}=j_{e}^{*}X_{p}. (2.24)
Theorem 2.12 (Central presentation and deletion–contraction).

Evaluation identifies the power quotient (2.21) with 𝒞~Gc\widetilde{\mathscr{C}}_{G}^{\mathrm{c}}. For every non-loop edge of a connected graph, there is an exact sequence of graded vector spaces

0⟶𝒞G/ec→πe∗𝒞Gc→δe𝒞G−ec​[−1]⟶0,0\longrightarrow\mathscr{C}_{G/e}^{\mathrm{c}}\xrightarrow{\pi_{e}^{*}}\mathscr{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{c}}\xrightarrow{\delta_{e}}\mathscr{C}_{G-e}^{\mathrm{c}}[-1]\longrightarrow 0, (2.25)

using the zero deletion term when ee is a bridge. Thus

H𝒞Gc​(t)={H𝒞G/ec​(t)+t​H𝒞G−ec​(t),e​ is not a bridge,H𝒞G/ec​(t),e​ is a bridge.H_{\mathscr{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{c}}}(t)=\begin{cases}H_{\mathscr{C}_{G/e}^{\mathrm{c}}}(t)+tH_{\mathscr{C}_{G-e}^{\mathrm{c}}}(t),&e\text{ is not a bridge},\\ H_{\mathscr{C}_{G/e}^{\mathrm{c}}}(t),&e\text{ is a bridge}.\end{cases} (2.26)

Loops may be deleted without changing 𝒞Gc\mathscr{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{c}}.

Proof.

We prove the presentation and exactness simultaneously by induction on the number of non-loop edges, as in Theorem 2.7. Disconnected graphs have both quotients zero. A connected graph without non-loop edges has one vertex; its incidence algebra and its power quotient are both 𝐤\mathbf{k}, irrespective of its loops.

For a non-loop edge e=u​ve=uv, Lemma 2.11 gives an injective contraction map on the incidence subalgebras. Equation (2.24) gives surjectivity of δe\delta_{e}: a polynomial representative Q⁡(X¯)Q(\overline{X}) lifts by choosing F∈RGF\in R_{G} with 𝒟e​F=Q\mathcal{D}_{e}F=Q. The antiderivative may be chosen homogeneous with degree raised by one.

If F⁡(X)∈ker⁡δeF(X)\in\ker\delta_{e}, the inductive presentation on G−eG-e gives 𝒟e​F∈ℐG−e(0)\mathcal{D}_{e}F\in\mathcal{I}_{G-e}^{(0)}. Lemma 2.6, with ϵ=0\epsilon=0, supplies H∈ℐG(0)H\in\mathcal{I}_{G}^{(0)} such that 𝒟e​H=𝒟e​F\mathcal{D}_{e}H=\mathcal{D}_{e}F. Then

P=F−H∈ker𝒟e=𝐤[xu+xv,xp:p≠u,v].P=F-H\in\ker\mathcal{D}_{e}=\mathbf{k}[x_{u}+x_{v},x_{p}:p\neq u,v].

Since H⁡(X)=0H(X)=0, the element F⁡(X)=P⁡(X)F(X)=P(X) belongs to the contraction image. This proves exactness on the incidence subalgebras.

To close the induction, suppose F⁡(X)=0F(X)=0. The same correction writes F=H+PF=H+P. Regard PP as a polynomial on G/eG/e, substituting xw=xu+xvx_{w}=x_{u}+x_{v} at the contracted vertex. Its evaluation on G/eG/e is zero because the ambient contraction map is injective. The inductive presentation puts it in ℐG/e(0)\mathcal{I}_{G/e}^{(0)}. The total relation maps to ρV\rho_{V}, and every proper cut of G/eG/e corresponds to a cut of GG containing both u,vu,v or neither, with the same size. Hence its ideal maps into ℐG(0)\mathcal{I}_{G}^{(0)}. Thus PP, and then FF, belongs to ℐG(0)\mathcal{I}_{G}^{(0)}, proving the presentation. All corrections can be made homogeneously. The Hilbert relation follows from exactness. Finally, loops occur in neither the cut sizes nor the incidence generators. ∎

Corollary 2.13 (Spanning-tree activity formula).

For a connected graph GG, with external activity α⁡(T)\alpha(T) defined as above,

H𝒞Gc​(t)=∑T​ spanning tree of ​Gt|E|−|V|+1−α⁡(T).H_{\mathscr{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{c}}}(t)=\sum_{T\text{ spanning tree of }G}t^{|E|-|V|+1-\alpha(T)}. (2.27)

In particular, dim𝒞Gc\dim\mathscr{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{c}} is the number of spanning trees. Equivalently, the series is t|E|−|V|+1​TG​(1,t−1)t^{|E|-|V|+1}T_{G}(1,t^{-1}).

Proof.

Choose the non-loop edge ee largest in the edge ordering. Trees containing ee correspond to trees of G/eG/e, with unchanged external activity and unchanged exponent in (2.27). Trees omitting ee correspond to trees of G−eG-e, again with unchanged activity, but with exponent increased by one when viewed in GG. If ee is a bridge, every spanning tree contains ee, so there are no trees omitting ee; this matches the bridge case of (2.26). A loop is externally active for every tree, so deleting it decreases both |E||E| and the external activity by one and leaves every exponent unchanged. The activity sum therefore satisfies (2.26) and has value 11 on a one-vertex graph, just as the Hilbert series. Induction proves the formula, and t=1t=1 gives the dimension. The last expression is the spanning-tree activity specialization of the Tutte polynomial. ∎

For example, a tree has central algebra 𝐤\mathbf{k}, an nn-cycle has central Hilbert series 1+(n−1)​t1+(n-1)t, and two vertices joined by mm parallel edges have central Hilbert series 1+t+⋯+tm−11+t+\cdots+t^{m-1}. For a disconnected graph one may instead define a componentwise central algebra by tensoring the connected ones. It counts spanning forests with one tree per component, but then the bridge case must remain separate; it is not the zero convention used in (2.25).

2.6 Recovery of the graphical matroid

The following classification was proved by Wagner [21, Theorem 1.10] and Nenashev [11, Theorem 2.1][12]. We give a proof in which the reconstruction is read directly from the highest-degree multiplication. Write G∘G^{\circ} for the graph obtained from GG by deleting all loops. Isolated vertices may also be discarded.

Theorem 2.14 (Wagner–Nenashev).

For any two graphs G1,G2G_{1},G_{2}, the following are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    𝒞G1\mathscr{C}_{G_{1}} and 𝒞G2\mathscr{C}_{G_{2}} are isomorphic as 𝐤\mathbf{k}-algebras;

  2. (ii)

    𝒞G1\mathscr{C}_{G_{1}} and 𝒞G2\mathscr{C}_{G_{2}} are isomorphic as graded 𝐤\mathbf{k}-algebras;

  3. (iii)

    the graphical matroids M⁡(G1∘)M(G_{1}^{\circ}) and M⁡(G2∘)M(G_{2}^{\circ}) are isomorphic.

Proof.

Loops do not occur in the generators XvX_{v}, so we may assume that the graphs are loopless. Let A=𝒞GA=\mathscr{C}_{G}, let N=|E⁡(G)|>0N=|E(G)|>0, and put W=A(1)W=A^{(1)}. For e∈E⁡(G)e\in E(G) let ℓe∈W∗\ell_{e}\in W^{*} be extraction of the coefficient of φe\varphi_{e}. Each ℓe\ell_{e} is nonzero. For every x∈Wx\in W,

xN=N!​(∏e∈E⁡(G)ℓe​(x))​∏e∈E⁡(G)φe.x^{N}=N!\left(\prod_{e\in E(G)}\ell_{e}(x)\right)\prod_{e\in E(G)}\varphi_{e}. (2.28)

Since 𝐤\mathbf{k} is infinite, there is an xx for which every ℓe​(x)\ell_{e}(x) is nonzero. Thus A(N)=𝐤​∏eφeA^{(N)}=\mathbf{k}\prod_{e}\varphi_{e} and A(j)=0A^{(j)}=0 for j>Nj>N.

Let 𝔪\mathfrak{m} be the maximal ideal of AA. Since AA is generated in degree one, 𝔪j=⨁k≥jA(k)\mathfrak{m}^{j}=\bigoplus_{k\geq j}A^{(k)}. In particular, NN is determined intrinsically by 𝔪N+1=0≠𝔪N\mathfrak{m}^{N+1}=0\neq\mathfrak{m}^{N}, and the homogeneous polynomial map

𝔪/𝔪2⟶𝔪N,x¯⟼xN\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^{2}\longrightarrow\mathfrak{m}^{N},\qquad\overline{x}\longmapsto x^{N}

is well-defined: changing xx by an element of 𝔪2\mathfrak{m}^{2} changes xNx^{N} by an element of 𝔪N+1=0\mathfrak{m}^{N+1}=0. After choosing an identification of the one-dimensional target with 𝐤\mathbf{k}, it is a polynomial QAQ_{A} on 𝔪/𝔪2≃W\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^{2}\simeq W, well-defined up to scalar. Formula (2.28) gives

QA≐∏e∈E⁡(G)ℓe,Q_{A}\doteq\prod_{e\in E(G)}\ell_{e},

where ≐\doteq means equality up to a nonzero scalar. Unique factorization recovers the multiset of lines {𝐤​ℓe:e∈E⁡(G)}⊂𝐏⁡(W∗)\{\mathbf{k}\ell_{e}:e\in E(G)\}\subset\mathbf{P}(W^{*}), including repeated factors. In vertex-potential coordinates these forms are au−ava_{u}-a_{v} for the oriented edges u​vuv, on the space of potentials modulo functions constant on connected components. Their dependence matroid is M⁡(G)M(G). An arbitrary algebra isomorphism preserves QAQ_{A} up to a linear change of variables and a scalar. This proves (i)⇒\Rightarrow(iii). If N=0N=0, the algebra is 𝐤\mathbf{k} and the loopless matroid is empty, so the same conclusion holds.

For (iii)⇒\Rightarrow(ii), use Whitney’s 22-isomorphism theorem [22]: after disregarding isolated vertices, graphs with isomorphic graphical matroids are related by identifications of vertices in distinct components, their inverse cleavings, and twists at a two-vertex separation. We check the induced cut spaces WG=Span⁡{Xv}⊂𝐤E⁡(G)W_{G}=\Span\{X_{v}\}\subset\mathbf{k}^{E(G)}. Identification and cleaving leave this space unchanged, since additive constants in vertex potentials can be chosen independently on the components. For a twist with boundary vertices u,vu,v, keep a potential aa on the first side and replace it on the second side by aw′=au+av−awa^{\prime}_{w}=a_{u}+a_{v}-a_{w}. This interchanges its boundary values and negates all edge differences on the second side. Hence negating the edge variables on that side maps the old cut space onto the new one. These sign changes, and the signed edge permutations induced by graph isomorphisms as in Proposition 2.4, extend to graded isomorphisms of the square-zero edge algebras. They therefore identify the subalgebras generated by the cut spaces. Finally, (ii)⇒\Rightarrow(i) is immediate. ∎

Remark 2.15.

The factorization argument also applies to a subalgebra of a square-zero algebra generated by the rows of a matrix with no zero columns. Its highest-power polynomial recovers the projective column configuration, with multiplicities, not merely its dependence matroid. Conversely, projectively equivalent configurations give isomorphic algebras by permuting and rescaling the edge variables. Thus, within this class, the highest-degree multiplication already determines the algebra. For graphs, this is more information than the dimensions of the graded pieces, whose Hilbert series is only a specialization of the Tutte polynomial.

The next section changes the filtration while retaining the underlying algebra. For loopless graphs without isolated vertices, multiple edges allowed, a nonzero quadratic coefficient makes this filtered invariant complete (Theorem 3.8).

3 Polynomially generated filtrations

3.1 Definition and general properties

We apply a power series to the vertex generators and filter the resulting subalgebra by the number of factors. For nondegenerate series this is a filtration of the fixed algebra 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G}; degenerate series may generate a smaller algebra. The notation 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f} includes both the subalgebra and its word filtration.

Definition 3.1.

A formal power series

f=a0+a1​u+a2​u2+⋯∈𝐤⁡[[u]]f=a_{0}+a_{1}u+a_{2}u^{2}+\cdots\in\mathbf{k}[[u]]

is called nondegenerate if a1≠0a_{1}\neq 0, i.e. when f′​(0)≠0f^{\prime}(0)\neq 0, and degenerate otherwise.

Definition 3.2.

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a graph and let f∈𝐤⁡[[u]]f\in\mathbf{k}[[u]] be a power series. The filtered external zonotopal algebra of GG associated to ff is the subalgebra 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f} of ΦG\Phi_{G} (2.2), with its filtration by degree in the generators

Yv:=f⁡(Xv)=f⁡(∑e∈Ecv,e​φe),v∈V,Y_{v}:=f(X_{v})=f\Bigl(\sum_{e\in E}c_{v,e}\varphi_{e}\Bigr),\ v\in V, (3.1)

where the coefficients cv,e∈{0,±1}c_{v,e}\in\{0,\pm 1\} are given by (2.5).

For nondegenerate ff the algebra 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}^{f}_{G} is all of 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} (Proposition 3.6); for degenerate ff it is in general a proper subalgebra (Section 3.7). If f=uf=u, then 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}^{f}_{G} is the usual zonotopal algebra 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} of GG, and if f=euf=e^{u}, the filtered algebra 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}^{f}_{G} is the KK-theoretic analog 𝒦G\mathscr{K}_{G} of 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} studied in [13].

Remark 3.3.

The generators Yv=f⁡(Xv)Y_{v}=f(X_{v}) are well-defined because φe2=0\varphi_{e}^{2}=0 implies that

Xvm=(∑e∈Ecv,e​φe)m=0, for ​m>deg⁡vX_{v}^{m}=\Bigl(\sum_{e\in E}c_{v,e}\varphi_{e}\Bigr)^{m}=0,\text{ for }m>\deg v (3.2)

and so the power series (3.1) terminates. This also shows that the terms of ff of degree higher than

Δ⁡(G):=maxv∈V⁡deg⁡v\Delta(G):=\max_{v\in V}\deg v

do not affect any of the generators YvY_{v} of 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f}. Therefore, we may restrict our attention to those f∈𝐤⁡[[u]]f\in\mathbf{k}[[u]] which are polynomials in uu of degree at most Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G).

The algebra 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}^{f}_{G} is endowed with an increasing filtration

𝐤=𝒞Gf,0⊂𝒞Gf,1⊂𝒞Gf,2⊂⋯⊂𝒞Gf,\mathbf{k}=\mathscr{C}^{f,0}_{G}\subset\mathscr{C}^{f,1}_{G}\subset\mathscr{C}^{f,2}_{G}\subset\cdots\subset\mathscr{C}^{f}_{G}, (3.3)

where the subspace 𝒞Gf,i\mathscr{C}^{f,i}_{G} is spanned by the monomials of degree at most ii in the generators Yv=f⁡(Xv)Y_{v}=f(X_{v}).

Remark 3.4.

Replacing ff by f+cf+c with c∈𝐤=𝒞Gf,0c\in\mathbf{k}=\mathscr{C}^{f,0}_{G} changes each YvY_{v} to Yv+cY_{v}+c, and multiplying ff by a nonzero scalar rescales the YvY_{v}. Neither changes the filtration (3.3). For nondegenerate ff we therefore assume from now on that f≡u(modu2)f\equiv u\pmod{u^{2}}; degenerate ff are treated in Section 3.7.

When f=uf=u, the filtration (3.3) coincides with the filtration induced on 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} by its standard grading.

Remark 3.5 (Functoriality).

Reorientation preserves these filtrations, since ηG​(f⁡(Xvω))=f⁡(Xvω′)\eta_{G}(f(X_{v}^{\omega}))=f(X_{v}^{\omega^{\prime}}); the maps of Remark 2.3 are filtered algebra isomorphisms. For a graph morphism ϕ=(γ,λ)\phi=(\gamma,\lambda),

ϕ∗​(Yv′G′)=f⁡(∑v∈γ−1​(v′)XvG).\phi^{*}(Y_{v^{\prime}}^{G^{\prime}})=f\left(\sum_{v\in\gamma^{-1}(v^{\prime})}X_{v}^{G}\right). (3.4)

After subtracting f⁡(0)f(0), which does not change the filtration, the images for injective γ\gamma are the YvGY_{v}^{G} and zeros. Thus ϕ∗​(𝒞G′f,i)=𝒞Gf,i\phi^{*}(\mathscr{C}_{G^{\prime}}^{f,i})=\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f,i} for all ii. In particular, graph isomorphisms induce filtered isomorphisms. When vertices are identified, the right side of (3.4) need not lie in the first filtered space; this is why filtered contraction is treated separately in Section 3.5.

Nondegenerate functions give filtrations of one fixed algebra. Degenerate functions, treated in Section 3.7, need not do so.

Proposition 3.6 ([13, Proposition 2]).

If f∈𝐤⁡[[u]]f\in\mathbf{k}[[u]] is a nondegenerate series, then 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}^{f}_{G} coincides, as a subalgebra of ΦG\Phi_{G}, with the usual zonotopal algebra 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G}.

Proof.

After subtracting the constant term, write f⁡(u)=c1​u+c2​u2+⋯f(u)=c_{1}u+c_{2}u^{2}+\cdots, with c1≠0c_{1}\neq 0. Each Yv=f⁡(Xv)Y_{v}=f(X_{v}) belongs to 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G}, so 𝒞Gf⊆𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f}\subseteq\mathscr{C}_{G}. The formal compositional inverse gg exists: its coefficients are determined successively by g⁡(f⁡(u))=ug(f(u))=u, since the coefficient of the next unknown is a nonzero power of c1c_{1}. Truncating gg after degree Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G) gives g⁡(f⁡(Xv))=Xvg(f(X_{v}))=X_{v} for every vertex. Thus every XvX_{v} belongs to 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f}, proving the reverse inclusion. ∎

The increasing word filtration varies with ff. By contrast, the decreasing filtration by powers of the maximal ideal recovers the original graded algebra. These are different filtrations on the same underlying algebra.

Corollary 3.7.

Let f∈u​𝐤​[[u]]f\in u\mathbf{k}[[u]] be a nondegenerate series and let JJ be the ideal of the algebra 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f} generated by the elements Yv=f⁡(Xv)Y_{v}=f(X_{v}), v∈Vv\in V. Then the associated graded algebra grJ⁡(𝒞Gf)\gr_{J}(\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f}) for the JJ-adic filtration

𝒞Gf⊃J⊃J2⊃⋯⊃0\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f}\supset J\supset J^{2}\supset\cdots\supset 0

is isomorphic to the graded algebra 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G}.

Proof.

By Proposition 3.6, 𝒞Gf=𝒞G\mathscr{C}^{f}_{G}=\mathscr{C}_{G} as algebras. The algebra 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} is local: it is the direct sum of 𝐤\mathbf{k} and its ideal 𝔪\mathfrak{m} of elements without constant term, and 𝔪\mathfrak{m} is nilpotent. Since 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} is generated by the elements XvX_{v}, the ideal 𝔪\mathfrak{m} is generated by them; moreover, Yv=f⁡(Xv)=Xv⋅uvY_{v}=f(X_{v})=X_{v}\cdot u_{v}, where uv=a1+a2​Xv+⋯u_{v}=a_{1}+a_{2}X_{v}+\cdots is a unit of 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} (a1≠0a_{1}\neq 0 by nondegeneracy), so J=(Yv:v∈V)=(Xv:v∈V)=𝔪J=(Y_{v}:v\in V)=(X_{v}:v\in V)=\mathfrak{m}. Finally, since the graded algebra 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} is generated in degree one, 𝔪k=⨁j≥k𝒞G(j)\mathfrak{m}^{k}=\bigoplus_{j\geq k}\mathscr{C}_{G}^{(j)}, whence

grJ⁡(𝒞Gf)=⨁k≥0𝔪k/𝔪k+1≅⨁k≥0𝒞G(k)=𝒞G.∎\gr_{J}(\mathscr{C}^{f}_{G})=\bigoplus_{k\geq 0}\mathfrak{m}^{k}/\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}\cong\bigoplus_{k\geq 0}\mathscr{C}_{G}^{(k)}=\mathscr{C}_{G}.\qed

3.2 Recovery of the graph from its filtration

The following result concerns filtered isomorphism types, rather than Hilbert functions. It applies to every ff with nonzero quadratic coefficient, not just to a generic parameter.

Theorem 3.8.

Let ff be a polynomial with nonzero linear and quadratic terms and let G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} be two loopless graphs without isolated vertices; multiple edges are allowed. Then 𝒞G1f\mathscr{C}^{f}_{G_{1}} and 𝒞G2f\mathscr{C}^{f}_{G_{2}} are isomorphic as filtered algebras if and only if the graphs G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} are isomorphic.

For simple graphs this is [13, Theorem 6], and for f=eu−1f=e^{u}-1 it is [13, Theorem 5]. Loops and isolated vertices do not occur in the generators f⁡(Xv)f(X_{v}). Hence, for arbitrary graphs, the filtered algebra determines the graph obtained by deleting all loops and isolated vertices, and nothing more.

Proof.

The implication from graph isomorphism follows from the signed pullback of Proposition 2.4 and (3.4). Conversely, let Ψ:𝒞Hf⟶𝒞Gf\Psi:\mathscr{C}_{H}^{f}\longrightarrow\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f} be a filtered algebra isomorphism. By the normalization in Remark 3.4, write f⁡(u)=u+α​u2+⋯f(u)=u+\alpha u^{2}+\cdots with α≠0\alpha\neq 0. We use the edge configuration reconstructed in the proof of Theorem 2.14, rather than reconstruct it a second time.

Put WG=𝔪G/𝔪G2W_{G}=\mathfrak{m}_{G}/\mathfrak{m}_{G}^{2} and define WHW_{H} similarly. The highest nonzero maximal-ideal power has degree N=|E⁡(G)|=|E⁡(H)|N=|E(G)|=|E(H)| and is one-dimensional. The intrinsic highest-power polynomial on WGW_{G} factors as QG≐∏eℓeQ_{G}\doteq\prod_{e}\ell_{e}, where ℓe\ell_{e} extracts the coefficient of φe\varphi_{e} in ordinary degree one. Two edges e,de,d give proportional forms if and only if they are parallel: parallel edges give ℓd=±ℓe\ell_{d}=\pm\ell_{e}, and if uu is an endpoint of ee but not of dd, then ℓe​(Xu)=±1\ell_{e}(X_{u})=\pm 1 while ℓd​(Xu)=0\ell_{d}(X_{u})=0. Here we use that the graphs are loopless. Thus the distinct lines 𝐤​ℓe\mathbf{k}\ell_{e} are indexed by the parallel classes of edges, and the multiplicity of a line in QGQ_{G} is the size of its class. Let GsG^{\mathrm{s}} be the simple graph obtained from GG by keeping one edge from each parallel class, and let m⁡(e)m(e) be the size of the class of ee. Unique factorization applied to the linear map Ψ¯:WH→WG\overline{\Psi}:W_{H}\to W_{G} therefore gives a bijection τ:E⁡(Gs)→E⁡(Hs)\tau:E(G^{\mathrm{s}})\to E(H^{\mathrm{s}}) with m⁡(τ⁡(e))=m⁡(e)m(\tau(e))=m(e), and nonzero scalars ses_{e} such that

ℓe∘Ψ¯=se​ℓτ⁡(e)′.\ell_{e}\circ\overline{\Psi}=s_{e}\ell^{\prime}_{\tau(e)}. (3.5)

The bijection preserves linear dependences, and hence the cycle matroid of GsG^{\mathrm{s}}, including its three-edge circuits, which are the triangles. If N=0N=0, both graphs are empty because isolated vertices are excluded, and there is nothing to prove.

Let Zw=Ψ⁡(f⁡(XwH))Z_{w}=\Psi(f(X_{w}^{H})). Since ZwZ_{w} is nilpotent and belongs to the first filtered space, it is a linear combination of the f⁡(XvG)f(X_{v}^{G}), with no constant term. Equation (3.5) gives

[φe]​Zw=se​cw,τ⁡(e)H.[\varphi_{e}]Z_{w}=s_{e}c^{H}_{w,\tau(e)}.

For g=f−1=u−α​u2+⋯g=f^{-1}=u-\alpha u^{2}+\cdots, the global incidence relation on HH gives ∑wg⁡(Zw)=0\sum_{w}g(Z_{w})=0. Take two disjoint edges e,de,d of GsG^{\mathrm{s}}. No f⁡(XvG)f(X_{v}^{G}) contains the monomial φe​φd\varphi_{e}\varphi_{d}, because its support uses only edges incident to vv. Thus no ZwZ_{w} contains that monomial either. Taking its coefficient in the inverse relation yields

0=−2αsesd∑w∈V⁡(H)cHw,τ⁡(e)cHw,τ⁡(d).0=-2\alpha s_{e}s_{d}\sum_{w\in V(H)}c^{H}_{w,\tau(e)}c^{H}_{w,\tau(d)}. (3.6)

The edges τ⁡(e),τ⁡(d)\tau(e),\tau(d) are not parallel, so they share at most one vertex. The sum is zero when they are disjoint and is 11 or −1-1 when they share a vertex. Thus τ⁡(e),τ⁡(d)\tau(e),\tau(d) are disjoint. Applying the same argument to Ψ−1\Psi^{-1} proves the converse. The bijection therefore preserves edge adjacency as well as triangles.

These data reconstruct the simple graph GsG^{\mathrm{s}}, which has no isolated vertices. Indeed, its stars at vertices of degree at least two are exactly the maximal sets of at least two pairwise incident edges containing no three-edge circuit. To check this, choose two edges with common vertex vv. Any edge meeting both either contains vv or completes a triangle with them; the latter possibility is excluded. Maximality then gives the full star at vv. Create a vertex for each such star. An edge belongs to zero, one, or two recovered stars; add respectively two, one, or no leaf endpoints. The zero-star case is an isolated K2K_{2} component. This recovers all vertices and incidences, so τ\tau is induced by an isomorphism Gs≃HsG^{\mathrm{s}}\simeq H^{\mathrm{s}}. Since τ\tau preserves the multiplicities mm, this isomorphism extends to an isomorphism G≃HG\simeq H.

The argument uses no extension of Ψ\Psi to an ambient edge algebra and no preservation of the original grading. Its linear data come from 𝔪/𝔪2\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^{2}, and its quadratic test comes from the actual first filtered space. ∎

If the quadratic term of the polynomial f⁡(u)f(u) vanishes, the corresponding algebras for non-isomorphic graphs can be isomorphic even as filtered algebras, as the following example shows.

Proposition 3.9.

Consider the trees G1=D6G_{1}=\mathrm{D}_{6} and G2=E6G_{2}=\mathrm{E}_{6} shown in Figure 2, and let f⁡(u)=u+u3f(u)=u+u^{3}. Then the filtered external zonotopal algebras 𝒞G1f\mathscr{C}^{f}_{G_{1}} and 𝒞G2f\mathscr{C}^{f}_{G_{2}} are isomorphic as filtered algebras.

For f=u+u3f=u+u^{3}, since φi2=φi′2=0\varphi_{i}^{2}=\varphi_{i}^{\prime 2}=0, we see that these sets of generators for 𝒞G1f\mathscr{C}_{G_{1}}^{f} and 𝒞G2f\mathscr{C}_{G_{2}}^{f} are, respectively,

S1={φ1,−φ1+φ2+φ5−6​φ1​φ2​φ5,φ3−φ2,φ4−φ3,−φ4,−φ5}S_{1}=\{\varphi_{1},-\varphi_{1}+\varphi_{2}+\varphi_{5}-6\varphi_{1}\varphi_{2}\varphi_{5},\varphi_{3}-\varphi_{2},\varphi_{4}-\varphi_{3},-\varphi_{4},-\varphi_{5}\}

and

S2={φ3′,φ2′−φ3′,φ1′−φ2′+φ5′−6​φ1′​φ2′​φ5′,−φ1′+φ4′,−φ4′,−φ5′}.S_{2}=\{\varphi_{3}^{\prime},\varphi_{2}^{\prime}-\varphi_{3}^{\prime},\varphi^{\prime}_{1}-\varphi^{\prime}_{2}+\varphi^{\prime}_{5}-6\varphi^{\prime}_{1}\varphi^{\prime}_{2}\varphi^{\prime}_{5},-\varphi^{\prime}_{1}+\varphi^{\prime}_{4},-\varphi_{4}^{\prime},-\varphi_{5}^{\prime}\}.

The linear subspaces generated by these sets in ΦG1\Phi_{G_{1}} and ΦG2\Phi_{G_{2}} are, respectively, L1=⟨S1⟩=⟨φi,φ1​φ2​φ5⟩L_{1}=\langle S_{1}\rangle=\langle\varphi_{i},\varphi_{1}\varphi_{2}\varphi_{5}\rangle and L2=⟨S2⟩=⟨φi′,φ1′​φ2′​φ5′⟩L_{2}=\langle S_{2}\rangle=\langle\varphi^{\prime}_{i},\varphi^{\prime}_{1}\varphi^{\prime}_{2}\varphi^{\prime}_{5}\rangle, i=1,…,5i=1,\ldots,5.
