∎

3.3 Generators and relations

Every element of the maximal ideal of ΦG\Phi_{G} is nilpotent, so the substitutions a↦f⁡(a)a\mapsto f(a) and a↦f−1​(a)a\mapsto f^{-1}(a) are defined on it and are mutually inverse (Proposition 3.6). Hence a polynomial relation ρ(Xv:v∈V)=0\rho(X_{v}:v\in V)=0 holds in 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} if and only if ρ(f−1(Yv):v∈V)=0\rho(f^{-1}(Y_{v}):v\in V)=0. Applied to the presentation of Theorem 2.7, this gives the relations among the filtered generators.

Corollary 3.10.

For a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) and a normalized nondegenerate f∈𝐤⁡[[u]]f\in\mathbf{k}[[u]], consider the ideal

IGf:=(yvdeg⁡v+1,(∑v∈If−1​(yv))DI+1)v∈V,I⊆V,|I|≥2I_{G}^{f}:=\left(y_{v}^{\deg v+1},\Bigl(\sum_{v\in I}f^{-1}(y_{v})\Bigr)^{D_{I}+1}\right)_{v\in V,\ I\subseteq V,\ |I|\geq 2} (3.7)

in 𝐤[yv:v∈V]\mathbf{k}[y_{v}:v\in V], where DID_{I}, as before, is the number of edges having one end in II and the other in the complementary subset V−IV-I, and deg⁡v=D{v}\deg v=D_{\{v\}} is the number of non-loop edges at vv.

Then IGfI_{G}^{f} is the ideal of relations for 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f}, i.e. it is the kernel of the epimorphism 𝐤[yv:v∈V]→𝒞Gf.\mathbf{k}[y_{v}\colon v\in V]\to\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f}~. Therefore

𝒞Gf≃𝐤[yv:v∈V]/IGf.\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f}\simeq\mathbf{k}[y_{v}\colon v\in V]/I_{G}^{f}~.
Proof.

First quotient by yvdeg⁡v+1y_{v}^{\deg v+1} for all vv. On this truncated polynomial algebra, the substitutions xv=f−1​(yv)x_{v}=f^{-1}(y_{v}) and yv=f⁡(xv)y_{v}=f(x_{v}) are mutually inverse automorphisms: the constant term of ff is zero and its linear coefficient is nonzero. In particular, xvdeg⁡v+1x_{v}^{\deg v+1} and yvdeg⁡v+1y_{v}^{\deg v+1} differ by a unit factor. Under this change of variables, the remaining cut-power generators of Theorem 2.7(i) become exactly the displayed relations. This proves both the presentation and that no further relations are needed. In the displayed ideal, each f−1​(yv)f^{-1}(y_{v}) may be truncated modulo yvdeg⁡v+1y_{v}^{\deg v+1}. ∎

Remark 3.11.

Modulo the component-sum relation ∑v∈Vf−1​(Yv)=0\sum_{v\in V}f^{-1}(Y_{v})=0, the cut sums for II and IcI^{c} are negatives of one another, and DI=DIcD_{I}=D_{I^{c}}. Hence one relation from each complementary pair suffices; keep the total-sum relation and all vertex nilpotence relations. For example, choose the representative with smaller cardinality, breaking ties arbitrarily. Section 6.3 gives examples of how the remaining relations depend on the parameter.

3.4 Hilbert series

We use the associated graded of the increasing word filtration to define its Hilbert function, as in the Introduction. For a general filtered vector space, the convention is the following.

Definition 3.12.

Let WW be a vector space with an exhaustive increasing filtration

W0⊂W1⊂⋯⊂Wi⊂⋯⊂WW^{0}\subset W^{1}\subset\cdots\subset W^{i}\subset\cdots\subset W

with W−1=0W^{-1}=0, whose associated graded space

gr⁡(W)=⨁i≥0Wi/Wi−1\gr(W)=\bigoplus_{i\geq 0}W^{i}/W^{i-1} (3.8)

has finite-dimensional components Wi/Wi−1W^{i}/W^{i-1}.

The sequence of integers

hi​(W)=dim𝐤Wi/Wi−1,i≥0,h_{i}(W)=\dim_{\mathbf{k}}W^{i}/W^{i-1},\ i\geq 0,

is called the Hilbert function of WW, and its generating function

ℋW​(t)=∑i≥0hi​(W)​ti\mathscr{H}_{W}(t)=\sum_{i\geq 0}h_{i}(W)t^{i} (3.9)

is called the Hilbert series of WW.

The Hilbert functions and Hilbert series of filtered external zonotopal algebras have some simple properties.

Proposition 3.13.

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) and let ff be any polynomial or formal power series. Write ℋGf​(t)=∑i≥0hi​ti\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f}(t)=\sum_{i\geq 0}h_{i}t^{i}. Then

  1. (i)

    ℋGf​(t)\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f}(t) is a polynomial in tt of degree d≤|E|d\leq|E|.

  2. (ii)

    hi≤(|V|+i−1i)\displaystyle h_{i}\leq\binom{|V|+i-1}{i} for all ii; in particular h0=1h_{0}=1.

  3. (iii)

    If ff has nonzero linear and quadratic terms and the loopless graph G∘G^{\circ} has no isolated vertices or isolated edges, then h1=|V|h_{1}=|V|.

  4. (iv)

    If G=G1⊔G2G=G_{1}\sqcup G_{2} is a disjoint union of two graphs G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}, then

    ℋGf​(t)=ℋG1f​(t)​ℋG2f​(t).\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f}(t)=\mathscr{H}_{G_{1}}^{f}(t)\,\mathscr{H}_{G_{2}}^{f}(t). (3.10)
Proof.

Subtract f⁡(0)f(0) using Remark 3.4. Then every generator YvY_{v} lies in the maximal ideal 𝔪=(φe:e∈E)\mathfrak{m}=(\varphi_{e}:e\in E) of ΦG\Phi_{G}. A product of more than |E||E| elements of 𝔪\mathfrak{m} vanishes, since every square-free monomial contains at most |E||E| variables; hence 𝒞Gf,i=𝒞Gf,|E|\mathscr{C}^{f,i}_{G}=\mathscr{C}^{f,|E|}_{G} for i≥|E|i\geq|E|, and hi=0h_{i}=0 for i>|E|i>|E|, proving (i).

For (ii), the graded quotient 𝒞Gf,i/𝒞Gf,i−1\mathscr{C}^{f,i}_{G}/\mathscr{C}^{f,i-1}_{G} is spanned by the images of the products of exactly ii generators, i.e. by the images of the degree-ii monomials in the |V||V| elements YvY_{v}; the number of such monomials is (|V|+i−1i)\binom{|V|+i-1}{i}.

For (iii), suppose ∑vcv​Yv∈𝐤\sum_{v}c_{v}Y_{v}\in\mathbf{k} for some scalars cvc_{v}. Comparing the linear parts in the edge variables gives ∑vcv​Xv=0\sum_{v}c_{v}X_{v}=0, which forces cvc_{v} to be constant on every connected component of GG, say cv=cCc_{v}=c_{C} for v∈Cv\in C.

Comparing the quadratic parts then gives a2​∑CcC​QC=0a_{2}\sum_{C}c_{C}\,Q_{C}=0, where QC=∑v∈CXv2Q_{C}=\sum_{v\in C}X_{v}^{2} and a2≠0a_{2}\neq 0 is the quadratic coefficient of ff. For every pair of distinct edges e,e′e,e^{\prime} sharing at least one vertex, the coefficient of φe​φe′\varphi_{e}\varphi_{e^{\prime}} in QCQ_{C} equals 2​∑v∈e∩e′cv,e​cv,e′2\sum_{v\in e\cap e^{\prime}}c_{v,e}c_{v,e^{\prime}}, which is ±2\pm 2 if the edges share one vertex and ±4\pm 4 if they are parallel; hence QC≠0Q_{C}\neq 0 unless the component CC is an isolated vertex or an isolated edge. Since the QCQ_{C} are supported on disjoint sets of variable pairs, all cCc_{C} vanish, so the classes of YvY_{v}, v∈Vv\in V, in 𝒞Gf,1/𝒞Gf,0\mathscr{C}^{f,1}_{G}/\mathscr{C}^{f,0}_{G} are linearly independent and h1=|V|h_{1}=|V|.

Finally, (iv) holds because ΦG1⊔G2=ΦG1⊗ΦG2\Phi_{G_{1}\sqcup G_{2}}=\Phi_{G_{1}}\otimes\Phi_{G_{2}}, the generators of 𝒞G1⊔G2f\mathscr{C}^{f}_{G_{1}\sqcup G_{2}} are those of the two factors, and consequently 𝒞G1⊔G2f,i=∑j+k≤i𝒞G1f,j⊗𝒞G2f,k\mathscr{C}^{f,i}_{G_{1}\sqcup G_{2}}=\sum_{j+k\leq i}\mathscr{C}^{f,j}_{G_{1}}\otimes\mathscr{C}^{f,k}_{G_{2}}; the Hilbert series of such a tensor product with the convolution filtration is the product of the Hilbert series. ∎

The first Hilbert coefficient also distinguishes the two cases in maximum degree two.

Proposition 3.14.

Let GG be a loopless graph of maximum degree at most two, and let f=u+α​u2+⋯f=u+\alpha u^{2}+\cdots be normalized and nondegenerate. Then ℋGf\mathscr{H}^{f}_{G} depends only on whether α=0\alpha=0. If GG has a vertex of degree two, the two series ℋGu\mathscr{H}^{u}_{G} and ℋGu+u2\mathscr{H}^{u+u^{2}}_{G} are different.

Proof.

Since Xv3=0X_{v}^{3}=0 for every vertex, Yv=Xv+α​Xv2Y_{v}=X_{v}+\alpha X_{v}^{2}, and scaling every edge variable by ε≠0\varepsilon\neq 0, and dividing the generators by ε\varepsilon, replaces α\alpha by ε​α\varepsilon\alpha. Thus all nonzero values of α\alpha give isomorphic filtered algebras. Let cc be the number of components of GG and c0c_{0} the number of those that are isolated vertices or isolated edges. For f=uf=u the relations among the XvX_{v} are spanned by the component sums, so h1=|V|−ch_{1}=|V|-c. For α≠0\alpha\neq 0, the proof of Proposition 3.13(iii) shows that a relation ∑vcv​Yv∈𝐤\sum_{v}c_{v}Y_{v}\in\mathbf{k} vanishes on every other component, so h1=|V|−c0h_{1}=|V|-c_{0}. A vertex of degree two lies in a component that is neither an isolated vertex nor an isolated edge, so c>c0c>c_{0}. ∎

3.5 Filtered deletion–contraction and strictness

For the graded algebras, the deletion–contraction sequence computes Hilbert series recursively. We now ask when it remains exact at each filtration level. It does so under mild conditions at an endpoint of degree at most two (Theorem 3.16), but not in general (Section 3.6). This failure is the reason for the boundary states of Section 4.

The underlying deletion–contraction sequence remains exact for every nondegenerate ff, but its restriction to filtration spaces need not be exact. The issue is strictness of the contraction embedding. Let e=u​ve=uv be a non-loop edge and let ww be the contracted vertex. In this subsection assume that the generators at these vertices are linear:

f⁡(Xu)=Xu,f⁡(Xv)=Xv,f⁡(Xw)=Xw.f(X_{u})=X_{u},\qquad f(X_{v})=X_{v},\qquad f(X_{w})=X_{w}. (3.11)

A sufficient condition is f≡u(modum)f\equiv u\pmod{u^{m}} with

m≥max⁡(deg⁡u+deg⁡v−1,deg⁡u+1,deg⁡v+1).m\geq\max(\deg u+\deg v-1,\deg u+1,\deg v+1). (3.12)

Indeed, the three relevant nilpotence orders are at most deg⁡u+1\deg u+1, deg⁡v+1\deg v+1, and deg⁡u+deg⁡v−1\deg u+\deg v-1, respectively. The corresponding endpoint generators after deleting ee are then linear as well, by applying je∗j_{e}^{*}.

Proposition 3.15 (The strictness defect).

Under (3.11), put

Fi=𝒞Gf,i,Bi=πe∗​(𝒞G/ef,i),Fi′′=𝒞G−ef,i.F_{i}=\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f,i},\qquad B_{i}=\pi_{e}^{*}(\mathscr{C}_{G/e}^{f,i}),\qquad F_{i}^{\prime\prime}=\mathscr{C}_{G-e}^{f,i}.

Then

Bi⊆Fi∩ker⁡δe,δe​(Fi)=Fi−1′′.B_{i}\subseteq F_{i}\cap\ker\delta_{e},\qquad\delta_{e}(F_{i})=F_{i-1}^{\prime\prime}. (3.13)

The obstruction above shows that filtered deletion–contraction alone does not control the attachment of graphs. The next section keeps two filtrations at a cut edge and computes directly with their joint birth degrees.

3.7 Degenerate functions

Let ff be degenerate. Every element of 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f} is a constant plus terms of degree at least two in the φe\varphi_{e}, so 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f} is a proper subalgebra of 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} as soon as GG has a non-loop edge. These filtered algebras are the algebras F​[f]GF[f]_{G} of [13, Section 3]. Nenashev and the first author asked for the combinatorial properties of their Hilbert series and, in particular, for the dimension of 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f} [13, Problem 4]. We answer this question for forests and for cycles. By Remark 3.4, subtracting the constant term does not change the filtration. A nonzero series with f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0 has order kk if f=c​uk+terms of higher degreef=cu^{k}+\text{terms of higher degree} with c≠0c\neq 0. It is degenerate exactly when k≥2k\geq 2 and for f=0f=0 the algebra is 𝐤\mathbf{k}. Loops occur in none of the XvX_{v}, so in this section all graphs are loopless.

Definition 3.19.

A partial orientation of a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) is a choice of orientations for the edges of a subset S⊆ES\subseteq E [9, Definition 2.1]. For e∈Se\in S let s⁡(e)s(e) be the vertex at which ee starts. The score vector of the partial orientation is a∈ℤ≥0Va\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}^{V}, where ava_{v} is the number of edges of SS starting at vv. The score vectors of partial orientations are the partial score vectors of GG [9, Definition 2.4]. For k≥1k\geq 1 put

sk​(G,t)=∑at|a|/k,|a|=∑v∈Vav,s_{k}(G;t)=\sum_{a}t^{|a|/k},\qquad|a|=\sum_{v\in V}a_{v},

the sum over the partial score vectors aa with k|avk\mid a_{v} for all v∈Vv\in V.

Removing an edge from SS shows that lowering an entry of a partial score vector gives a partial score vector. By [9, Corollary 2.6], s1​(G,t)s_{1}(G;t) is the Hilbert series of the external bizonotopal algebra (Remark 2.8).

Theorem 3.20.

Let GG be a forest, let k≥2k\geq 2, and let f∈𝐤⁡[u]f\in\mathbf{k}[u] have order kk. Put

ℰG,k\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{G,k} ={m∈ℤ≥0V⁡(G):k​m​ is a partial score vector of ​G},\displaystyle=\{m\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}^{V(G)}:km\text{ is a partial score vector of }G\},
IG,k\displaystyle I_{G,k} =(zm:m∉ℰG,k)⊆𝐤[zv:v∈V(G)].\displaystyle=(z^{m}:m\notin\mathcal{E}_{G,k})\subseteq\mathbf{k}[z_{v}:v\in V(G)].

Evaluation induces an isomorphism of filtered algebras

𝐤[zv:v∈V(G)]/IG,k→∼𝒞Gf,zv⟼f(Xv),\mathbf{k}[z_{v}:v\in V(G)]/I_{G,k}\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \mathscr{C}_{G}^{f},\qquad z_{v}\longmapsto f(X_{v}), (3.23)

where the quotient on the left has its standard degree filtration. Consequently

ℋGf(t)=sk(G;t),𝒞Gf≃𝒞Gukas filtered algebras.\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f}(t)=s_{k}(G;t),\qquad\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f}\simeq\mathscr{C}_{G}^{u^{k}}\quad\text{as filtered algebras}.

In particular, the filtered isomorphism type depends only on GG and kk, and its dimension counts the partial score vectors with every entry divisible by kk.

  2. (ii)

    For the star with NN leaves, ℋSN+1f=1+t+⋯+t⌊N/k⌋\mathscr{H}_{S_{N+1}}^{f}=1+t+\cdots+t^{\lfloor N/k\rfloor}.

    If k>Δ⁡(G)k>\Delta(G), then all YvY_{v} vanish and 𝒞Gf=𝐤\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f}=\mathbf{k}; this holds for every graph.

For a∈ℤ≥0Va\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}^{V}, expanding the powers with φe2=0\varphi_{e}^{2}=0 gives

∏v∈VXvav=∏v∈Vav!⋅∑S(∏e∈Scs⁡(e),e)​φS,φS=∏e∈Sφe,\prod_{v\in V}X_{v}^{a_{v}}=\prod_{v\in V}a_{v}!\cdot\sum_{S}\Bigl(\prod_{e\in S}c_{s(e),e}\Bigr)\varphi_{S},\qquad\varphi_{S}=\prod_{e\in S}\varphi_{e}, (3.24)

the sum over the partial orientations with score vector aa. Indeed, XvavX_{v}^{a_{v}} is av!a_{v}! times the sum of the products of ava_{v} distinct terms cv,e​φec_{v,e}\varphi_{e}. Choosing such a product for every vv amounts to orienting the chosen edges away from vv, and the product of the choices vanishes unless all the chosen edges are distinct. In particular, ∏vXvav=0\prod_{v}X_{v}^{a_{v}}=0 unless aa is a partial score vector.

Lemma 3.22.

Let GG be a graph and let f∈𝐤⁡[u]f\in\mathbf{k}[u] have order k≥1k\geq 1. Then 𝒞Gf,d\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f,d} is spanned by the products ∏vYvmv\prod_{v}Y_{v}^{m_{v}} with ∑vmv≤d\sum_{v}m_{v}\leq d for which k​mkm is a partial score vector. Since f​(u)mvf(u)^{m_{v}} is divisible by uk​mvu^{km_{v}}, the product ∏vYvmv\prod_{v}Y_{v}^{m_{v}} is a linear combination of products ∏vXvjv\prod_{v}X_{v}^{j_{v}} with jv≥k​mvj_{v}\geq km_{v} for all vv. For a vertex vv let ej​(v)e_{j}(v) be the jjth elementary symmetric polynomial in the variables φe\varphi_{e} of the edges at vv, with e0​(v)=1e_{0}(v)=1 and ej​(v)=0e_{j}(v)=0 for j<0j<0, and put Pa=∏veav​(v)P_{a}=\prod_{v}e_{a_{v}}(v). Lemma 3.23.

Let GG be a forest and, for each v∈Vv\in V, let Av⊆ℤ≥0A_{v}\subseteq{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0} be a set that contains no two consecutive integers. Then the nonzero elements PaP_{a} with a∈∏vAva\in\prod_{v}A_{v} are linearly independent.

Proof.

We use induction on the number of edges. If there are none, only P0=1P_{0}=1 occurs. Otherwise let ℓ\ell be a leaf, let e=ℓ​pe=\ell p be its edge and let G′=G−ℓG^{\prime}=G-\ell. If aℓ=1a_{\ell}=1, then Pa=φe​Pa′′P_{a}=\varphi_{e}\,P^{\prime}_{a^{\prime}}, because φe​ej​(p)=φe​ej′​(p)\varphi_{e}\,e_{j}(p)=\varphi_{e}\,e^{\prime}_{j}(p). If aℓ=0a_{\ell}=0, then eap​(p)=eap′​(p)+φe​eap−1′​(p)e_{a_{p}}(p)=e^{\prime}_{a_{p}}(p)+\varphi_{e}\,e^{\prime}_{a_{p}-1}(p) gives

Pa=Pa′′+φe​Pa′−δp′,P_{a}=P^{\prime}_{a^{\prime}}+\varphi_{e}\,P^{\prime}_{a^{\prime}-\delta_{p}},

where δp\delta_{p} is the indicator vector of pp. Since ΦG=ΦG′⊕φe​ΦG′\Phi_{G}=\Phi_{G^{\prime}}\oplus\varphi_{e}\Phi_{G^{\prime}}, a relation ∑aca​Pa=0\sum_{a}c_{a}P_{a}=0 splits into ∑aca​Pa′′=0\sum_{a}c_{a}P^{\prime}_{a^{\prime}}=0 and ∑aca​Pa′−δp′=0\sum_{a}c_{a}P^{\prime}_{a^{\prime}-\delta_{p}}=0. The vectors a′a^{\prime} lie in ∏v≠ℓAv\prod_{v\neq\ell}A_{v}, so by induction ca=0c_{a}=0 whenever Pa′′≠0P^{\prime}_{a^{\prime}}\neq 0. For the remaining aa we have Pa=φe​Pa′−δp′≠0P_{a}=\varphi_{e}\,P^{\prime}_{a^{\prime}-\delta_{p}}\neq 0. The vectors a′−δpa^{\prime}-\delta_{p} are distinct and lie in the product of the sets AvA_{v}, v≠ℓ,pv\neq\ell,p, and {x−1:x∈Ap,x≥1}\{x-1:x\in A_{p},\ x\geq 1\}, which again contains no two consecutive integers. The hypothesis is needed: for the path with two edges and Av=ℤ≥0A_{v}={\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}, eight elements PaP_{a} are nonzero, in an algebra of dimension four.

Proof of Theorem 3.20.

Partial score feasibility is downward closed. Hence ℰG,k\mathcal{E}_{G,k} is a finite order ideal, IG,kI_{G,k} is a monomial ideal, and the residue classes of {zm:m∈ℰG,k}\{z^{m}:m\in\mathcal{E}_{G,k}\} form a basis of 𝐤[zv:v∈V(G)]/IG,k\mathbf{k}[z_{v}:v\in V(G)]/I_{G,k}. Lemma 3.22 shows that every generator of IG,kI_{G,k} evaluates to zero. It remains to prove the independence of the feasible products ∏vYvmv\prod_{v}Y_{v}^{m_{v}}. A forest is bipartite; orient every edge from one class V+V_{+} of a bipartition to the other class V−V_{-} (Remark 3.5). Then cv,e=±1c_{v,e}=\pm 1 for v∈V±v\in V_{\pm} and every edge ee at vv, and (3.24) becomes ∏vXvav=±∏vav!⋅Pa\prod_{v}X_{v}^{a_{v}}=\pm\prod_{v}a_{v}!\cdot P_{a}. The component of lowest degree in the φe\varphi_{e} of ∏vYvmv\prod_{v}Y_{v}^{m_{v}} is

c∑vmv∏vXvk​mv=±c∑vmv∏v(kmv)!⋅Pk​m≠0.c^{\sum_{v}m_{v}}\prod_{v}X_{v}^{km_{v}}=\pm c^{\sum_{v}m_{v}}\prod_{v}(km_{v})!\cdot P_{km}\neq 0.

Since k≥2k\geq 2, the set k​ℤ≥0k{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0} contains no two consecutive integers, and Lemma 3.23 shows that these lowest components are linearly independent. Elements whose lowest components are linearly independent are linearly independent: in a nontrivial relation, consider the smallest degree of a lowest component with nonzero coefficient. Hence evaluation modulo IG,kI_{G,k} is injective as well as surjective. It maps the span of the standard monomials of degree at most dd onto 𝒞Gf,d\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f,d} for every dd, proving the filtered isomorphism and its Hilbert formula. ∎

Remark 3.24.

The presentation gives 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f} a grading in which the YvY_{v} have degree one. This grading need not agree with ordinary edge degree in ΦG\Phi_{G}. The same proof permits a different function fvf_{v} at each vertex, of order kv≥2k_{v}\geq 2: the standard monomials are those for which (kv​mv)v(k_{v}m_{v})_{v} is a partial score vector. Only the orders kvk_{v} matter. Indeed, apply Lemma 3.23 with Av=kv​ℤ≥0A_{v}=k_{v}{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0} to the lowest-degree components of the products.

Corollary 3.25.

Let GG be a graph and let f∈𝐤⁡[u]f\in\mathbf{k}[u] have order k≥2k\geq 2, with coefficient cc of its lowest nonzero term. Then for all dd

dim𝒞Guk,d≤dim𝒞Gf,d≤∑m≤d[tm]​sk​(G,t),\dim\mathscr{C}_{G}^{u^{k},d}\leq\dim\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f,d}\leq\sum_{m\leq d}[t^{m}]\,s_{k}(G;t),

with equality for forests.

Proof.

The upper bound is Lemma 3.22. An orientation of GG defines a homomorphism from the partial orientation algebra of [9] onto ΦG\Phi_{G} that maps the external bizonotopal algebra ℬG\mathcal{B}_{G} onto 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} and its generators yvy_{v} to XvX_{v} [9, Section 2]. 4 Boundary states, assembly, and path recurrences

We compute Hilbert series under attachment by retaining two filtrations at a marked leaf edge. Their joint birth degrees determine the local closing, branching, and path-extension rules. We establish these rules first and then apply them to the tail and neck families of Theorem C. Figure 3 fixes the notation.

Splitting, assembly, and the gap bound hold for every normalized nondegenerate ff. For extension through bivalent vertices and the tail and neck recurrences we assume f=u+α​u2+β​u3+⋯f=u+\alpha u^{2}+\beta u^{3}+\cdots with α≠0\alpha\neq 0. We use the generators Yv=f⁡(Xv)Y_{v}=f(X_{v}) of (3.1). For a finite set SS in a commutative algebra, ⟨S⟩i\langle S\rangle^{i} denotes the span of products of at most ii elements of SS. Every filtration is zero in negative degrees. Only α\alpha enters the path-extension rule and only α,β\alpha,\beta enter the terminal calculations; the attached boundary data may depend on higher coefficients.

4.1 Boundary filtrations and their states

Let rr be a leaf edge of a graph GG, joining a leaf vertex aa to a′a^{\prime}. Write rr also for its edge variable φr\varphi_{r}. Deleting rr isolates aa, so 𝒞G−rf\mathscr{C}^{f}_{G-r} is naturally identified with 𝒞G/rf\mathscr{C}^{f}_{G/r}. Under this identification the deletion map jr∗j_{r}^{*} is evaluation at r=0r=0. Since Ya=±rY_{a}=\pm r, omitting the leaf generator gives the open filtration

Pi=⟨Yw:w∈V(G)∖{a}⟩i⊂𝒞Gf.P_{i}=\bigl\langle Y_{w}:w\in V(G)\smallsetminus\{a\}\bigr\rangle^{i}\subset\mathscr{C}^{f}_{G}. (4.1)

This filtration is exhaustive. Indeed, Xa=−∑w≠aXwX_{a}=-\sum_{w\neq a}X_{w}, and each XwX_{w} is a polynomial in YwY_{w}, by Proposition 3.6. Thus the omitted generator Ya=f⁡(Xa)Y_{a}=f(X_{a}) belongs to the algebra generated by the other YwY_{w}. The full, or closed, filtration is Pi+r​Pi−1P_{i}+rP_{i-1}.

Example 4.2.

The lifts in (4.2) can be removed from all local calculations. This is the principle behind every rule below. The old graph spaces serve as coefficient spaces; the new multiplications involve only the displayed boundary and vertex variables. The required changes of basis are linear over these local variables, not algebra automorphisms of the old graph algebras.

Lemma 4.3 (Block decomposition).

Keep the notation of Lemma 4.1, and let Λ\Lambda be the algebra of finitely many further edge variables, adjoined at the leaf aa. The Λ⁡[r]/(r2)\Lambda[r]/(r^{2})-linear map

Ψ:U⊗Λ⁡[r]/(r2)⟶U⊗Λ⁡[r]/(r2),Ψ⁡(eλ)=eλ+r​aλ,\Psi\colon U\otimes\Lambda[r]/(r^{2})\longrightarrow U\otimes\Lambda[r]/(r^{2}),\qquad\Psi(e_{\lambda})=e_{\lambda}+ra_{\lambda},

To record a boundary calculation without choosing an adapted basis, let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be the free abelian group on symbols [p,q][p,q], with p,q≥0p,q\geq 0. Give it the ℤ⁡[t]{\mathbb{Z}}[t]-module structure

t⁡[p,q]=[p+1,q+1].t[p,q]=[p+1,q+1].

This finite sum has nonnegative integer coefficients. Formal differences in 𝒮\mathcal{S} will be used only to express linear identities between such sums. When a state sum is written as ∑jaj​(t)​[0,j]\sum_{j}a_{j}(t)[0,j], its constant term means ∑jaj​(0)​[0,j]\sum_{j}a_{j}(0)[0,j]; the exponents of tt retain the common birth-degree shifts.

4.2 Assembly and bounded gaps

Let ee be a bridge of GG. Cutting GG at ee gives two marked graphs; each contains ee as its marked leaf edge, whose leaf is the endpoint of ee on the other side. The generators of GG are the open generators of the two sides. Hence the Hilbert series of GG is the sum, over all pairs of states [p,q][p,q] and [p′,q′][p^{\prime},q^{\prime}] of the two sides, of the closing evaluation

𝖤⁡([p,q],[p′,q′])=tp+p′+tmin⁡(q+p′,p+q′).\mathsf{E}([p,q],[p^{\prime},q^{\prime}])=t^{p+p^{\prime}}+t^{\min(q+p^{\prime},p+q^{\prime})}. (4.6)

Indeed, by Lemma 4.3 applied on both sides it suffices to take one state on each side. Since r2=0r^{2}=0, the products of 11 and rr from the two sides give 11 in degree p+p′p+p^{\prime} and rr in degree min⁡(q+p′,p+q′)\min(q+p^{\prime},p+q^{\prime}). Reorienting the shared edge on one side, with the signed identification just described, changes neither birth degree.

Fix a bound DD for the vertex degrees. Consider a vertex vv of degree r+1≤Dr+1\leq D, with one incoming edge variable xjx_{j} for each of the pairwise disjoint incoming marked pieces B1,…,BrB_{1},\ldots,B_{r} joined at vv, and an outgoing variable zz (Figure 4(b)). Its new generator is

y=f⁡(z−x1−⋯−xr)inΦrloc=𝐤⁡[x1,…,xr,z]/(x12,…,xr2,z2).y=f(z-x_{1}-\cdots-x_{r})\quad\text{in}\quad\Phi^{\rm loc}_{r}=\mathbf{k}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{r},z]/(x_{1}^{2},\ldots,x_{r}^{2},z^{2}).

4.3 Extending a path by one edge

In this subsection f=u+α​u2+⋯f=u+\alpha u^{2}+\cdots with α≠0\alpha\neq 0. Start with a graph whose marked leaf edge has variable rr and whose open filtration is P∙P_{\bullet}. Attach one new edge, with variable ss, at the marked leaf. The old leaf becomes a bivalent vertex; the new leaf is the marked open endpoint. With compatible orientations, the new vertex generator is

y=f⁡(s−r)=s−r−2​α​r​s,y=f(s-r)=s-r-2\alpha rs,

P~i=∑k≥0yk​Pi−k=Pi+y​Pi−1+r​s​Pi−2.\widetilde{P}_{i}=\sum_{k\geq 0}y^{k}P_{i-k}=P_{i}+yP_{i-1}+rsP_{i-2}.

We call this operation path extension. The following lemma shows that 𝖲⁡(P~∙)\mathsf{S}(\widetilde{P}_{\bullet}) depends only on 𝖲⁡(P∙)\mathsf{S}(P_{\bullet}) and defines the path-extension operator T:𝒮→𝒮T:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{S}. Iterating TT corresponds to successive one-edge extensions; it is an operator on state sums, not a graph-algebra homomorphism.

Lemma 4.5 (One-edge extension).

The identity 𝖲⁡(P~∙)=T​𝖲​(P∙)\mathsf{S}(\widetilde{P}_{\bullet})=T\mathsf{S}(P_{\bullet}) holds, where TT is the ℤ⁡[t]{\mathbb{Z}}[t]-linear operator

T⁡[p,q]={[p,p+1]+[q,q+1],q≤p,[p,p+2]+[p+1,p+1],q=p+1,[p,q]+[p+1,p+2],q≥p+2.T[p,q]=\begin{cases}[p,p+1]+[q,q+1],&q\leq p,\\ [p,p+2]+[p+1,p+1],&q=p+1,\\ [p,q]+[p+1,p+2],&q\geq p+2.\end{cases} (4.11)

By the preceding change of basis it suffices to start with a single state [p,q][p,q] in 𝐤⁡[r]/(r2)\mathbf{k}[r]/(r^{2}). Since y2=−2​r​sy^{2}=-2rs, r​y=r​sry=rs, and y3=r​y2=0y^{3}=ry^{2}=0, the new filtration is spanned by

1​from degree ​p,r​from degree ​q,y​from degree ​p+1,r​s​from degree ​min⁡(p+2,q+1).1\ \text{from degree }p,\quad r\ \text{from degree }q,\quad y\ \text{from degree }p+1,\quad rs\ \text{from degree }\min(p+2,q+1).

Qinew=Span{1:p≤i,r:a≤i},Rinew=Span{r:b≤i, 1−2αr:c≤i}.Q_{i}^{\rm new}=\Span\{1:p\leq i,\ r:a\leq i\},\qquad R_{i}^{\rm new}=\Span\{r:b\leq i,\ 1-2\alpha r:c\leq i\}. (4.12)

Indeed, the image of yy is −r-r, and its cancellation with rr gives y+r=s⁡(1−2​α​r)y+r=s(1-2\alpha r). These are all possibilities for a kernel element. In the three cases of (4.11), simultaneous adapted bases for (4.12) are respectively

(1−2​α​r,r),(1,1−2​α​r),(1,r).(1-2\alpha r,r),\qquad(1,1-2\alpha r),\qquad(1,r).

Their birth degrees give the table. The middle pair is a basis because α≠0\alpha\neq 0. ∎

In Example 4.2, the passage from one edge to the open path with two edges is the case q=p+1q=p+1 of (4.11): T⁡[0,1]=[0,2]+[1,1]T[0,1]=[0,2]+[1,1].

We next identify the polynomial governing TT. Put

e0=[0,0],e1=[0,1],e2=[0,2],𝒱=ℤ⁡[t]​e0⊕ℤ⁡[t]​e1⊕ℤ⁡[t]​e2.e_{0}=[0,0],\qquad e_{1}=[0,1],\qquad e_{2}=[0,2],\qquad\mathcal{V}={\mathbb{Z}}[t]e_{0}\oplus{\mathbb{Z}}[t]e_{1}\oplus{\mathbb{Z}}[t]e_{2}.
Lemma 4.6 (The path-extension operator and its stationary part).

The submodule 𝒱\mathcal{V} is TT-invariant. In the ordered basis e0,e1,e2e_{0},e_{1},e_{2}, the restriction of TT has transfer matrix

M=(0t020t011),χ⁡(z)=det(z​I−M)=z3−z2−3​t​z+2​t.M=\begin{pmatrix}0&t&0\\ 2&0&t\\ 0&1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\chi(z)=\det(zI-M)=z^{3}-z^{2}-3tz+2t. (4.13)

Proposition 4.7 (Intrinsic stationary boundary data).

For an open boundary filtration P∙P_{\bullet} on A=U⊕r​UA=U\oplus rU, put

Write y=s−r−2​α​r​sy=s-r-2\alpha rs. Since y2=−2​r​sy^{2}=-2rs and y3=0y^{3}=0,

These quotients measure the change from P∙P_{\bullet} to the enlarged filtration P^i=Pi+r​Pi−2\widehat{P}_{i}=P_{i}+rP_{i-2}, in which multiplication by rr has filtration degree at most two. They give a basis-independent interpretation of the stationary state differences.

4.4 The calculus in summary

Theorem 4.8 (Boundary-state calculus).

Let ff be normalized and nondegenerate, and let DD bound the vertex degrees, with D≥1D\geq 1.

  1. (i)

    Closing. If a bridge ee cuts GG into two marked graphs with boundary states sλs_{\lambda} and sμ′s^{\prime}_{\mu} at ee, then ℋGf=∑λ,μ𝖤⁡(sλ,sμ′)\mathscr{H}^{f}_{G}=\sum_{\lambda,\mu}\mathsf{E}(s_{\lambda},s^{\prime}_{\mu}), with 𝖤\mathsf{E} as in (4.6).

  2. (ii)

    Branching. Let B1,…,BrB_{1},\ldots,B_{r} be incoming marked pieces, pairwise disjoint before attachment, with marked edge variables x1,…,xrx_{1},\ldots,x_{r}. Identify their open leaf endpoints at a new vertex vv, and attach one further edge zz with an open leaf endpoint. The states at zz are obtained by summing, over all tuples of states [pj,qj][p_{j},q_{j}] of the branches, the outgoing states of the local filtration (4.7), multiplied by t∑jpjt^{\sum_{j}p_{j}}. The local computation takes place in an algebra of dimension 2r+12^{r+1} and depends only on the gaps qj−pjq_{j}-p_{j} and on ff modulo ur+2u^{r+2}.

  3. (iii)

    Path extension. If α≠0\alpha\neq 0 and r=1r=1, the rule in (ii) is the operator TT of (4.11).

  4. (iv)

    Gaps. Every state satisfies 2−D≤q−p≤D2-D\leq q-p\leq D.

In particular, the Hilbert series of a tree is computed by rooting it at an edge, starting with the state [0,1][0,1] at each leaf, applying (ii) at each vertex, and closing by (i).

Proof.

Part (i) is (4.6). Part (ii) is the discussion following (4.7), which uses Lemma 4.3 for each branch and the rank formula (4.8); only ff modulo ur+2u^{r+2} enters, because (z−∑jxj)r+2=0(z-\sum_{j}x_{j})^{r+2}=0. Part (iii) is Lemma 4.5, and (iv) is Lemma 4.4. A leaf, regarded as a branch, is a single edge with one open endpoint and has the state [0,1][0,1] (Example 4.2). ∎

4.5 Tail families

Given a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) with a marked vertex v∈Vv\in V, we consider three families of graphs with tails: the straight-tail GnG_{n}, the forked-tail G~n\widetilde{G}_{n}, and the double-edged GnbG^{b}_{n} extensions of GG (Figure 5).

The straight-tail extension GnG_{n}, for n≥0n\geq 0, attaches at vv a path of length nn, with vertices v0=v,v1,…,vnv_{0}=v,v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}. The forked-tail extension G~n\widetilde{G}_{n}, for n≥2n\geq 2, attaches two new leaf edges at the terminal vertex vn−2v_{n-2} of Gn−2G_{n-2}; here v0=vv_{0}=v when n=2n=2. The double-edged extension GnbG_{n}^{b}, for n≥2n\geq 2, is GnG_{n} with one additional edge joining vn−1v_{n-1} to vnv_{n}.

The three families satisfy the same third-order recurrence. For the forked and double-edged families, it follows from identities with the straight-tail series. We use the operator

L⁡(an)=an−an−1−3​t​an−2+2​t​an−3,L(a_{n})=a_{n}-a_{n-1}-3t\,a_{n-2}+2t\,a_{n-3}, (4.18)

whenever the four terms are defined.

Theorem 4.9.

Let GG be a graph with a marked vertex vv. Let Gn,G~nG_{n},\widetilde{G}_{n}, and GnbG^{b}_{n} be the straight, forked and double-edged extensions defined above. Let Hn​(t),H~n​(t),H_{n}(t),\ \widetilde{H}_{n}(t), and Hnb​(t)H^{b}_{n}(t) be the Hilbert series of the corresponding algebras 𝒞Gnf,𝒞G~nf\mathscr{C}^{f}_{G_{n}},\ \mathscr{C}^{f}_{\widetilde{G}_{n}}, and 𝒞Gnbf\mathscr{C}^{f}_{G^{b}_{n}}, where

f=u+α​u2+β​u3+…,α≠0.f=u+\alpha u^{2}+\beta u^{3}+\ldots,\qquad\alpha\neq 0. (4.19)

Then:

  1. (i)

    The straight-tail Hilbert series satisfy the third-order recurrence L⁡(Hn)=0L(H_{n})=0, that is,

    Hn=Hn−1+3​t​Hn−2−2​t​Hn−3,n≥4.H_{n}=H_{n-1}+3tH_{n-2}-2tH_{n-3},\qquad n\geq 4. (4.20)
  2. (ii)

    The forked tail family has the same Hilbert series as the straight tail:

    H~n=Hn,n≥3.\widetilde{H}_{n}=H_{n},\qquad n\geq 3.
  3. (iii)

    For the double-edged family one has

    Hnb=Hn+1−t​Hn−1,n≥2.H_{n}^{b}=H_{n+1}-tH_{n-1},\qquad n\geq 2.

    Consequently the double-edged Hilbert series satisfy the same recurrence L⁡(Hnb)=0L(H^{b}_{n})=0, that is,

    Hnb=Hn−1b+3​t​Hn−2b−2​t​Hn−3b,n≥5.H_{n}^{b}=H_{n-1}^{b}+3tH_{n-2}^{b}-2tH_{n-3}^{b},\qquad n\geq 5.

For a boundary state define two ℤ⁡[t]{\mathbb{Z}}[t]-linear evaluations

𝖼⁡[p,q]=tp+tmin⁡(q,p+1),𝗇⁡[p,q]=tp+tmin⁡(q,p+2).\mathsf{c}[p,q]=t^{p}+t^{\min(q,p+1)},\qquad\mathsf{n}[p,q]=t^{p}+t^{\min(q,p+2)}. (4.21)

They give its contributions to the Hilbert series of the closed filtration Pi+r​Pi−1P_{i}+rP_{i-1} and the augmented filtration Pi+r​Pi−2P_{i}+rP_{i-2}, respectively. To see this, use (4.2): the lift of the quotient class still enters in degree pp, whereas its rr-multiple enters either in degree qq or by multiplying that lift, with the indicated shift.

Lemma 4.10.

For every state s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S},

The three terminal configurations can also be handled uniformly.

Lemma 4.11 (Terminal evaluation).

Let E=B⊗𝐤⁡[r]/(r2)E=B\otimes\mathbf{k}[r]/(r^{2}), where BB is a finite-dimensional commutative unital algebra and dimB=d\dim B=d. Suppose terminal generators define a filtration MℓM_{\ell} on EE with

{(tp+tq)​(1+(d−1)​t),q≤p,tp​(1+d​t+(d−1)​t2),q=p+1,tp​(1+(d−1)​t+d​t2),q≥p+2.\begin{cases}(t^{p}+t^{q})(1+(d-1)t),&q\leq p,\\ t^{p}(1+dt+(d-1)t^{2}),&q=p+1,\\ t^{p}(1+(d-1)t+dt^{2}),&q\geq p+2.\end{cases}

Each equals (4.24). ∎

Lemma 4.12 (The three ends).

For an incoming state ss, the straight two-edge end and the forked end both contribute 3​t​𝖼​(s)+𝗇⁡(s)3t\mathsf{c}(s)+\mathsf{n}(s). The doubled one-edge end contributes 2​t​𝖼​(s)+𝗇⁡(s)2t\mathsf{c}(s)+\mathsf{n}(s).

g1=f⁡(s−r),g2=f⁡(u−s),g3=u.g_{1}=f(s-r),\qquad g_{2}=f(u-s),\qquad g_{3}=u.

For the forked end the generators are h=f⁡(s+u−r),s,uh=f(s+u-r),s,u. Their images modulo rr, together with 11, again form a basis of E/(r)E/(r). The identities

(h−s−u)2=−4​α​r​s​u,h​s=s​u−r​s−2​α​r​s​u,h​u=s​u−r​u−2​α​r​s​u(h-s-u)^{2}=-4\alpha rsu,\qquad hs=su-rs-2\alpha rsu,\qquad hu=su-ru-2\alpha rsu

For the doubled end let s,s′s,s^{\prime} be its two parallel edge variables and put σ=s+s′\sigma=s+s^{\prime}. Then σ2=2​s​s′\sigma^{2}=2ss^{\prime} and σ3=0\sigma^{3}=0. The terminal generators lie in E=𝐤⁡[r,σ]/(r2,σ3)E=\mathbf{k}[r,\sigma]/(r^{2},\sigma^{3}), with d=3d=3, and are

5 Symmetry reductions: parallel edges and attached leaves

The two families considered here admit local reductions that also apply inside larger graphs. A parallel class enters every vertex generator only through the sum of its edge variables. When several leaves are attached at one vertex, their generators give the individual leaf-edge variables. The reduction in this case uses the Jordan decomposition of multiplication by the sum of these variables. We first develop the one-variable calculations and then apply them to leaves attached to an arbitrary graph, retaining the boundary states needed for Section 4.2. Throughout this section,

f⁡(u)=u+∑i≥2αi​ui∈𝐤⁡[[u]].f(u)=u+\sum_{i\geq 2}\alpha_{i}u^{i}\in\mathbf{k}[[u]]. (5.1)

Only finitely many coefficients of ff enter each calculation, since the elements to which ff is applied are nilpotent.

5.1 Parallel edges and truncated polynomials

Proposition 5.1 (Compression of parallel classes).

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be the set of non-loop parallel classes of a graph GG, and let mbm_{b} be the size of the class bb. Orient all edges in each class consistently, and write cv,bc_{v,b} for their common incidence coefficient. This may be done using the filtered reorientation isomorphisms of Section 3. There is an injective graded homomorphism

ΠG:=𝐤[zb:b∈ℬ]/(zbmb+1:b∈ℬ)⟶ΦG,zb⟼∑e∈bφe,\Pi_{G}:=\mathbf{k}[z_{b}:b\in\mathcal{B}]/(z_{b}^{m_{b}+1}:b\in\mathcal{B})\longrightarrow\Phi_{G},\qquad z_{b}\longmapsto\sum_{e\in b}\varphi_{e}, (5.2)

from the parallel-class algebra ΠG\Pi_{G} of GG. Its image contains 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G}, and under this map 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f} is identified, as a filtered algebra, with the subalgebra of ΠG\Pi_{G} generated by

f⁡(∑b∈ℬcv,b​zb),v∈V⁡(G).f\left(\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}c_{v,b}z_{b}\right),\qquad v\in V(G).
Proof.

For 0≤j≤mb0\leq j\leq m_{b}, the jjth power of the sum of the variables in bb is j!j! times their elementary square-free sum of degree jj. These powers are nonzero and have distinct degrees. Products over different classes have distinct multidegrees, so the homomorphism is injective. Each incidence sum XvX_{v}, and hence f⁡(Xv)f(X_{v}), is in its image. Since the displayed generators correspond, so do their word filtrations. Loops do not contribute to the incidence sums. ∎

Thus the ambient dimension can be reduced from 2∑bmb2^{\sum_{b}m_{b}} to ∏b(mb+1)\prod_{b}(m_{b}+1) without changing any filtered rank. In particular, let EmE_{m} be the graph of two vertices joined by mm parallel edges. Setting s=∑e∈E⁡(Em)φes=\sum_{e\in E(E_{m})}\varphi_{e} gives

𝒞Emf=𝐤⁡[s]/(sm+1),𝒞Emf,d=Span⁡{f​(s)i​f​(−s)j:i+j≤d}.\mathscr{C}_{E_{m}}^{f}=\mathbf{k}[s]/(s^{m+1}),\qquad\mathscr{C}_{E_{m}}^{f,d}=\Span\{f(s)^{i}f(-s)^{j}:i+j\leq d\}. (5.3)

For m=0m=0 the algebra is 𝐤\mathbf{k}. The total dimension is m+1m+1 for every nondegenerate ff.

5.1.1 An odd-coordinate normal form

5.1.2 The generic Hilbert series and an exceptional locus

We will use the following elementary Taylor-coefficient calculation both here and for stars.

Lemma 5.3 (Truncated exponential series).

Let λ1,…,λa∈𝐤\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{a}\in\mathbf{k} be distinct, and let r1,…,rar_{1},\ldots,r_{a} be positive integers. Put K=∑jrjK=\sum_{j}r_{j}. For every M≥0M\geq 0, the images of

zi​exp⁡(λj​z),1≤j≤a,0≤i<rj,z^{i}\exp(\lambda_{j}z),\qquad 1\leq j\leq a,\quad 0\leq i<r_{j},

in 𝐤⁡[z]/(zM)\mathbf{k}[z]/(z^{M}) span a space of dimension min⁡(M,K)\min(M,K).

Proof.

For 0≤n<K0\leq n<K, the nnth derivative at zero of zi​exp⁡(λj​z)z^{i}\exp(\lambda_{j}z) is the iith derivative of unu^{n} at u=λju=\lambda_{j}. Thus the transpose of the first KK derivative rows is the Hermite-evaluation map on polynomials of degree less than KK. Its kernel has zeros of total multiplicity KK, and is therefore zero. The first KK rows form an invertible square matrix. Any smaller initial set of rows is independent, while for M≥KM\geq K the columns remain independent. Passing from derivatives to coefficients rescales the rows by nonzero factorials. ∎

Theorem 5.4 (The generic Hilbert series of two-vertex multigraphs).

For all m,d≥0m,d\geq 0, the largest possible cumulative dimension is

dim𝒞Emgen,d=min⁡{⌊m2⌋+1,⌊(d+2)24⌋}+min⁡{⌈m2⌉,⌊(d+1)24⌋}.\begin{split}\dim\mathscr{C}_{E_{m}}^{{\rm gen},d}={}&\min\left\{\left\lfloor\frac{m}{2}\right\rfloor+1,\left\lfloor\frac{(d+2)^{2}}{4}\right\rfloor\right\}\\ &+\min\left\{\left\lceil\frac{m}{2}\right\rceil,\left\lfloor\frac{(d+1)^{2}}{4}\right\rfloor\right\}.\end{split} (5.7)

These maxima are attained simultaneously for every m,dm,d by

f∗​(u)=u+exp⁡(u2)−1.f_{*}(u)=u+\exp(u^{2})-1.

They are the generic cumulative dimensions on the normalized parameter space; the generic Hilbert series is obtained by successive differences.

Proof.

There are Kd=⌊(d+2)2/4⌋K_{d}=\lfloor(d+2)^{2}/4\rfloor pairs (a,j)(a,j) with 2​a+j≤d2a+j\leq d, so the right side of (5.7) is an upper bound by Proposition 5.2. For f∗f_{*} we have B⁡(z)=exp⁡(z)−1B(z)=\exp(z)-1. Triangular changes between the powers of exp⁡(z)−1\exp(z)-1 and exp⁡(z)\exp(z) show that Wd​(B)W_{d}(B) is spanned by

za​exp⁡(j​z),0≤j≤d,0≤a≤⌊d−j2⌋.z^{a}\exp(jz),\qquad 0\leq j\leq d,\quad 0\leq a\leq\left\lfloor\frac{d-j}{2}\right\rfloor.

Lemma 5.3 shows that every truncation of this space has the maximal rank. Apply it also to Wd−1​(B)W_{d-1}(B). For each fixed mm, only finitely many word lengths are needed, and the matrix entries are polynomials in the coefficients of ff through degree mm. The simultaneously attained maxima therefore hold on a nonempty Zariski open set. ∎

For completeness, the small values can be stated without any genericity assumption.

Proposition 5.7 (The untruncated plane equation).

For ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2, the kernel of 𝐤⁡[A,B]→𝐤⁡[s]\mathbf{k}[A,B]\to\mathbf{k}[s], A↦a⁡(s)A\mapsto a(s), B↦b⁡(s)B\mapsto b(s), is generated by

A2​r−∑j=0r−1A2​r−2​j−2​B2​j+1if ​ℓ=2​r,A^{2r}-\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}A^{2r-2j-2}B^{2j+1}\quad\text{if }\ell=2r, (5.9)

For odd ℓ\ell, use a=s⁡(1+b)a=s(1+b), invert 1+B1+B, and put s=A/(1+B)s=A/(1+B). Equation (5.10) then becomes B=∑j=1rs2​jB=\sum_{j=1}^{r}s^{2j}; its polynomial has no factor 1+B1+B, so the same argument applies.

The highest total-degree terms of these equations are respectively AℓA^{\ell} and BℓB^{\ell}. A product with the defining equation has degree exactly ℓ\ell plus the degree of its multiplier. Let AA be a finite-dimensional standard graded algebra, let ℓ∈A(1)\ell\in A^{(1)}, and choose a homogeneous multiplication-string basis

A homogeneous string basis is the graded Jordan decomposition of multiplication by ℓ\ell, equivalently the decomposition into shifted cyclic modules over 𝐤⁡[ℓ]\mathbf{k}[\ell]. Since AA is standard graded, the ddth filtered space is

∑j+k≤df​(ℓ)k​A(≤j).\sum_{j+k\leq d}f(\ell)^{k}A^{(\leq j)}.

For every normalized nondegenerate ff and every N≥0N\geq 0,

5.3 The symmetric-group decomposition

The symmetric-group action refines the numerical star formula to a representation-valued Hilbert series. The group ΣN\Sigma_{N} acts on ΦN\Phi_{N} by permuting the edge variables and commutes with the three operators of Proposition 5.10. Thus each primitive space WpW_{p} is a ΣN\Sigma_{N}-module.

Proposition 5.14 (Symmetric-group and 𝔰​𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_{2} structure).

The modules WpW_{p}, 0≤p≤⌊N/2⌋0\leq p\leq\lfloor N/2\rfloor, are absolutely irreducible and pairwise nonisomorphic, of dimensions

dimWp=(Np)−(Np−1)=(Np)​N−2​p+1N−p+1.\dim W_{p}=\binom{N}{p}-\binom{N}{p-1}=\binom{N}{p}\frac{N-2p+1}{N-p+1}. (5.26)

The homogeneous pieces decompose as

ΦN(k)≃⨁p=0min⁡(k,N−k)Wp,ΦN(k)≃ΦN(N−k).\Phi_{N}^{(k)}\simeq\bigoplus_{p=0}^{\min(k,N-k)}W_{p},\qquad\Phi_{N}^{(k)}\simeq\Phi_{N}^{(N-k)}. (5.27)

If VjV_{j} denotes the (j+1)(j+1)-dimensional simple 𝔰​𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_{2}-module, then

ΦN≃⨁p=0⌊N/2⌋Wp⊗VN−2​pas a ​ΣN×𝔰​𝔩2​-module.\Phi_{N}\simeq\bigoplus_{p=0}^{\lfloor N/2\rfloor}W_{p}\otimes V_{N-2p}\quad\text{as a }\Sigma_{N}\times\mathfrak{sl}_{2}\text{-module}. (5.28)

Moreover, in the representation ring of ΣN\Sigma_{N},

∑d≥0[𝒞SN+1f,d/𝒞SN+1f,d−1]​td=∑p=0⌊N/2⌋[Wp]​tp​hN−2​pf​(t).\sum_{d\geq 0}[\mathscr{C}_{S_{N+1}}^{f,d}/\mathscr{C}_{S_{N+1}}^{f,d-1}]t^{d}=\sum_{p=0}^{\lfloor N/2\rfloor}[W_{p}]t^{p}h_{N-2p}^{f}(t). (5.29)
Proof.

The complement map on subsets gives the second assertion in (5.27), and the first follows already from (5.19). To prove irreducibility, work first over an algebraic closure. For permutation modules on finite sets X,YX,Y, the dimension of the equivariant Hom space is the number of orbits on X×YX\times Y. A pair of subsets of sizes i,j≤N/2i,j\leq N/2 is classified by the size of their intersection. Hence

⟨ΦN(i),ΦN(j)⟩:=dimHomΣN⁡(ΦN(i),ΦN(j))=min⁡(i,j)+1.\left\langle\Phi_{N}^{(i)},\Phi_{N}^{(j)}\right\rangle:=\dim\Hom_{\Sigma_{N}}(\Phi_{N}^{(i)},\Phi_{N}^{(j)})=\min(i,j)+1. (5.30)

In the representation ring, [Wp]=[ΦN(p)]−[ΦN(p−1)][W_{p}]=[\Phi_{N}^{(p)}]-[\Phi_{N}^{(p-1)}], where ΦN(−1)=0\Phi_{N}^{(-1)}=0. Taking successive differences of (5.30) in both indices gives ⟨Wp,Wq⟩=δp​q\langle W_{p},W_{q}\rangle=\delta_{pq}. The WpW_{p} are actual modules, and representations of a finite group in characteristic zero are semisimple; they are therefore irreducible and pairwise nonisomorphic. They are defined as kernels of the same operators over 𝐤\mathbf{k}, so this proves absolute irreducibility there. (In the notation of [6], WpW_{p} is the Specht module S(N−p,p)S^{(N-p,p)}, realized as a kernel intersection.)

The lowest-weight space of each string is WpW_{p}, and the commuting 𝔰​𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_{2}-action generates VN−2​pV_{N-2p}. This proves (5.28). Finally, the star filtration is ΣN\Sigma_{N}-invariant, and (5.22) is equivariant, with trivial group action on PN−2​pP_{N-2p}. Taking classes of successive quotients proves (5.29). ∎

Each summand in (5.28) has the consistently graded form

Wpdegree ​p→𝑠s​Wpdegree ​p+1→𝑠⋯→𝑠sN−2​p​Wpdegree ​N−p.\underset{\text{degree }p}{W_{p}}\xrightarrow{\ s\ }\underset{\text{degree }p+1}{sW_{p}}\xrightarrow{\ s\ }\cdots\xrightarrow{\ s\ }\underset{\text{degree }N-p}{s^{N-2p}W_{p}}.

The raising operator EE shifts the word filtration by one, so only the ΣN\Sigma_{N}-part of (5.28) is used in (5.29).

5.4 Several attached leaves and boundary states

Let (G,v)(G,v) be an arbitrary marked graph, and let Gv+NG_{v}^{+N} be obtained by attaching NN new leaves at vv. Put

AG,v;M=𝒞G⊗𝐤⁡[x]/(xM+1)(M≥0),A_{G,v;M}=\mathscr{C}_{G}\otimes\mathbf{k}[x]/(x^{M+1})\qquad(M\geq 0), (5.31)

and endow it with the word filtration AG,v;Mf,dA_{G,v;M}^{f,d} generated by

x,f⁡(Xv+x),f⁡(Xu)(u≠v).x,\qquad f(X_{v}+x),\qquad f(X_{u})\quad(u\neq v). (5.32)

These elements generate the entire underlying algebra: formal inversion recovers Xv+xX_{v}+x and all the other XuX_{u}, and xx is included. Let JG,v;Mf​(t)J_{G,v;M}^{f}(t) be its Hilbert series.

Theorem 5.15 (Reduction for attached leaves).

For every G,v,NG,v,N and normalized nondegenerate ff,

ℋGv+Nf​(t)=∑p=0⌊N/2⌋mN,p​tp​JG,v;N−2​pf​(t).\mathscr{H}_{G_{v}^{+N}}^{f}(t)=\sum_{p=0}^{\lfloor N/2\rfloor}m_{N,p}\,t^{p}J_{G,v;N-2p}^{f}(t). (5.33)

More precisely, there is a ΣN\Sigma_{N}-equivariant decomposition of filtered vector spaces

𝒞Gv+Nf,d≃⨁p=0⌊N/2⌋Wp⊗AG,v;N−2​pf,d−p.\mathscr{C}_{G_{v}^{+N}}^{f,d}\simeq\bigoplus_{p=0}^{\lfloor N/2\rfloor}W_{p}\otimes A_{G,v;N-2p}^{f,d-p}. (5.34)

The group permutes the new leaves and acts trivially on each factor AG,v;N−2​pA_{G,v;N-2p}.

Proof.

Orient the new edges away from vv, write their variables as φ1,…,φN\varphi_{1},\ldots,\varphi_{N}, and put s=∑iφis=\sum_{i}\varphi_{i}. As an unfiltered algebra,

𝒞Gv+N=𝒞G⊗ΦN.\mathscr{C}_{G_{v}^{+N}}=\mathscr{C}_{G}\otimes\Phi_{N}.

Indeed, the generators at the new leaves recover all the new edge variables, while subtracting ss from the modified incidence sum at vv recovers XvX_{v}. The filtered space is the sum of

ΦN(≤a)​f​(Xv+s)k​∏u≠vf​(Xu)iu,a+k+∑u≠viu≤d.\Phi_{N}^{(\leq a)}f(X_{v}+s)^{k}\prod_{u\neq v}f(X_{u})^{i_{u}},\qquad a+k+\sum_{u\neq v}i_{u}\leq d.

Apply (5.19) to the factor ΦN\Phi_{N}. On the string starting in degree pp, multiplication by ss is multiplication by xx in PN−2​pP_{N-2p}. Every polynomial in ss with coefficients in 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G} preserves this decomposition, so f⁡(Xv+s)f(X_{v}+s) acts as f⁡(Xv+x)f(X_{v}+x). The starting degree contributes pp, and all other generators act on the factor 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G}. This gives (5.34). It is equivariant by Proposition 5.14; taking dimensions of successive quotients gives (5.33). ∎

When GG has one vertex, JG,v;Mf=hMfJ_{G,v;M}^{f}=h_{M}^{f}, and the theorem reduces to the star formula. In general, the filtration on AG,v;MA_{G,v;M} is not the tensor-product filtration of 𝒞Gf\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f} and PMP_{M}: the generator f⁡(Xv+x)f(X_{v}+x) depends on both factors. Instead of working with the 2N2^{N}-dimensional algebra ΦN\Phi_{N}, the theorem reduces the calculation to ⌊N/2⌋+1\lfloor N/2\rfloor+1 filtered algebras AG,v;N−2​pA_{G,v;N-2p}, with one-variable factors of dimension at most N+1N+1 and explicit multiplicities. There is no restriction on cycles in GG.

Corollary 5.16 (Compatibility with boundary states).

Suppose GG has a marked leaf edge rr, with leaf vertex aa, and that v≠av\neq a. Form the open filtration by omitting the generator at aa. The decomposition (5.34) also holds for this open filtration and respects projection modulo rr and multiplication by its edge variable. Consequently the boundary states of Gv+NG_{v}^{+N} are obtained from the open filtrations on AG,v;N−2​pA_{G,v;N-2p} with generators (5.32), omitting the generator at aa, by shifting both birth degrees by pp and repeating them mN,pm_{N,p} times.

Proof.

Omitting the generator at aa does not change the string decomposition of ΦN\Phi_{N}. Projection modulo rr and multiplication by φr\varphi_{r} act on 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G}, so they preserve this direct-sum decomposition. Thus the image filtration, the kernel-coefficient filtration, and all their intersections decompose into the same summands, with both indices shifted by pp. Taking their joint birth multiplicities as in Lemma 4.1 proves the statement. These open filtrations on AG,v;MA_{G,v;M} are exhaustive: the missing edge variable can be recovered from the component relation among the XuX_{u}, using xx and the inverse series applied to the retained generators. ∎

This supplies boundary-state sums for the path-extension and gluing rules of Section 4.2, not just closed Hilbert series. Leaves attached at several vertices can be treated simultaneously: take the independent string decompositions, multiply their multiplicities, add their initial degrees, and replace the generator at each attachment vertex vv by f⁡(Xv+xv)f(X_{v}+x_{v}).

The two symmetry reductions now have a common description. In a parallel class, every graph generator depends only on the sum of the edge variables, so only the invariant string 1,s,…,sN1,s,\ldots,s^{N} occurs. For leaves attached at one vertex, the individual leaf-edge variables are generators, and all the strings of (5.19) occur. A parallel class of size m>1m>1 has boundary algebra 𝐤⁡[z]/(zm+1)\mathbf{k}[z]/(z^{m+1}) rather than the dual numbers, so the boundary states [p,q][p,q] of Section 4 do not describe it. Ordinary marked leaf edges elsewhere in the graph retain that boundary calculus.

5.5 Generic stars and distinguished parameters

The ranks rm,dfr_{m,d}^{f} of the one-variable filtrations in (5.17) give particularly simple comparisons between the exponential and inverse-polynomial parameters. They also exhibit how the two symmetry reductions detect different identities of the same function.

Proposition 5.17 (The generic Hilbert series of stars).

For all m,d≥0m,d\geq 0,

rm,dexp⁡(u)−1=min⁡{m+1,(d+22)}.r_{m,d}^{\exp(u)-1}=\min\left\{m+1,\binom{d+2}{2}\right\}. (5.35)

The exponential therefore has the generic Hilbert series on every star. In the star formula (5.21), the generic local coefficients are

[td]​hmgen=min⁡{m+1,(d+22)}−min⁡{m+1,(d+12)}.[t^{d}]h_{m}^{\rm gen}=\min\left\{m+1,\binom{d+2}{2}\right\}-\min\left\{m+1,\binom{d+1}{2}\right\}.

For any ff, there are only K=(d+22)K=\binom{d+2}{2} products of degree at most dd, giving the stated upper bound. For f=exp⁡(u)−1f=\exp(u)-1, triangular changes of generators give the span of

xi​exp⁡(j​x),0≤j≤d,0≤i≤d−j.x^{i}\exp(jx),\qquad 0\leq j\leq d,\quad 0\leq i\leq d-j.

Apply Lemma 5.3, with multiplicities d−j+1d-j+1, to obtain (5.35). The positive shifted sum in Theorem 5.11 shows that every cumulative star rank attains its maximum. As in Theorem 5.4, these simultaneously attained maxima are the generic values. ∎

Corollary 5.18 (Inversion and quadratic inverses on stars).

For every nondegenerate ff and every star SnS_{n},

ℋSnf=ℋSnf−1.\mathscr{H}_{S_{n}}^{f}=\mathscr{H}_{S_{n}}^{f^{-1}}. (5.36)

If f−1​(u)=u+c​u2f^{-1}(u)=u+cu^{2} with c≠0c\neq 0, then

rm,df=min⁡{m+1,2​d+1}.r_{m,d}^{f}=\min\{m+1,2d+1\}. (5.37)

Such a function is nongeneric on every SnS_{n} with n≥6n\geq 6; its quadratic Hilbert coefficient is one less than the generic one.

Proof.

The coordinate y=f⁡(x)y=f(x) in PmP_{m} changes the generators x,f⁡(x)x,f(x) to f−1​(y),yf^{-1}(y),y. Hence the local ranks for ff and f−1f^{-1} agree, and (5.36) follows from Theorem 5.11. For a quadratic inverse the new generators span y,y2y,y^{2}, giving (5.37). At total filtration degree two in the star decomposition, only the unshifted Pn−1P_{n-1} summand differs from the generic value: for n≥6n\geq 6 its cumulative rank is five rather than six. The other summands have at most one unit of word degree left and give the same ranks. The first filtered dimensions are also equal, proving the one-unit coefficient difference. ∎

The inversion identity is special to stars. It fails already for the tree E6\mathrm{E}_{6}: the function f=u+u2+2​u3f=u+u^{2}+2u^{3} lies in the exceptional subcubic cell, whereas f−1=u−u2+O⁡(u4)f^{-1}=u-u^{2}+O(u^{4}) is generic, and E6\mathrm{E}_{6} separates the two (Table 3 and Theorem 6.7). The distinction from the parallel-edge filtrations is explicit: stars compare xx with f⁡(x)f(x), whereas parallel edges compare f⁡(x)f(x) with f⁡(−x)f(-x). The exponential has maximal star ranks, but the identity (1+f⁡(x))​(1+f⁡(−x))=1(1+f(x))(1+f(-x))=1 gives a quadratic relation for parallel edges. Proposition 5.17 thus answers [13, Problem 3] for stars: the exponential is generic on every star. Further parameter comparisons appear in Section 6.8.

6 Parameter spaces and Hilbert stratification

The rank description gives a finite Hilbert stratification for each fixed graph. Boundary states yield a stronger algebraic theorem: one finite partition works for all trees of bounded maximum degree. The explicit partitions for maximum degrees three and four use exact symbolic local rank calculations. The finite-field computations of Section 6.10 have a different status, explained there.

6.1 Determinantal strata and specialization

For a graph GG, put D=max⁡(1,Δ⁡(G))D=\max(1,\Delta(G)) and let

𝒜G=𝒜D={u+∑j=2Daj​uj}≃𝔸𝐤D−1.{\mathscr{A}}_{G}={\mathscr{A}}_{D}=\left\{u+\sum_{j=2}^{D}a_{j}u^{j}\right\}\simeq\mathbb{A}^{D-1}_{\mathbf{k}}. (6.1)

Thus 𝒜G{\mathscr{A}}_{G} parametrizes normalized polynomially generated filtrations; if GG has no non-loop edges, its only relevant parameter is uu. All algebras have the same underlying vector space 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G}. For a polynomial H⁡(t)=∑hi​tiH(t)=\sum h_{i}t^{i}, let

SGH={f∈𝒜G:ℋGf=H}S_{G}^{H}=\{f\in{\mathscr{A}}_{G}:\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f}=H\}

be its Hilbert stratum. We use the cumulative partial order

H⪯cumH′⟺∑j=0i[tj]H≤∑j=0i[tj]H′for every i.H\preceq_{\rm cum}H^{\prime}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sum_{j=0}^{i}[t^{j}]H\leq\sum_{j=0}^{i}[t^{j}]H^{\prime}\quad\text{for every }i. (6.2)

Cumulative dominance implies the corresponding lexicographic inequality, but the converse need not hold; lexicographic order extends this partial order.

Choose a homogeneous basis of 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G}, and set A=𝐤⁡[a2,…,aD]A=\mathbf{k}[a_{2},\ldots,a_{D}]. The universal generators are Yv=Xv+∑j=2Daj​Xvj∈𝒞G⊗AY_{v}=X_{v}+\sum_{j=2}^{D}a_{j}X_{v}^{j}\in\mathscr{C}_{G}\otimes A. Let MG,iM_{G,i} be the matrix of all products of at most ii such generators, in the fixed basis. Its entries are polynomials in AA, and

rG,i​(f):=dim𝒞Gf,i=rk⁡MG,i​(f).r_{G,i}(f):=\dim\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f,i}=\rank M_{G,i}(f). (6.3)

Only 0≤i≤N0\leq i\leq N is needed, where NN is the number of non-loop edges.

Theorem 6.1 (Hilbert strata).

For a fixed graph GG:

  1. (i)

    Each cumulative dimension rG,ir_{G,i} is lower semicontinuous. Every SGHS_{G}^{H} is locally closed, and only finitely many are nonempty.

  2. (ii)

    If f∈SGH¯f\in\overline{S_{G}^{H}}, then ℋGf⪯cumH\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f}\preceq_{\rm cum}H. There is a nonempty Zariski open stratum whose Hilbert function is simultaneously maximal in every cumulative degree.

  3. (iii)

    On every reduced Hilbert stratum, the universal filtration spaces are subbundles of the constant bundle 𝒞G⊗𝒪\mathscr{C}_{G}\otimes\mathcal{O}, and their successive quotients are locally free. They form a finite locally free family of associated graded algebras.

Proof.

The locus rG,i≤rr_{G,i}\leq r is cut out by the (r+1)(r+1)-minors of MG,iM_{G,i} (see [3] for determinantal loci). This proves lower semicontinuity. An equality of ranks is an intersection of an open and a closed condition. Intersecting these conditions over the finitely many indices proves (i). All minors vanishing on a stratum vanish on its closure, proving the specialization assertion. Each matrix attains its maximum rank on a nonempty open set; these finitely many open sets have nonempty intersection since 𝒜G{\mathscr{A}}_{G} is irreducible. This is the asserted generic stratum. On a reduced rank-constant locus, all minors above the specified rank vanish as regular functions. Locally choose a nonvanishing maximal minor. Row and column operations reduce the matrix to a block identity with a zero complementary block, showing that its image is a subbundle. The same argument for inclusions of successive filtration spaces gives locally free quotients, compatible with base change. Multiplication in the constant algebra induces the associated graded algebra structure. ∎

Remark 6.2.

Using the images in a fixed ambient vector space is essential. Freeness of abstract filtration modules alone does not imply constancy of their images after specialization. For example, in 𝐤⁡[s,z]/(z3)\mathbf{k}[s,z]/(z^{3}) the algebra generators z,s​z2z,sz^{2} give the free module F1=𝐤⁡[s]​{1,z,s​z2}F_{1}=\mathbf{k}[s]\{1,z,sz^{2}\}, but its image in the fibre has dimension three for s≠0s\neq 0 and two for s=0s=0. The matrices in (6.3) avoid this base-change issue.

6.2 Scaling and inverse-series coordinates

Proposition 6.3.

The action

f⁡(u)⟼fε​(u)=ε−1​f​(ε​u)=u+∑j=2Dεj−1​aj​uj,ε∈𝐤∗,f(u)\longmapsto f_{\varepsilon}(u)=\varepsilon^{-1}f(\varepsilon u)=u+\sum_{j=2}^{D}\varepsilon^{j-1}a_{j}u^{j},\qquad\varepsilon\in\mathbf{k}^{*}, (6.4)

preserves the filtered isomorphism class and hence each Hilbert stratum. The point uu lies in the closure of every nonempty stratum. Consequently ℋGu⪯cumℋGf\mathscr{H}_{G}^{u}\preceq_{\rm cum}\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f} for all ff, and the largest possible Hilbert degree is NN, attained at f=uf=u.

Proof.

Scaling every edge variable by ε\varepsilon sends f⁡(Xv)f(X_{v}) to f⁡(ε​Xv)=ε​fε​(Xv)f(\varepsilon X_{v})=\varepsilon f_{\varepsilon}(X_{v}), which gives the filtered isomorphism. The displayed orbit map extends to ε=0\varepsilon=0, with value uu. Apply Theorem 6.1 to its closure. The general degree bound is NN, and the highest-power calculation (2.28) shows that 𝒞G(N)≠0\mathscr{C}_{G}^{(N)}\neq 0 when N>0N>0; the edgeless case has series 11. ∎

The weights are 1,2,…,D−11,2,\ldots,D-1. The action need not be free: the stabilizer of a nonzero parameter is the group of roots of unity whose order divides every j−1j-1 with aj≠0a_{j}\neq 0. Over an algebraic closure, for D≥2D\geq 2, the quotient of 𝒜G∖{u}{\mathscr{A}}_{G}\setminus\{u\} is the weighted projective space 𝐏⁡(1,2,…,D−1)\mathbf{P}(1,2,\ldots,D-1), with its induced Hilbert partition. The point uu has the least Hilbert function, but its stratum need not be a singleton: for two-vertex multigraphs every odd ff has the same Hilbert series as uu. For D=1D=1 the punctured parameter space is empty.

The determinantal ideals above are weighted homogeneous. Indeed, in a homogeneous basis of 𝒞G\mathscr{C}_{G}, the coefficient of edge degree kk in a product of ss generators has parameter weight k−sk-s. Every term in a minor therefore has the same weight (the sum of its row degrees minus the sum of its column lengths).

For relations it is often preferable to use the coefficients of g=f−1g=f^{-1}, truncated modulo uD+1u^{D+1}. Inversion is a polynomial involution of 𝒜D{\mathscr{A}}_{D} commuting with scaling. Explicitly,

f⁡(u)=u+α​u2+β​u3+γ​u4+⋯,g⁡(u)=u−α​u2+(2​α2−β)​u3+(−5​α3+5​α​β−γ)​u4+⋯.\begin{split}f(u)&=u+\alpha u^{2}+\beta u^{3}+\gamma u^{4}+\cdots,\\ g(u)&=u-\alpha u^{2}+(2\alpha^{2}-\beta)u^{3}+(-5\alpha^{3}+5\alpha\beta-\gamma)u^{4}+\cdots.\end{split} (6.5)

This is a change of parameter coordinates; in general ℋGf≠ℋGf−1\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f}\neq\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f^{-1}} (see the discussion after Corollary 5.18). In particular, on the chart α≠0\alpha\neq 0, normalizing the quadratic coefficient to one identifies the actual cubic coordinate λ=β/α2\lambda=\beta/\alpha^{2} with 2−λ2-\lambda in normalized inverse coordinates. In all statements of this section, parameters refer to the actual function Yv=f⁡(Xv)Y_{v}=f(X_{v}).

6.3 Small parameter spaces

The two-vertex and star families of Section 5 give immediate examples. For E2,E3E_{2},E_{3} the strata are α=0\alpha=0 and α≠0\alpha\neq 0; for E4E_{4} they are α=γ=0\alpha=\gamma=0, α=0,γ≠0\alpha=0,\gamma\neq 0, and α≠0\alpha\neq 0. For S4S_{4} there are the origin and its complement. For S5S_{5} the four strata are successively determined by whether α\alpha, then β\beta, then γ\gamma is the first nonzero coefficient. Their series are those of Corollary 5.13. Two examples with non-coordinate exceptional loci will be useful.

Proposition 6.4.

Let f=u+α​u2+β​u3f=u+\alpha u^{2}+\beta u^{3}. For the triangle with one doubled edge, the complete Hilbert partition is

conditionℋGfα=β=01+2​t+3​t2+3​t3+t4(α,β)≠(0,0),α⁡(β−2​α2)​(3​β−2​α2)=01+3​t+4​t2+2​t3α⁡(β−2​α2)​(3​β−2​α2)≠01+3​t+5​t2+t3\begin{array}[]{c|l}\text{condition}&\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f}\\ \hline\cr\alpha=\beta=0&1+2t+3t^{2}+3t^{3}+t^{4}\\ (\alpha,\beta)\neq(0,0),\quad\alpha(\beta-2\alpha^{2})(3\beta-2\alpha^{2})=0&1+3t+4t^{2}+2t^{3}\\ \alpha(\beta-2\alpha^{2})(3\beta-2\alpha^{2})\neq 0&1+3t+5t^{2}+t^{3}\end{array}

For G=K4G=K_{4} it is

conditionℋK4fα=β=01+3​t+6​t2+10​t3+11​t4+6​t5+t6α=0,β≠01+4​t+9​t2+12​t3+8​t4+3​t5+t6α≠0,β=2​α21+4​t+9​t2+15​t3+5​t4+3​t5+t6α≠0,β≠2​α21+4​t+10​t2+14​t3+5​t4+3​t5+t6.\begin{array}[]{c|l}\text{condition}&\mathscr{H}_{K_{4}}^{f}\\ \hline\cr\alpha=\beta=0&1+3t+6t^{2}+10t^{3}+11t^{4}+6t^{5}+t^{6}\\ \alpha=0,\ \beta\neq 0&1+4t+9t^{2}+12t^{3}+8t^{4}+3t^{5}+t^{6}\\ \alpha\neq 0,\ \beta=2\alpha^{2}&1+4t+9t^{2}+15t^{3}+5t^{4}+3t^{5}+t^{6}\\ \alpha\neq 0,\ \beta\neq 2\alpha^{2}&1+4t+10t^{2}+14t^{3}+5t^{4}+3t^{5}+t^{6}.\end{array}
Proof.

Scaling reduces the nonzero-quadratic locus to f=u+u2+λ​u3f=u+u^{2}+\lambda u^{3}. Construct the matrices (6.3) in the square-free edge basis. Exact elimination over ℚ⁡(λ)\mathbb{Q}(\lambda) gives the generic series in the tables. For the doubled triangle the only factors inverted in this elimination, up to constants, are λ−2\lambda-2, λ−2/3\lambda-2/3, and λ−10/3\lambda-10/3. Recomputing from the original generators at these three values gives the second row at 2,2/32,2/3 and the generic row at 10/310/3. For K4K_{4} the excluded values are 2,2/3,4/3,8/32,2/3,4/3,8/3, and only 22 changes the ranks. The remaining cases α=0\alpha=0 reduce, after a field extension, to β=0\beta=0 or 11 and give the displayed series. All these are exact rational calculations; the complete matrices and elimination procedure are specified by the executable certificates in Appendix A. For the locus β=2​α2\beta=2\alpha^{2}, the extra relation also follows directly from

∑vYv−α​∑vYv2=(β−2​α2)​∑vXv3\sum_{v}Y_{v}-\alpha\sum_{v}Y_{v}^{2}=(\beta-2\alpha^{2})\sum_{v}X_{v}^{3} (6.6)

on every subcubic graph. ∎

6.4 A common stratification for bounded-degree trees

For a marked tree, a boundary state records more information than its closed Hilbert series. The gap bound of Lemma 4.4 turns this into a finite set of local types for bounded valency.

The branching columns (4.7), intersection ranks (4.8), and closing rule (4.6) have already been established in Section 4.2. We apply them uniformly in the coefficients of ff.

Theorem 6.5 (Uniform parameter partition for trees).

Fix D≥1D\geq 1. There is a finite partition of 𝒜D{\mathscr{A}}_{D} into locally closed subsets on each of which ℋTf\mathscr{H}_{T}^{f} is constant in ff simultaneously for every finite tree TT of maximum degree at most DD. The partition is determined by finitely many polynomial coefficient matrices with at most 2D2^{D} rows, independently of the size of TT.

Proof.

For D=1D=1 every component is an edge or an isolated vertex, and the assertion is immediate. For D≥2D\geq 2, root a tree across an edge. A leaf gives [0,1][0,1]. Each rooted branch, with its outgoing edge and an open auxiliary leaf, has maximum degree at most DD. By Lemma 4.4, every gap lies in {2−D,…,D}\{2-D,\ldots,D\}. There are therefore only finitely many normalized input tuples for vertices of valency at most DD. For each tuple, form the columns (4.7), their zz-multiples, and the concatenations in (4.8). Their entries are polynomials in the coefficients of ff and their row space has dimension at most 2r+1≤2D2^{r+1}\leq 2^{D}. There are only finitely many relative filtration thresholds. Partition 𝒜D{\mathscr{A}}_{D} by all these finitely many ranks. Every part is locally closed and all its local transition tables are fixed. Induction over the tree fixes every boundary-state sum, and (4.6) fixes its Hilbert series. The one-vertex tree has series 11 and requires no closing step. ∎

Thus equality of the pointwise profiles f↦ℋTff\mapsto\mathscr{H}_{T}^{f} of two bounded-degree trees can be decided by finitely many tests, using one geometric representative from each nonempty cell of the common partition. Individual trees may merge some of its parts.

For D=3D=3, the common partition has a particularly simple form. Put ej=[0,j]e_{j}=[0,j], 0≤j≤30\leq j\leq 3, and normalize α=1\alpha=1 when α≠0\alpha\neq 0, writing λ=β/α2\lambda=\beta/\alpha^{2}. The bivalent rule is

Theorem 6.7 (The four subcubic cells).

For every tree of maximum degree at most three, its Hilbert series depends on f=u+α​u2+β​u3f=u+\alpha u^{2}+\beta u^{3} only through the following four cells:

On α≠0\alpha\neq 0, a leaf starts with e1e_{1}, and the bivalent path-extension rule and (6.7) preserve the span of e0,e1,e2,e3e_{0},e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}. Their only distinction in the parameter is λ=2\lambda=2. Induction and (4.6) prove constancy on the two cells. On α=0\alpha=0, the nonzero cubic coefficient can be normalized to one after a field extension, which does not change dimensions. Finally, the tree E6=T⁡(1,2,2)\mathrm{E}_{6}=T(1,2,2) has four distinct series on these four cells (Table 3; the values follow from the path-extension and branching rules above). Hence no two cells can be merged for all subcubic trees. ∎

Remark 6.8.

At λ=2\lambda=2, the span of e0,e1,e2e_{0},e_{1},e_{2} is closed under both path extension and branching. Thus no gap-three state is created in a subcubic tree. This gives a boundary interpretation of the inverse-quadratic locus [u3]​f−1=0[u^{3}]f^{-1}=0 and its relation to the stationary contribution in Theorem 4.16.

6.6 Which trees detect the exceptional subcubic cell?

An individual tree need not distinguish all four cells of Theorem 6.7. We now characterize when the two nonzero-quadratic cells have different Hilbert series. For a subcubic tree TT, write

HTg=ℋTu+u2,HTs=ℋTu+u2+2​u3.H_{T}^{\mathrm{g}}=\mathscr{H}_{T}^{\,u+u^{2}},\qquad H_{T}^{\mathrm{s}}=\mathscr{H}_{T}^{\,u+u^{2}+2u^{3}}.

The superscripts denote the generic and special nonzero-quadratic cells. At a vertex of TT, each incident branch is considered with that vertex as its open leaf endpoint. Its boundary-state sum is the element of 𝒮\mathcal{S} defined in (4.5); it does not include the generator of the vertex at which the branches meet.

Proposition 6.9 (Graphical detection of the exceptional cell).

Let TT be a finite tree of maximum degree at most three. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    HTg≠HTsH_{T}^{\mathrm{g}}\neq H_{T}^{\mathrm{s}};

  2. (ii)

    TT has a trivalent vertex with at least two neighbors that are not leaves;

  3. (iii)

    TT contains as a subtree the six-vertex tree with arm lengths 1,2,21,2,2 (the tree of type E6\mathrm{E}_{6}).

Moreover,

HTg−HTs=t2​(1−t)​CT​(t),CT​(t)∈ℤ≥0​[t].H_{T}^{\mathrm{g}}-H_{T}^{\mathrm{s}}=t^{2}(1-t)C_{T}(t),\qquad C_{T}(t)\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}[t]. (6.9)

If the equivalent conditions hold, then CT​(0)=1C_{T}(0)=1; in particular,

[t2]​HTg−[t2]​HTs=1.[t^{2}]H_{T}^{\mathrm{g}}-[t^{2}]H_{T}^{\mathrm{s}}=1. (6.10)
Proof.

The equivalence of (ii) and (iii) follows by extending two of the three edges at the trivalent vertex by one edge each. In a tree the additional vertices are distinct and introduce no further edges.

Let 𝖡g\mathsf{B}_{\mathrm{g}} and 𝖡s\mathsf{B}_{\mathrm{s}} be the two branching operations in (6.7), and put Δ​𝖡=𝖡g−𝖡s\Delta\mathsf{B}=\mathsf{B}_{\mathrm{g}}-\mathsf{B}_{\mathrm{s}}. Their only nonzero differences on unordered pairs of basis states are

Δ​𝖡​(e2,e2)\displaystyle\Delta\mathsf{B}(e_{2},e_{2}) =e3−e2+t2​(e0−e1).\displaystyle=e_{3}-e_{2}+t^{2}(e_{0}-e_{1}).

(6.11)

Thus the three incident branches can be treated symmetrically, although the branching notation designates one outgoing edge.

For this proof, assign to each trivalent vertex a function fv∈{fg,fs}f_{v}\in\{f_{\mathrm{g}},f_{\mathrm{s}}\}, where fg=u+u2f_{\mathrm{g}}=u+u^{2} and fs=u+u2+2​u3f_{\mathrm{s}}=u+u^{2}+2u^{3}. Replacing fv=fsf_{v}=f_{\mathrm{s}} by fv=fgf_{v}=f_{\mathrm{g}} at a single trivalent vertex, while fixing all other choices, therefore changes the closed Hilbert series by

by (6.11). Summing over a succession of such replacements proves (6.9).

First assign fsf_{\mathrm{s}} to every trivalent vertex. The constant term of the boundary-state sum of a branch is e1e_{1} if the branch is a single edge and e2e_{2} otherwise. Here the constant term means evaluation at t=0t=0 in the state module. For the smallest tree satisfying these conditions, the difference is exactly t2​(1−t)t^{2}(1-t):

Proof of Theorem 6.10.

We follow the proof of Theorem 6.5, keeping track of the parameters. On α≠0\alpha\neq 0 normalize α=1\alpha=1 by scaling and write f=u+u2+b​u3+c​u4f=u+u^{2}+bu^{3}+cu^{4}.

Iteration of the local branching rules. Start from the leaf state, of gap one. For every multiset of at most three incoming gaps that has occurred, form the local columns (4.7) and compute the ranks (4.8) by exact elimination over ℚ⁡(b,c)\mathbb{Q}(b,c), recording every factor by which a pivot is divided. Add the outgoing gaps and repeat until no new gap appears. This gives the gaps 0,…,40,\ldots,4, fifty-five local tables, and only three nonconstant pivot factors:

b−2,c−5​b+5,c−b2−b+1.b-2,\qquad c-5b+5,\qquad c-b^{2}-b+1.

The first two are −[u3]​g-[u^{3}]g and −[u4]​g-[u^{4}]g.

On b=2b=2 and on c=5​b−5c=5b-5 some tables change; on c=b2+b−1c=b^{2}+b-1 (equivalently g2​g4=g32g_{2}g_{4}=g_{3}^{2}) all tables agree with the generic ones. In each of the three calculations the only pivot factor is c−5c-5 (on b=2b=2) or b−2b-2 (on the other two curves), and it vanishes on the curve only at (b,c)=(2,5)(b,c)=(2,5). As in Appendix A, the tables of each curve therefore hold at all its points except (2,5)(2,5).

The common point (2,5)(2,5) is a separate part of the partition. Before normalization it consists of f=u+α​u2+2​α2​u3+5​α3​u4f=u+\alpha u^{2}+2\alpha^{2}u^{3}+5\alpha^{3}u^{4}, α≠0\alpha\neq 0, a single scaling orbit. Constancy on this part follows from scaling, not from specializing the generic curve tables.

The locus α=0\alpha=0. Scaling, after a field extension, reduces it to f=u+u3+γ​u4f=u+u^{3}+\gamma u^{4}, to u+u4u+u^{4}, and to uu. Over ℚ⁡(γ)\mathbb{Q}(\gamma) the first family has the single pivot factor γ\gamma, so its local tables are constant for γ≠0\gamma\neq 0. The specialization γ=0\gamma=0, represented by u+u3u+u^{3}, and the remaining cases u+u4u+u^{4} and uu each form a single scaling orbit. Constancy on each of these parts again follows from scaling.

Field extensions do not change ranks, and Hilbert functions are constant on scaling orbits. Hence all local tables are constant on each of the eight cells, and by induction over the tree and the closing rule (4.6) so is every Hilbert series of a tree with Δ≤4\Delta\leq 4. The separating trees above were found by evaluating all trees with Δ≤4\Delta\leq 4 and at most ten vertices at one point of each cell. All arithmetic is exact. The corresponding scripts are described in Appendix A. ∎

The pattern of Theorem 6.10 does not persist. This locus is invariant under f↦f−1f\mapsto f^{-1}, as Corollary 5.18 requires, and it contains the inverse quadratics and u/(1−u)u/(1-u). It is not, however, the vanishing locus of an individual coefficient of f−1f^{-1}. We have not recomputed the intersections of these surfaces or the locus α=0\alpha=0, so the complete partition for D=5D=5 is open (Section 8). The smallest tree detecting g5=0g_{5}=0 was found by an exhaustive search over trees with Δ≤5\Delta\leq 5 and at most fourteen vertices.

6.8 Distinguished functions and graph-dependent exceptionality

A parameter ff is Hilbert-exceptional for GG if ℋGf\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f} differs from the generic series of Theorem 6.1(ii). The exponential and inverse polynomials are distinguished for different elementary reasons.

Let g=f−1g=f^{-1}. On each connected component the defining relations give

∑vg⁡(Yv)=0.\sum_{v}g(Y_{v})=0. (6.12)

If gg is a polynomial of degree ss, this is a relation of filtration degree at most ss, regardless of the vertex degrees. In particular, g⁡(u)=u+c​u2g(u)=u+cu^{2} gives ∑vYv+c​∑vYv2=0\sum_{v}Y_{v}+c\sum_{v}Y_{v}^{2}=0. Whether such a short relation lowers a Hilbert value depends on the graph. For the inverse-quadratic truncation through degree three on subcubic trees, Proposition 6.9 gives the exact test.

Proposition 6.12 (Inverse degree and boundary gaps).

If f−1f^{-1} is a polynomial of degree at most ss, then every boundary state of every marked graph satisfies q−p≤sq-p\leq s. In particular, for an inverse quadratic f−1​(u)=u+c​u2f^{-1}(u)=u+cu^{2}, c≠0c\neq 0, every long-neck family with arbitrary side graphs satisfies

L⁡(Hn)=0(n≥5).L(H_{n})=0\qquad(n\geq 5). (6.13)

For a fixed graph, the same gap bound holds whenever the relevant truncation of f−1f^{-1} through the maximum vertex degree has degree at most ss.

Proof.

At a marked leaf aa with edge variable rr, the identity Xa=−∑v≠aXv=−∑v≠ag(Yv)X_{a}=-\sum_{v\neq a}X_{v}=-\sum_{v\neq a}g(Y_{v}) gives r∈Psr\in P_{s}. Multiplying a lift of u∈Qiu\in Q_{i} by rr then gives r​u∈Pi+sru\in P_{i+s}, so Qi⊆Ri+sQ_{i}\subseteq R_{i+s}. The bound follows from a simultaneous adapted basis. For an inverse quadratic, both side graphs in the neck construction have no gap greater than two. Theorem 4.16 gives (6.13). ∎

For the exponential parameter f⁡(u)=(exp⁡(c​u)−1)/cf(u)=(\exp(cu)-1)/c, c≠0c\neq 0, the simplification instead concerns addition:

1+c​f​(x+x′)=(1+c​f​(x))​(1+c​f​(x′)).1+cf(x+x^{\prime})=(1+cf(x))(1+cf(x^{\prime})).

Internal edge contributions cancel across a cut, so

(∏v∈I(1+c​Yv)−1)DI+1=0,∏v∈V⁡(C)(1+c​Yv)=1\left(\prod_{v\in I}(1+cY_{v})-1\right)^{D_{I}+1}=0,\qquad\prod_{v\in V(C)}(1+cY_{v})=1 (6.14)

for each connected component CC. These are the multiplicative cut relations of [13, Theorem 3], after normalization. The inverse series is logarithmic, not polynomial. At a square-zero boundary rr,

f⁡(x+r)=f⁡(x)+r⁡(1+c​f​(x)),f(x+r)=f(x)+r(1+cf(x)),

so coefficient extraction gives δr​(Pi)⊆Qi\delta_{r}(P_{i})\subseteq Q_{i} and hence Ri⊆QiR_{i}\subseteq Q_{i}. All exponential boundary gaps are therefore nonnegative, rather than bounded above by two.

The contrast is already visible in the examples. The normalized cubic ratio λ=β/α2\lambda=\beta/\alpha^{2} is 22 for the inverse quadratic and 2/32/3 for the exponential (Figure 7). The first is detected by subcubic trees. The exponential, in contrast, lies in the generic cell for every tree of maximum degree at most four: its inverse log⁡(1+u)\log(1+u) has [u3]=1/3[u^{3}]=1/3 and [u4]=−1/4[u^{4}]=-1/4, so Theorem 6.10 applies. It also avoids the five loci of Remark 6.11. By Proposition 5.17 and Corollary 5.18, the exponential is generic on every star, while an inverse quadratic is exceptional on every star with at least six vertices.

The exponential is exceptional, however, for small graphs with cycles. The first examples are the multigraphs of [13, Example 2]: for the 44-cycle with two opposite edges doubled and for the 44-cycle with two adjacent edges doubled, the exponential gives 1+4​t+10​t2+14​t3+3​t41+4t+10t^{2}+14t^{3}+3t^{4} and 1+4​t+10​t2+15​t3+2​t41+4t+10t^{2}+15t^{3}+2t^{4}, while the generic series are 1+4​t+10​t2+15​t3+2​t41+4t+10t^{2}+15t^{3}+2t^{4} and 1+4​t+10​t2+16​t3+t41+4t+10t^{2}+16t^{3}+t^{4}. We confirmed these values by exact computation. Besides the doubled triangle (Proposition 6.4) and the unicycles G​8G8 (Table 5), four simple graphs with five vertices and maximum degree three have this property: the triangle with a path of length two attached at one endpoint, the house, the kite (K4K_{4} minus an edge, with a leaf edge) and K2,3K_{2,3}. For the first of them the series at u+u2u+u^{2} and at eu−1e^{u}-1 are

1+5​t+13​t2+8​t3+t4and1+5​t+13​t2+7​t3+2​t4.1+5t+13t^{2}+8t^{3}+t^{4}\qquad\text{and}\qquad 1+5t+13t^{2}+7t^{3}+2t^{4}.

Six graphs with five vertices and Δ=4\Delta=4 are added in Proposition 6.20. For [13, Problem 3], which asks for which graphs the exponential is generic, the answer therefore depends on the graph: it is affirmative for stars and for all trees with Δ≤4\Delta\leq 4, and negative for these graphs with cycles. Functional identities single out parameter loci, but the graph determines which of them are Hilbert-exceptional.

Remark 6.13 (Complete profiles of small graphs).

For each of the eighteen graphs of maximum degree three with four or five vertices in Tables B1–B3 of [18, tables/], the complete Hilbert partition of the cubic parameter plane was computed exactly: the generic ranks over ℚ⁡(λ)\mathbb{Q}(\lambda) with all pivot factors recorded, then a recomputation over the residue field of every factor, and separately the two orbits with α=0\alpha=0. In every case the only exceptional values are λ=2\lambda=2 (for twelve of the graphs) and λ=2/3\lambda=2/3 (for six graphs, all of which contain a cycle and are also exceptional at λ=2\lambda=2). On these graphs the inverse quadratic and the exponential therefore give the only exceptional parameters with α≠0\alpha\neq 0, after truncation through degree three. The full profiles are listed in those tables.

6.9 Universal Hilbert equivalence and exact collisions

Recall that universal Hilbert equivalence means equality of the nondegenerate profiles at the same parameter. We compare the profiles on a common space 𝒜D{\mathscr{A}}_{D}, with D≥max⁡{1,Δ⁡(G),Δ⁡(G′)}D\geq\max\{1,\Delta(G),\Delta(G^{\prime})\}.

Proposition 6.14 (A determinantal criterion).

Over an algebraically closed field, universal Hilbert equivalence is equivalent to

Ir+1​(MG,i)=Ir+1​(MG′,i)for every ​i,r.\sqrt{I_{r+1}(M_{G,i})}=\sqrt{I_{r+1}(M_{G^{\prime},i})}\quad\text{for every }i,r. (6.15)

Only finitely many i,ri,r are needed.

Proof.

We view the entries of MG,iM_{G,i} and MG′,iM_{G^{\prime},i} as polynomials on the common space 𝒜D{\mathscr{A}}_{D}. The ones in MG,iM_{G,i} involve only aja_{j} with j≤Δ⁡(G)j\leq\Delta(G). By (6.3), the zero set of Ir+1​(MG,i)I_{r+1}(M_{G,i}) in 𝒜D​(𝐤){\mathscr{A}}_{D}(\mathbf{k}) is the set of ff with dim𝒞Gf,i≤r\dim\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f,i}\leq r. The Hilbert series ℋGf\mathscr{H}^{f}_{G} is determined by the cumulative dimensions dim𝒞Gf,i\dim\mathscr{C}_{G}^{f,i}, i≥0i\geq 0, and conversely. Hence ℋGf=ℋG′f\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f}=\mathscr{H}_{G^{\prime}}^{f} for all ff if and only if, for every ii and rr, the two determinantal loci have the same 𝐤\mathbf{k}-points. Over an algebraically closed field this is equivalent to (6.15), by the Nullstellensatz. Let NN and N′N^{\prime} be the numbers of non-loop edges of GG and G′G^{\prime}. For i≥max⁡(N,N′)i\geq\max(N,N^{\prime}) both cumulative dimensions are the total dimensions, so these conditions coincide with the one for i=max⁡(N,N′)i=\max(N,N^{\prime}). For r≥max⁡(dim𝒞G,dim𝒞G′)r\geq\max(\dim\mathscr{C}_{G},\dim\mathscr{C}_{G^{\prime}}) both ideals are zero. Thus only finitely many pairs (i,r)(i,r) give distinct conditions. ∎

Proposition 6.15 (Universal collisions).

Each pair in (6.16) consists of nonisomorphic universally Hilbert equivalent graphs over every characteristic-zero field. Their complete pointwise Hilbert profiles are given in Tables 5–8. Unspecified coefficients in the conditions are arbitrary, and all coefficients beyond the maximum vertex degree are irrelevant.

Each unicyclic graph has a unique four-cycle and a unique path of length two attached to that cycle at one endpoint.
