Remark 6.17 (Bizonotopal Hilbert series).

The Hilbert series of the external bizonotopal algebra counts partial score vectors by weight [9, Corollary 2.6]. It separates the two graphs of each pair in (6.16): the coefficients of t5t^{5} are 330330 and 329329 for G​8G8, and the coefficients of t4t^{4} are 403403 and 402402 for T​1T1, 436436 and 437437 for T​2T2, and 411411 and 412412 for T​3T3. Thus the external bizonotopal Hilbert series separates T​3T3, whereas no Hilbert series obtained from generators f⁡(Xv)f(X_{v}) does. The bizonotopal algebra uses opposite-arrow variables whose product is zero; it is not obtained by ordinary parallel-edge doubling. In the terms of Theorem 3.20: for the two trees of T​3T3 the numbers of partial score vectors with all entries divisible by 22, and by 33, agree in each weight, while the numbers of all partial score vectors differ.

Proposition 6.18 (Collisions among small graphs).
  1. (i)

    No two nonisomorphic trees with at most nine vertices are universally Hilbert equivalent. Among the 106106 trees with ten vertices, the pairs T​1T1, T​2T2, T​3T3 are the only universally Hilbert equivalent pairs.

  2. (ii)

    Among connected unicyclic simple graphs with at most eight vertices, G​8G8 is the only universally Hilbert equivalent pair.

Proof.

Two graphs whose Hilbert series differ at a single nondegenerate ff are not universally Hilbert equivalent. Enumerate up to isomorphism all 201201 trees with at most ten vertices and all 143143 connected unicyclic simple graphs with at most eight vertices, and compute their Hilbert series exactly at the six functions

u,u+u2,u+u2+u3,u+u2+2​u3,u+u3,u+u4.u,\quad u+u^{2},\quad u+u^{2}+u^{3},\quad u+u^{2}+2u^{3},\quad u+u^{3},\quad u+u^{4}.

Any two nonisomorphic graphs with the same number of vertices are separated by one of them, except the two graphs in each of the pairs T​1T1, T​2T2, T​3T3 and G​8G8. These pairs are universally Hilbert equivalent by Proposition 6.15. For trees the Hilbert series were computed twice, by the boundary-state calculus and directly in the edge algebra, with identical results. For unicyclic graphs they were computed directly. The enumeration reproduces the known numbers of trees and of connected unicyclic graphs (sequences A000055 and A001429 of [14]). ∎

In this particular six-function separating set, u+u4u+u^{4} is needed to distinguish some trees with a vertex of degree at least four. Without it the remaining five functions do not separate, for example, the star with four leaves from the tree with five vertices and a vertex of degree three.

For subcubic trees, Theorem 6.7 turns comparison at four points into a complete test of universal Hilbert equivalence, and Theorem 6.10 does the same with eight points for Δ≤4\Delta\leq 4. These complete tests give the statistics in Table 10. The table records the frequency of collisions in these finite ranges. Among the enumerated subcubic trees, classes of three first appear at sixteen vertices.

In the enumerated classes, the complete nondegenerate profile distinguishes more graphs than any individual tested parameter. The largest numbers of distinct Hilbert series in these tests occur at exceptional parameters (Table 10). For example, among the 1102011020 subcubic trees with eighteen vertices the generic point separates 22982298 classes and the inverse-quadratic point u+u2+2​u3u+u^{2}+2u^{3} separates 32023202, while the complete nondegenerate profile separates 1085010850.

Up to fifteen vertices, every subcubic collision pair differs by exchanging two paths of different lengths, each attached to the rest of the tree at one endpoint. No single tested exchange type preserves the nondegenerate profile in general. For example, the exchange relating the two trees T​2T2 swaps a leaf edge and a path of length three attached at opposite ends of an edge. It preserves the profile in only 1616 of the 250250 cases with at most fourteen vertices. At sixteen vertices, four pairs require more than one exchange.

Remark 6.19 (Consequences of the profiles).

Along the locus 3​β=2​α23\beta=2\alpha^{2}, α≠0\alpha\neq 0, every subcubic tree has its generic Hilbert series, whereas either graph of the pair G​8G8 has a nongeneric series. For T​1T1, the nested exceptional conditions are exactly [u3]​f−1=0[u^{3}]f^{-1}=0 and then [u4]​f−1=0[u^{4}]f^{-1}=0, as Theorem 6.10 predicts. The two Hilbert functions are therefore incomparable under ⪯cum\preceq_{\rm cum}. Inspection of Table 5 shows that the projectivized partition has no least Hilbert function under this order.

Universal Hilbert equivalence also need not be preserved by attaching a leaf at corresponding marked vertices. Attach one edge at vertex 66 of the two trees T​2T2. At f=u+u2+2​u3f=u+u^{2}+2u^{3} their Hilbert functions are

(1,11,59,192,392,369),(1,11,59,192,386,375),(1,11,59,192,392,369),\qquad(1,11,59,192,386,375),

as follows from the same branching algorithm. Their difference is 6​t4​(1−t)6t^{4}(1-t). Thus equality of nondegenerate Hilbert profiles does not imply equality of the boundary-state sums at specified vertices. For α≠0\alpha\neq 0 the filtered algebras in each pair are not isomorphic, by Theorem 3.8.

6.10 The exponential and the generic series of small graphs

We return to [13, Problem 3]: for which graphs does the exponential have the generic Hilbert series? Exact rational and symbolic calculations, and modular ranks attaining a proved upper bound, give the computer-assisted results below. The remaining finite-field scans are experimental; unproved generic values are called candidates, and unproved exceptional loci proposed. Appendix A specifies these distinctions.

For a normalized nondegenerate series, write f=u+α​u2+β​u3+γ​u4+⋯f=u+\alpha u^{2}+\beta u^{3}+\gamma u^{4}+\cdots, g=f−1g=f^{-1}, and put

vf​(u)=f′​(g⁡(u))=1g′​(u)=1+v1​u+v2​u2+v3​u3+⋯.v_{f}(u)=f^{\prime}\bigl(g(u)\bigr)=\frac{1}{g^{\prime}(u)}=1+v_{1}u+v_{2}u^{2}+v_{3}u^{3}+\cdots. (6.19)

Thus v1=2​αv_{1}=2\alpha, v2=3​β−2​α2v_{2}=3\beta-2\alpha^{2} and v3=4​(α3−2​α​β+γ)v_{3}=4(\alpha^{3}-2\alpha\beta+\gamma). These vjv_{j} are coefficients of a formal series, not Hilbert coefficients. We reserve hjh_{j} for [tj]​ℋGf[t^{j}]\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f}. The equation vf​(u)=1+c​uv_{f}(u)=1+cu is equivalent to f′​(u)=1+c​f​(u)f^{\prime}(u)=1+cf(u), f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0, and hence characterizes f=(ec​u−1)/cf=(e^{cu}-1)/c for c≠0c\neq 0. An inverse quadratic g⁡(u)=u+c​u2g(u)=u+cu^{2} instead has 1/vf=g′=1+2​c​u1/v_{f}=g^{\prime}=1+2cu.

Proposition 6.20 (Exact exponential exceptions on five vertices; computer-assisted).

The exponential f=eu−1f=e^{u}-1 is Hilbert-exceptional for the following six simple graphs with five vertices and Δ=4\Delta=4: K4K_{4} minus an edge with a leaf edge at a vertex of degree three (the dart), K4K_{4} with a leaf edge, the wheel (a 44-cycle together with a vertex joined to all of its vertices), the house with both diagonals of its square, K5−eK_{5}-e and K5K_{5}. Its Hilbert functions on these graphs are those of Table 11.

Proof.

The Hilbert functions at f=eu−1f=e^{u}-1 (truncated at u4u^{4}) and at f5=u+u2+u4f_{5}=u+u^{2}+u^{4} (Table B4 of [18, tables/]) were computed by exact rational arithmetic in the square-free edge algebra. In each case the cumulative dimensions at the exponential are smaller than those at f5f_{5} in some degree, so the exponential does not lie in the open stratum of Theorem 6.1. ∎

Together with the exact examples in Section 6.8, this proves exceptionality for at least ten of the thirty connected simple graphs on two to five vertices. Genericity is proved for sixteen others: the graphs with Δ≤2\Delta\leq 2, the three additional trees, and the six remaining graphs with Δ=3\Delta=3, by Proposition 3.14, Theorem 6.10 and Remark 6.13, respectively. For four graphs—the triangle with two leaf edges at one vertex, two triangles sharing a vertex, the cone over the four-vertex path, and K1,1,3K_{1,1,3}—the exponential agrees with the candidate generic value in Table 11, and the scans below found no larger cumulative ranks. The one-vertex graph has series 11 for every ff.

For the multigraphs with four vertices and Δ=3\Delta=3 (Table B2 of [18, tables/]), the previously established profiles identify the exponential exceptions as the 44-cycles with one doubled edge and with two opposite doubled edges. The exponential is generic on E2,E3,E4E_{2},E_{3},E_{4} (Section 6.3). The last row of Table 11 also includes the adjacent-doubled-edge example from [13, Example 2].

Remark 6.22 (Two algebraic features of the proposed loci).

The equations themselves have two useful properties. On v1≠0v_{1}\neq 0, the conic QQ, v1​v3=v22v_{1}v_{3}=v_{2}^{2}, is equivalent to

vf​(u)≡1+σ​u1+τ​u(modu4),σ=v1−v2v1,τ=−v2v1.v_{f}(u)\equiv\frac{1+\sigma u}{1+\tau u}\pmod{u^{4}},\qquad\sigma=v_{1}-\frac{v_{2}}{v_{1}},\quad\tau=-\frac{v_{2}}{v_{1}}.

Indeed, the first three nonconstant coefficients of the fraction are σ−τ,−τ⁡(σ−τ),τ2​(σ−τ)\sigma-\tau,-\tau(\sigma-\tau),\tau^{2}(\sigma-\tau). Taking its reciprocal and integrating yields

g⁡(u)≡{τσ​u+σ−τσ2​log⁡(1+σ​u),σ≠0,u+τ2​u2,σ=0,(modu5).g(u)\equiv\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\tau}{\sigma}u+\frac{\sigma-\tau}{\sigma^{2}}\log(1+\sigma u),&\sigma\neq 0,\\[6.0pt] u+\dfrac{\tau}{2}u^{2},&\sigma=0,\end{cases}\pmod{u^{5}}.

The quadratic limiting case is essential: it includes KK and cannot be omitted in favor of a logarithmic expression with finite coefficients.

The quartic WW is absolutely irreducible. Set a=v2/v12a=v_{2}/v_{1}^{2} and b=v3/v13b=v_{3}/v_{1}^{3}. Its equation, divided by v18v_{1}^{8}, is

b2+(2​a2−6​a+2)​b−4​a4+8​a3−3​a2=0.b^{2}+(2a^{2}-6a+2)b-4a^{4}+8a^{3}-3a^{2}=0.

Its discriminant as a quadratic in bb is 4​(a−1)2​(5​a2−4​a+1)4(a-1)^{2}(5a^{2}-4a+1). The last factor has two distinct roots in characteristic zero, so this is not a square even in 𝐤¯​(a)\overline{\mathbf{k}}(a). The monic quadratic is therefore irreducible over that field and in 𝐤¯​[a,b]\overline{\mathbf{k}}[a,b]. In the chart α=1\alpha=1, (a,b)(a,b) are an invertible affine change of (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu), proving the assertion for the displayed plane curve.

Conjecture 6.25.

Let GG be a connected simple graph that is not a tree, and let ff be generic.

  1. (i)

    If GG has at least four vertices and is neither the 44-cycle nor the triangle with a leaf edge, then equality holds for h2h_{2} in (6.20).

  2. (ii)

    If GG is bridgeless, with |E⁡(G)|−|V⁡(G)|+1≥3|E(G)|-|V(G)|+1\geq 3, and G≠K4G\neq K_{4}, then equality holds for h3h_{3} in (6.20).

In these ranges, the highest-degree parts of the displayed relations would span all initial relations in the indicated degree. This concerns the associated graded algebra: an initial relation need not itself be an exact homogeneous relation among the YvY_{v}.

Proposition 6.26 (Conjecture 6.25 for at most seven vertices; computer-assisted).

Conjecture 6.25 holds for all graphs with at most seven vertices: part (i) for the 968968 graphs to which it applies, and part (ii) for the 557557 graphs to which it applies. For f=eu−1f=e^{u}-1, equality holds in part (i) for all 968968 graphs and in part (ii) for 555555 of the 557557 graphs. The two exceptions are (a) a diamond and a triangle sharing a vertex of degree two of the diamond, and (b) the triangular prism with one of the three edges between its triangles removed. On each, h3h_{3} at the exponential is one less than the bound, so the exponential is Hilbert-exceptional.

so attaining UdU_{d} modulo pp proves dimFd=Ud\dim F_{d}=U_{d} at that parameter. For generic ff the rank is at least the rank at any parameter and at most the bound for generic ff, which is at most the bound at the parameter; so equality then also holds for generic ff.

The script low_certificate.py [18] computes these ranks modulo p=1048573p=1048573 for all 970970 connected simple graphs with four to seven vertices that are not trees, at a random integer parameter and at the exponential, whose coefficients 1/k!1/k! (k≤6k\leq 6) have denominators prime to pp. At the random parameter the modular ranks attain U2U_{2} for all 968968 graphs of part (i) and U3U_{3} for all 557557 graphs of part (ii); at the exponential they do so except for U3U_{3} on the two graphs named in the statement. For a connected graph, its cyclomatic number is |E|−|V|+1|E|-|V|+1. The listed exclusions are necessary. For C4C_{4} and the triangle with a leaf edge, h2=7h_{2}=7 rather than 99, and the cubic bound is not attained for K4K_{4} or for cycles. Modular computations suggest that it is also not attained for eight of the fourteen bridgeless graphs of cyclomatic number two with at most seven vertices, nor for the tested graphs with a bridge. On the doubled triangle and on the 44-cycle with one doubled edge, the exponential’s smaller quadratic value is part of the earlier exact profiles.

7 Cycle graphs

For graphs of maximum degree two, all normalized nondegenerate series with nonzero quadratic coefficient give the same Hilbert series. The linear case is separate, as are the degenerate cases of Proposition 3.29.

7.1 The coefficients through degree three

The low-degree calculation can be made independently of the more involved closing argument for the top term. We prove completeness of the relations of word degree at most three, rather than infer their ranks from finite computations. In this subsection write xi=φix_{i}=\varphi_{i}, ℓi=xi+1−xi\ell_{i}=x_{i+1}-x_{i} and qi=xi​xi+1q_{i}=x_{i}x_{i+1}; thus Yi=ℓi−qiY_{i}=\ell_{i}-q_{i}. All indices are taken modulo nn.

Span{zi3,zi2zi+1+zizi+12:i∈ℤ/nℤ}.\Span\{z_{i}^{3},\ z_{i}^{2}z_{i+1}+z_{i}z_{i+1}^{2}:i\in{\mathbb{Z}}/n{\mathbb{Z}}\}. (7.3)

Yi2=−2​qi,Yi​Yi+1=qi−xi​xi+2+qi+1.Y_{i}^{2}=-2q_{i},\qquad Y_{i}Y_{i+1}=q_{i}-x_{i}x_{i+2}+q_{i+1}. (7.4)

We prove that they account for every cubic relation by comparing ordinary edge degrees, starting with the highest one.

A product Yi​Yj​YkY_{i}Y_{j}Y_{k} with distinct, pairwise nonadjacent indices has edge-degree-six term −qi​qj​qk-q_{i}q_{j}q_{k}. These monomials are distinct: their supports are proper subsets of the cycle, since n≥7n\geq 7, and each run of consecutive vertices in such a support has a unique covering by disjoint adjacent pairs. Every other cubic word contains a square or an adjacent pair, and has edge degree at most four by (7.4). Thus the coefficients of all the pairwise nonadjacent triples vanish in a relation.

Modulo (7.3), the remaining words are represented by adjacent doubles Yi2​Yi+1Y_{i}^{2}Y_{i+1} and by

Di​j=Yi2​Yj(i,j​ nonadjacent),Ai=Yi​Yi+1​Yi+2,Bi​j=Yi​Yi+1​Yj,D_{ij}=Y_{i}^{2}Y_{j}\quad(i,j\text{ nonadjacent}),\qquad A_{i}=Y_{i}Y_{i+1}Y_{i+2},\qquad B_{ij}=Y_{i}Y_{i+1}Y_{j},

In the second, two descriptions would require the isolated vertex to be at distance two from both endpoints of the run of three, which is possible only on a cycle of length six. 7.2 The top term

Theorem 7.3 (The top term for cycles).

For every n≥3n\geq 3,

g=λ​Ω2​m−1+c+ga​(a)+gb​(b),g=\lambda\Omega_{2m-1}+c+g_{a}(a)+g_{b}(b), (7.23)

where ga,gbg_{a},g_{b} have zero constant term.

It remains to impose the closing condition on one parity class. Choose one of Y2​j,Y2​j+1Y_{2j},Y_{2j+1} for each jj, recording the choice by εj∈{0,1}\varepsilon_{j}\in\{0,1\}. Up to an overall sign, the coefficient of b0⋯bm−1b_{0}\cdots b_{m-1} in the resulting product is ∏j(1+uj​aj)\prod_{j}(1+u_{j}a_{j}), where uj=εj−1+εj−1u_{j}=\varepsilon_{j-1}+\varepsilon_{j}-1. Km(h)(ε)=[a0⋯am−1]h(a)∏j(1+ujaj).K_{m}(h)(\varepsilon)=[a_{0}\cdots a_{m-1}]h(a)\prod_{j}(1+u_{j}a_{j}). (7.24)
Lemma 7.6.

For m≥2m\geq 2,

ker⁡Km\displaystyle\ker K_{m} =𝒵odd​(a),\displaystyle=\mathcal{Z}_{\rm odd}(a), (7.25)
{h:Km​(h)​ vanishes on nonconstant ​ε}\displaystyle\{h:K_{m}(h)\text{ vanishes on nonconstant }\varepsilon\} =𝒵odd​(a)⊕𝐤​ 1⊕𝐤​a0.\displaystyle=\mathcal{Z}_{\rm odd}(a)\oplus\mathbf{k}\,1\oplus\mathbf{k}a_{0}. (7.26)

Km​(h)​(σ)=∑T⊇DhT​∏j∉Tuj.K_{m}(h)(\sigma)=\sum_{T\supseteq D}h_{T}\prod_{j\notin T}u_{j}.

Proof of Proposition 7.5.

For a nonconstant choice sequence ε\varepsilon, the chosen generators do not cover all the aa-variables: a transition from 00 to 11 leaves one aja_{j} absent. Hence their product pairs to zero with the constant term and with gbg_{b} in (7.23). g=λ​Ω2​m−1+c+μ​a0+ν​b0+za+zb,za∈𝒵odd​(a),zb∈𝒵odd​(b).g=\lambda\Omega_{2m-1}+c+\mu a_{0}+\nu b_{0}+z_{a}+z_{b},\qquad z_{a}\in\mathcal{Z}_{\rm odd}(a),\quad z_{b}\in\mathcal{Z}_{\rm odd}(b).

Conversely, a polynomial in the aa-variables can pair nontrivially with a product of at most mm generators only if that product chooses exactly one of Y2​j,Y2​j+1Y_{2j},Y_{2j+1} for every jj. Completion of the proof of Theorem 7.3.

For n=2​mn=2m, Proposition 7.5 and (7.19) give dimFm⟂=2m−1+2\dim F_{m}^{\perp}=2^{m-1}+2. 7.6 The cycle conjecture

Theorem 7.3 fixes the top term of HnH_{n}, and Theorem 7.1 proves the first three stable coefficients. The conjecture extends this agreement to all degrees below half the cycle length, using the trace of the transfer matrix M=M⁡(t)M=M(t) of (4.13). Put trn​(t)=tr⁡M​(t)n\mathrm{tr}_{n}(t)=\operatorname{tr}M(t)^{n}.

The trace has the following weighted independent-set interpretation. For a set SS of vertices of CnC_{n}, let c⁡(S)c(S) be the number of vertices outside SS both of whose neighbors lie in SS.

Proposition 7.7 (A weighted independence form).

For w∈𝐤w\in\mathbf{k}, let Mw​(t)M_{w}(t) be the matrix (4.13) with the entry 22 replaced by w−1w-1, so that M3=MM_{3}=M. For n≥3n\geq 3,

tr⁡Mw​(t)n=∑Swc⁡(S)​t|S|,\operatorname{tr}M_{w}(t)^{n}=\sum_{S}w^{c(S)}t^{|S|},

the sum over the independent sets SS of vertices of CnC_{n}. In particular trn​(t)=∑S3c⁡(S)​t|S|\mathrm{tr}_{n}(t)=\sum_{S}3^{c(S)}t^{|S|}, and tr⁡M1​(t)n=I⁡(Cn,t)\operatorname{tr}M_{1}(t)^{n}=I(C_{n};t).

Proof.

The potentially nonzero transition weights of MwM_{w} are w−1w-1 from e0e_{0} to e1e_{1}, tt from e1e_{1} to e0e_{0}, 11 from e1e_{1} to e2e_{2}, tt from e2e_{2} to e1e_{1} and 11 from e2e_{2} to e2e_{2}. Thus tr⁡Mwn\operatorname{tr}M_{w}^{n} is the sum, over the sequences (si)i∈ℤ/n​ℤ(s_{i})_{i\in{\mathbb{Z}}/n{\mathbb{Z}}} of states, of the products of the entries from sis_{i} to si+1s_{i+1}. Put S={i:si=e1}S=\{i:s_{i}=e_{1}\} and D={i:si=e0}D=\{i:s_{i}=e_{0}\}. There is no entry from e1e_{1} to e1e_{1}, so SS is independent, and e0e_{0} is entered and left only through e1e_{1}, so every element of DD has both neighbors in SS. Conversely, every pair (S,D)(S,D) of this kind comes from exactly one sequence, with si=e2s_{i}=e_{2} outside S∪DS\cup D. Each element of DD contributes the factor tt of its entering step; each element of SS contributes w−1w-1 if it is entered from DD and tt otherwise. Since the elements of SS entered from DD correspond to the elements of DD, the product is t|S|​(w−1)|D|t^{|S|}(w-1)^{|D|}, and summing over DD gives t|S|​wc⁡(S)t^{|S|}w^{c(S)}. ∎

Conjecture 7.8 (Cycle congruence).

Let α≠0\alpha\neq 0 and Hn=ℋCnfH_{n}=\mathscr{H}^{f}_{C_{n}}. For every n≥3n\geq 3,

Hn​(t)≡trn​(t)−t2(modt⌈n/2⌉).H_{n}(t)\equiv\mathrm{tr}_{n}(t)-t^{2}\pmod{t^{\lceil n/2\rceil}}. (7.27)

Equivalently, for every d≥0d\geq 0 with 2​d<n2d<n,

[td]​Hn=∑S⊆V⁡(Cn)​ independent|S|=d3c⁡(S)−δd,2.[t^{d}]H_{n}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq V(C_{n})\text{ independent}\\ |S|=d\end{subarray}}3^{c(S)}-\delta_{d,2}.

Thus each independent set is weighted by a factor of three for each vertex outside it whose two neighbors lie in the set.

For d=2d=2 and n≥5n\geq 5, the weighted sum is 3​n+n⁡(n−5)/2=(n+12)3n+n(n-5)/2=\binom{n+1}{2}, consistent with the stable quadratic coefficient. Setting w=1w=1 gives I⁡(Cn,t)I(C_{n};t), which differs by tt from the matching-quotient series of Remark 7.10. At t=1t=1 the weighted sum is 2n+(−1)n​ℓn2^{n}+(-1)^{n}\ell_{n}, as used below.

The conjecture agrees with the series HnH_{n} for n≤17n\leq 17, computed modulo two primes [18, cycles/] by the method of Proposition 7.12. It was first found in the following equivalent form, as a recurrence for the operator LL of (4.18). Here ℓk\ell_{k} are the Lucas numbers defined in Proposition 3.29.

Proposition 7.9 (Equivalent forms of the conjecture).

Given Theorem 7.3, Conjecture 7.8 is equivalent to the recurrence

L⁡(Hn)={t3+(2n/2−2+1)​tn/2​(1−t)if n is even,t3+(ℓn−4−1+2​t)​(1−t)​t(n−1)/2if n is odd,n≥6,L(H_{n})=\begin{cases}t^{3}+(2^{n/2-2}+1)t^{n/2}(1-t)&\text{if $n$ is even},\\ t^{3}+(\ell_{n-4}-1+2t)(1-t)t^{(n-1)/2}&\text{if $n$ is odd,}\end{cases}\qquad n\geq 6, (7.28)

together with the initial values

H3=1+3​t+2​t2+t3,H4=1+4​t+7​t2+3​t3,H5=1+5​t+14​t2+10​t3+t4.H_{3}=1+3t+2t^{2}+t^{3},\quad H_{4}=1+4t+7t^{2}+3t^{3},\quad H_{5}=1+5t+14t^{2}+10t^{3}+t^{4}.

It is also equivalent to the closed formulas (7.29) and (7.30) below.

Proof.

The characteristic polynomial of MM is z3−z2−3​t​z+2​tz^{3}-z^{2}-3tz+2t by (4.13), so Cayley–Hamilton gives L⁡(trn)=0L(\mathrm{tr}_{n})=0, that is, trn=trn−1+3​t​trn−2−2​t​trn−3\mathrm{tr}_{n}=\mathrm{tr}_{n-1}+3t\mathrm{tr}_{n-2}-2t\mathrm{tr}_{n-3} for n≥3n\geq 3. The initial values tr0=3\mathrm{tr}_{0}=3, tr1=1\mathrm{tr}_{1}=1 and tr2=1+6​t\mathrm{tr}_{2}=1+6t, together with this recurrence, give deg⁡trn≤⌊n/2⌋\deg\mathrm{tr}_{n}\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor by induction. Moreover

det(z​I−M⁡(1))=(z−2)​(z2+z−1),trn​(1)=2n+(−1)n​ℓn.\det(zI-M(1))=(z-2)(z^{2}+z-1),\qquad\mathrm{tr}_{n}(1)=2^{n}+(-1)^{n}\ell_{n}.

Since dim𝒞Cn=2n−1\dim\mathscr{C}_{C_{n}}=2^{n}-1 by (7.9), the congruence and the top-term theorem leave just one coefficient undetermined, and evaluation at t=1t=1 determines it. Writing Am=2m−1+1A_{m}=2^{m-1}+1, the resulting formulas are

H2​m\displaystyle H_{2m} =tr2​m−t2−(ℓ2​m+Am)​tm+Am​tm+1\displaystyle=\mathrm{tr}_{2m}-t^{2}-(\ell_{2m}+A_{m})t^{m}+A_{m}t^{m+1} (m≥2),\displaystyle(m\geq 2), (7.29)
H2​m+1\displaystyle H_{2m+1} =tr2​m+1−t2+(ℓ2​m+1−1)​tm+1+tm+2\displaystyle=\mathrm{tr}_{2m+1}-t^{2}+(\ell_{2m+1}-1)t^{m+1}+t^{m+2} (m≥1).\displaystyle(m\geq 1). (7.30)

Substitution in LL, using ℓn=ℓn−1+ℓn−2\ell_{n}=\ell_{n-1}+\ell_{n-2}, gives the two lines of the conjectured recurrence. The formulas also give its initial values. Conversely, that recurrence and those initial values uniquely determine the sequence, so they imply (7.29)–(7.30), and hence the congruence. ∎

Remark 7.10 (The matching quotient and the Lucas contribution).

The number ℓn\ell_{n} counts all independent vertex subsets of CnC_{n}. There is an unconditional occurrence of this count: if J=(φiφi+1:i∈ℤ/nℤ)⊂ΦnJ=(\varphi_{i}\varphi_{i+1}:i\in{\mathbb{Z}}/n{\mathbb{Z}})\subset\Phi_{n}, then J⊂𝒞CnJ\subset\mathscr{C}_{C_{n}} and the induced quotient filtration has series I⁡(Cn,t)−tI(C_{n};t)-t, where I⁡(Cn,t)I(C_{n};t) is the independence polynomial. Indeed, modulo JJ the generators become linear differences, and (7.9) contains every surviving monomial of degree at least two and all but one linear direction. Thus this quotient has dimension ℓn−1\ell_{n}-1 for both parities.

This quotient is the Dunkl matching algebra of the cycle in Grinberg–Kirillov–Shapiro [4]. Their matching algebra ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{M}(G) is the quotient of the square-zero edge algebra by products of incident edges; 𝒟⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G) is its subalgebra generated by the signed incidence sums. In ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{M}(G) every Xv2=0X_{v}^{2}=0, so all normalized generators f⁡(Xv)f(X_{v}) have the same image XvX_{v}. For G=CnG=C_{n}, the additional ideal is precisely JJ, and hence 𝒞Cnf/J≃𝒟⁡(Cn)\mathscr{C}_{C_{n}}^{f}/J\simeq\mathcal{D}(C_{n}) with its degree filtration. Their unicyclic formula [4, Theorem 5.16] gives the same series I⁡(Cn,t)−tI(C_{n};t)-t (matchings of a cycle correspond to independent sets of its line graph, again a cycle). This identifies the quotient, not the induced filtration on JJ, and therefore does not prove the full cycle formula.

In the conjectural trace formulas the Lucas part is bn=(−1)n+1​ℓn​t⌈n/2⌉b_{n}=(-1)^{n+1}\ell_{n}t^{\lceil n/2\rceil}. Directly from the Lucas recurrence,

L⁡(bn)=0​(n​ even),L⁡(bn)=ℓn−4​t(n−1)/2​(1−t)​(n​ odd).L(b_{n})=0\ (n\text{ even}),\qquad L(b_{n})=\ell_{n-4}t^{(n-1)/2}(1-t)\ (n\text{ odd}).

Thus the even recurrence has no explicit Lucas term because of a cancellation, although the independent sets contribute for both parities.

Remark 7.11 (An exact boundary-operator formulation).

For 2​d<n2d<n, every product of at most dd cyclic generators omits two consecutive generators. Let Pn−1(i),dP_{n-1}^{(i),d} be the open path obtained by omitting Yi−1,YiY_{i-1},Y_{i}, and put Ei,d=(Pn−1(i),d)⟂E_{i,d}=(P_{n-1}^{(i),d})^{\perp} in the algebra on the other variables. Then

Fd⟂=kerDn,d,Dn,d:Φn⟶⨁i𝐤[φj:j≠i]/(φj2)/Ei,d,g⟼([∂φig])i.F_{d}^{\perp}=\ker D_{n,d},\qquad D_{n,d}:\Phi_{n}\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{i}\mathbf{k}[\varphi_{j}:j\neq i]/(\varphi_{j}^{2})\big/E_{i,d},\quad g\longmapsto([\partial_{\varphi_{i}}g])_{i}.

Consequently (7.27) is equivalent to

rkDn,d=∑j=0d[tj]trn−𝟏{d≥2},2d<n.\rank D_{n,d}=\sum_{j=0}^{d}[t^{j}]\mathrm{tr}_{n}-\mathbf{1}_{\{d\geq 2\}},\qquad 2d<n.

This rank identity is open. It encodes the condition that the separate path coefficients come from one polynomial, which the trace of the transfer matrix alone does not see.

Proposition 7.12 (An interpolation matrix for the cycle filtration).

For every n≥3n\geq 3 and d≥0d\geq 0, let An,dA_{n,d} be the integer matrix with rows indexed by S⊆ℤ/n​ℤS\subseteq{\mathbb{Z}}/n{\mathbb{Z}} and columns indexed by m∈ℤ≥0nm\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}^{n} with |m|≤d|m|\leq d, and entries

(An,d)S,m=∏i∈S(mi−1−mi).(A_{n,d})_{S,m}=\prod_{i\in S}(m_{i-1}-m_{i}). (7.31)

Then dimFd=rkℚ⁡An,d\dim F_{d}=\rank_{\mathbb{Q}}A_{n,d}.

Proof.

In the normalization (7.1), Yi=exp⁡(φi+1−φi)−1Y_{i}=\exp(\varphi_{i+1}-\varphi_{i})-1 because the cube of that difference is zero. Replacing the generators YiY_{i} by 1+Yi1+Y_{i} preserves every word-filtration level: binomial expansion gives inclusions in both directions without increasing the number of factors. Thus FdF_{d} is spanned by

∏i(1+Yi)mi=exp⁡(∑i(mi−1−mi)​φi)=∏i(1+(mi−1−mi)​φi),|m|≤d.\prod_{i}(1+Y_{i})^{m_{i}}=\exp\!\left(\sum_{i}(m_{i-1}-m_{i})\varphi_{i}\right)=\prod_{i}\bigl(1+(m_{i-1}-m_{i})\varphi_{i}\bigr),\qquad|m|\leq d.

Their coefficients in the square-free basis are exactly (7.31). Since these coefficients are integers, their rank is the same over every characteristic-zero field. ∎

For 2​d<n2d<n, Conjecture 7.8 is therefore equivalent to

rkℚAn,d=∑j=0d[tj]trn−𝟏{d≥2}.\rank_{\mathbb{Q}}A_{n,d}=\sum_{j=0}^{d}[t^{j}]\mathrm{tr}_{n}-\mathbf{1}_{\{d\geq 2\}}.

The unresolved step is the rank of these columns, which retain the joint cyclic compatibility. Theorem 7.1 settles it through d=3d=3 in the stable range.

8 Outlook

We conclude with several questions suggested by the results.

Cycles.

The rank formulations in Section 7.6 retain the joint endpoint compatibility needed to close a path.

Problem 8.1.

Prove the cycle congruence (7.27), equivalently the rank identity of Remark 7.11.

Subdivision.

Let WW have a marked non-loop edge ee, and let WnW_{n} replace ee by a path with nn edges. For a bridge, Theorem 4.16 makes L⁡(ℋWnf)L(\mathscr{H}^{f}_{W_{n}}) constant for n≥5n\geq 5. For a doubled edge, Wn=Cn+1W_{n}=C_{n+1}, and the cycle conjecture predicts that each fixed coefficient stabilizes. The same behavior is observed for the theta graph and K4K_{4}, in the ranges n≤8n\leq 8 and n≤5n\leq 5, respectively [18, checks/subdivision.py].

Conjecture 8.2 (Subdivision stabilization).

Let f=u+α​u2+⋯f=u+\alpha u^{2}+\cdots, with α≠0\alpha\neq 0. For every graph WW with a marked non-loop edge, and every jj, the coefficient of tjt^{j} in L⁡(ℋWnf)L(\mathscr{H}^{f}_{W_{n}}) is independent of nn for all sufficiently large nn.

Parameter partitions.

The inverse-coefficient description for D≤4D\leq 4 fails in degree five (Remark 6.11).

Problem 8.3.

Determine the common parameter partition for trees of maximum degree five. For general DD, is it described by a finite list of explicit types of conditions, such as inverse coefficients, star determinants and Hankel conditions?

Problem 8.4.

Is there a common finite parameter partition for all graphs of bounded maximum degree and bounded cycle rank?

The tree proof uses finitely many gap types at one boundary; it does not classify several interacting boundary actions.

Collisions.

Marked boundary data retain information not determined by the nondegenerate Hilbert profile (Remark 6.19).

Problem 8.5.

Which graph operations preserve the nondegenerate profile f↦ℋGff\mapsto\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f}, and which preserve the all-polynomial profile? Are there infinitely many pairs of nonisomorphic trees whose Hilbert series agree for every polynomial ff?

Distinguished functions.

The exponential is generic on all stars and on trees with Δ≤4\Delta\leq 4, but not on every graph. The proposed loci of Remark 6.21 suggest different mechanisms for its exceptionality.

Problem 8.6.

Which graphs detect a given functional identity of ff, such as a low inverse degree or an addition law, and at which filtration level?

The exponential case includes [13, Problem 3]. A proof of the proposed locus description, with an explanation comparable to (6.6), would go beyond the present scans. For generic ff, Conjecture 6.25 concerns degrees two and three; a graphical description of the fourth coefficient is also open.

Degenerate functions.

For graphs with cycles the partial-score bound need not be attained, and the Hilbert series can depend on higher coefficients of ff (Remark 3.30).

Problem 8.7.

Compute ℋGf\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f} for degenerate ff when GG has cycles. For which graphs does it depend only on the order of ff? Is there a splitting rule as in Lemma 3.28 for vertices of higher degree?

Central and internal algebras.

Nenashev and the first author also consider the filtered spanning-tree algebras 𝒞Gc,f\mathscr{C}_{G}^{{\mathrm{c}},f} generated by the elements f⁡(Xv)f(X_{v}) in ΦGc\Phi_{G}^{\mathrm{c}} of Section 2.5. A bridge of GG represents 𝒞Gc,f\mathscr{C}_{G}^{{\mathrm{c}},f} as the tensor product of the algebras for the two sides [13, Proposition 5]. Thus 𝒞Gc,f\mathscr{C}_{G}^{{\mathrm{c}},f} depends only on the bridgeless part and reconstruction of that part is [13, Problem 7]. The edge-algebra realizations of the central and internal algebras in [8, Theorem 7] also permit polynomial filtrations. Do they admit boundary-state descriptions and common parameter partitions?

Unimodality.

The computed Hilbert functions are consistent with unimodality, including the modular values in Section 6.10. All 20642064 Hilbert functions computed in the proof of Proposition 6.18 are log-concave, and all entries of the supplementary tables [18, tables/] are unimodal. So are the 442442 Hilbert functions of Section 6.10.

Log-concavity in general fails already for K4K_{4} and generic ff, whose Hilbert function is (1,4,10,14,5,3,1)(1,4,10,14,5,3,1) (Proposition 6.4). Is ℋGf\mathscr{H}_{G}^{f} unimodal for every graph GG and every nondegenerate ff? Compare the related questions for bizonotopal algebras in [9, Section 5].

Joint boundaries.

Cyclic gluing requires both endpoint actions on the same object, not only the one-boundary birth pairs. The next step is to identify data that retain this compatibility under path extension and closing. Rees modules may organize the resulting filtration defects; their homological interpretation is left to subsequent work.

Characteristic.

Characteristic zero is used for nonzero factorial coefficients, cut-power antiderivatives, and semisimplicity in Section 5.3. The finite-field calculations serve as evidence or as certificates for characteristic-zero ranks, not as a positive-characteristic version of the theory.

Appendix A Computer calculations

The programs behind every computer-assisted statement, their recorded output, and the data for the conjectures are in the repository [18]. Its file README.md lists, for each statement, the directory, the command, the kind of computation and the output file, and records the environment of the recorded run; the script run_all.sh reruns all computations. The requirements are Python 3 with SymPy, NumPy and networkx, and a C++17 compiler with the GMP library for one certificate. The directories are:

  • •

    certificates/: the parameter certificates of Section 6 (the subcubic branching table, small graphs and the collision pairs);

  • •

    strata/: maximum degree four and five, and the collision statistics of Tables 10 and 10;

  • •

    search/: the exhaustive searches of Proposition 6.18, the checks of the collision pairs, of degenerate functions and of Proposition 6.20; it is written independently of the other directories and uses only the Python standard library;

  • •

    checks/: the remaining checks, and in its subdirectory generic_exp/ the computations modulo a prime of Section 6.10;

  • •

    cycles/: the series HnH_{n} of Section 7.6 and the annihilators of Section 7;

  • •

    tables/: the Hilbert functions of the connected graphs with four or five vertices and maximum degree three (complete cubic profiles, Tables B1–B3) and of the connected simple graphs with five vertices and maximum degree four (nine parameters, Table B4), with a script that recomputes every entry exactly from the drawings of the graphs.

Every computation is of one of three kinds. Exact computations use integer, rational, rational-function-field or number-field arithmetic. A certified modular computation computes a rank modulo a prime and compares it with an upper bound proved in the text; by (6.21), attaining the bound proves equality over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. All other computations modulo a prime are evidence. Only the first two kinds are used in proofs.

The certificates of Section 6 work as follows. The local vertex algorithm forms the finitely many columns (4.7). For each threshold it computes the image modulo the outgoing variable and the coefficient space of the kernel, then their intersections and the differences (4.4). Exact elimination over a rational-function field records every nonconstant factor inverted during a pivot. The same matrices have the certified ranks on the complement of these factors. Each excluded locus is recomputed from the original columns over its own function field, again recording the inverted factors; the zeros of these new factors on the locus are recomputed in turn or, where they form a single scaling orbit, covered by scaling. For the subcubic table the only factor is λ−2\lambda-2, and the calculation at λ=2\lambda=2 inverts none. For T​1T1 and for Theorem 6.10 the excluded curves are (6.17). On each of them the recomputation inverts only β−2\beta-2, or γ−5\gamma-5 on β=2\beta=2; these vanish on the curves only at (2,5)(2,5), where the calculation inverts nothing. Thus no parameter value is omitted by a generic calculation.

The unicycle algorithm works in the full square-free edge basis. Starting with F0=𝐤F_{0}=\mathbf{k}, a basis of FiF_{i} is obtained from a basis of Fi−1F_{i-1} and its products with all YvY_{v}. Only the newly added basis vectors need to be multiplied: products of older vectors already belong to Fi−1F_{i-1}. Multiplying only newly added basis vectors gives the same filtration spaces and ranks. The unfiltered dimension is 240240, so attaining that dimension certifies exhaustion. All generic pivot factors divide (6.18). The computation is restarted over ℚ⁡[λ]/(p)\mathbb{Q}[\lambda]/(p) for every irreducible factor pp, including both quadratic factors, as well as in the two zero-quadratic cases. These residue computations, together with the generic localization, cover the parameter line over an algebraic closure and hence over every characteristic-zero field. The driver verify_parameter_results.py in certificates/ runs these certificates and stops with an error if the subcubic branching table, the profiles of the tree pairs or the unicycle profiles differ from the values stated in Section 6. Its recorded output lists the states on every curve and intersection used for the tree pairs, so the final closing calculation can also be checked independently of the elimination.

The strengthened monomial presentation in Theorem 3.20 and the cycle results of Theorems 7.1 and 7.3 have algebraic proofs in the text. The interpolation identity of Proposition 7.12 is also proved directly. No extrapolation from finite ranks is used for these statements.

Computer calculations enter the proofs of Lemma 6.6 (a finite calculation in an eight-dimensional algebra, used for Theorem 6.7), Propositions 6.4, 6.15, 6.16, 6.18, 6.20 and 6.26, and Theorem 6.10; they also produce the data in Remarks 3.30, 6.11, 6.13, 6.17, 6.21 and 6.23 and in the tables. The certified modular kind is used only for Proposition 6.26.

The evidence for Conjectures 7.8 and 8.2, the proposed loci and the six-vertex data of Remarks 6.21 and 6.23, the checks of Theorem 3.20 and Proposition 3.29, and the observations in the Outlook are not used in any proof.
